legal_issues.issue: Whether Martin Perera has capacity and statutory power to dispose of his house by last will to a person who is not an heir.
Whether he may exclude his children from the will without stating any reason, and whether the children have any statutory claim against a valid will.
What formalities the will must satisfy for that disposition to be valid, including who may attest it.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Martin Perera may execute a last will devising his house to his helper Siripala while leaving nothing to his two adult children, without stating any reason for excluding them, and on what statutory conditions the validity of such a will depends.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Wills Ordinance s.2(1) makes it lawful for any person who has reached the age of eighteen years and is residing within or outside Sri Lanka to execute a will disposing of movable and immovable property belonging to him at the time of death which would otherwise devolve on his heirs, in favour of a person not legally incapacitated from taking. Wills Ordinance s.2(2) gives every testator full power to make such testamentary disposition as he feels disposed and, in the exercise of that right, to exclude any child, parent, relative or descendant, or to disinherit or omit to mention any such person, without assigning any reason, notwithstanding any law, usage or custom to the contrary. The preferential right of children in Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.24 sits in the Part of that Ordinance dealing with inheritance ab intestato and so operates only over property not validly disposed of by will. Freedom of testation must, however, be exercised in the prescribed form: under Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4 no will containing a devise of immovable property or a bequest of movable property is valid unless it is in writing and the testator signs it and affixes his thumb impression at the foot or end before a notary public and two witnesses present at the same time. Under Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11 a benefit given by the will to a person who attests it, or to that person's spouse, is null and void so far as concerns that attesting witness, although the will itself remains valid. Wills Ordinance s.9 confirms that landed property in the Ordinance extends to houses and buildings.
gold_answer_draft.application: Martin is seventy-two, of sound mind and under no disability, so he satisfies the age and capacity condition in s.2(1), and he is governed by the general law rather than by Kandyan law, Thesawalamai or Muslim law. The house at No. 47/3, Temple Lane, Nugegoda is his own immovable property, held as sole owner, and it would devolve on Anusha and Dinesh if he did not dispose of it; Siripala, an unrelated domestic helper, is not legally incapacitated from taking it. His decision to leave the children nothing, and to give no explanation for that in the will, falls squarely within the words of s.2(2), and because the children's preferential right in Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.24 applies only on intestacy, they have no statutory claim against a will that disposes of the house. Two conditions must nevertheless be met. The will must be in writing and Martin must sign it and place his thumb impression at the end of it before a notary public and two witnesses present at the same time, as Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4 requires. The attesting witnesses must not be beneficiaries or the spouses of beneficiaries, which the proposed neighbours are not; had Siripala or his wife attested the will, Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11 would render the devise of the house to him null and void. Nothing in the facts shows whether the children are in need of support, and no maintenance claim against the estate arises from the provisions relied on here.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Yes. Martin Perera may execute the last will leaving the house to Siripala and giving his children nothing, and he need not assign any reason for excluding them, because Wills Ordinance s.2(2) confers that power in terms and notwithstanding any contrary law, usage or custom. The exclusion cannot be attacked merely because no reason is given. The advice is qualified only by the requirement that the will be executed in the manner required by Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4 and that neither Siripala nor his spouse attest it, failing which the will or the devise to him would fail on grounds unconnected with the absence of reasons.

answer_claims.claim_text: A person who has reached eighteen years and is residing in or outside Sri Lanka may execute a will disposing of movable and immovable property belonging to him at death which would otherwise devolve on his heirs, in favour of a person not legally incapacitated from taking.
Every testator has full power to exclude, disinherit or omit to mention any child without assigning any reason, notwithstanding any law, usage or custom to the contrary.
The preferential right of children to a parent's estate operates in inheritance ab intestato and therefore does not defeat a valid testamentary disposition.

A will containing a devise of immovable property or a bequest of movable property is valid only if it is in writing and the testator signs it and affixes his thumb impression at the foot or end before a notary public and two witnesses present at the same time.
A benefit given by a will to a person who attests it, or to that person's spouse, is null and void so far as concerns that attesting witness.
Martin Perera, aged seventy-two, of sound mind and governed by the general law, satisfies the statutory age and capacity condition for executing a will.

The house at Nugegoda is Martin's own immovable property which would otherwise devolve on his two adult children, and Siripala, an unrelated helper, is not legally incapacitated from taking it under the will.
Because Martin's children take only on intestacy, they acquire no claim to the house against a valid will and cannot attack the exclusion on the ground that the will gives no reason for it.

The proposed execution before a notary public and two disinterested neighbours, with Martin's signature and thumb impression at the end of the will, meets the statutory form, and since neither witness benefits under the will the devise to Siripala is not avoided.

Martin Perera may execute the will leaving his house to Siripala and nothing to his children without assigning any reason, provided the will is executed in the prescribed form and no beneficiary or beneficiary's spouse attests it.

legal_issues.issue: What Nihal, as the executor holding the will, must do with the will immediately after Martin's death and in which court.
How and within what time he must apply to have the will proved and probate granted to him, and what the application must contain.
What steps follow the court's order, namely the oath, the inventory and valuation, the administration of the estate and the final account.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What steps Nihal, as the executor named in Martin Perera's last will and the person who found the original will, is required to take after Martin's death in order to obtain probate and to administer and wind up the estate.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.9 requires that a will be duly proved and recorded after the testator's death in the District Court empowered to grant probate. Civil Procedure Code s.516 requires the person in whose custody the will was, or who finds it after the death, to produce it to the District Court of the district in which he resides or in which the testator died, as soon as reasonably may be, with an affidavit verifying the time and place of death and the nature and value of the property left. Under s.517 the person appointed executor may apply to the District Court of the district in which he resides, in which the testator resided at death, or in which land of the estate is situate, within the time limit and in the manner specified in s.524, to have the will proved and probate granted to him; s.518 shows the process is not optional, since if no application is made the court itself proceeds to grant probate to the named executor or administration to another competent person. Section 524 requires the application to be made within three months of the finding of the will, by petition and affidavit setting out in numbered paragraphs the making of the will, the details and situation of the property, the heirs to the best of the petitioner's knowledge, the grounds of entitlement and the character claimed, with the will annexed or brought into court, evidence proving due execution, and the charges for the notice under s.529. Section 529 requires the Probate Officer to publish notice in Sinhala, Tamil and English calling for written objections supported by affidavit. If no objection is filed, s.531(1)(a)(i) requires the court, on prima facie proof of the due making of the will and the petitioner's character, to declare the will proved, declare the applicant executor and direct the grant of probate; if objections are filed, issues are framed and under s.534 probate is granted if the prima facie proof is not rebutted. Section 539 then requires the executor to take the oath of an executor within fifteen days of the order and to file an inventory and valuation within one month of the oath, whereupon probate issues. By s.542 an unlimited grant carries power over the whole of the deceased's movable and immovable property in Sri Lanka. Section 551 requires a true and final account of the executorship, verified on oath with receipts and vouchers, within twelve months of the issue of probate or such further time as the court allows, and s.552 makes an executor who fails to pay over what is due within a year of the grant personally liable for interest.
gold_answer_draft.application: Nihal found the original will in Martin's safe on 17 February 2026, three days after the death, so he is the finder within the meaning of s.516 and must produce the will to the District Court of Colombo, being both the district in which Martin died and the district in which Nihal resides, as soon as reasonably may be, supporting it with an affidavit of the time and place of death and of the house and bank balance left within that jurisdiction. As the executor named in the will he should then petition the same court under ss.517 and 524 by 17 May 2026, within three months of finding the will, setting out the making of the will of 20 August 2024, the details of the house at No. 47/3 on Lot A in Plan No. 2214 and of the savings account, the heirs Anusha and Dinesh as well as the legatee Siripala, the ground on which he claims and his character as executor, annexing the will and affidavit evidence of the notary and attesting witnesses to prove due execution, and tendering the charges for publication. The Probate Officer will publish the notice under s.529 and the children may file written objections supported by affidavit within the period stated in it. If they do not, the court will declare the will proved and direct that probate issue to Nihal under s.531; if they do object, the matter goes to a final hearing on framed issues and probate follows under s.534 unless the prima facie proof is rebutted. Within fifteen days of that order Nihal must take the executor's oath, and within one month of the oath file the inventory and valuation of the house, the bank balance and the debts under s.539, on which probate will be issued to him. Holding an unlimited grant he may then get in the bank balance, pay the funeral expenses and the hospital bill of about Rs. 350,000, transfer the house at No. 47/3 to Siripala in terms of the will, and file his final account within twelve months of the grant under s.551, remembering that under s.552 delay beyond a year in paying over what is due exposes him to interest out of his own funds. Whether an extension of time will be needed, and what duty is payable on the estate, cannot be settled on the facts given.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Nihal must produce the will to the District Court of Colombo with the prescribed affidavit as soon as reasonably may be after the death, and within three months of finding it petition that court by petition and affidavit to have the will proved and probate granted to him, allow the Probate Officer's notice to be published and any objections to be dealt with, and on the order declaring the will proved take the executor's oath within fifteen days and file the inventory and valuation within a month of the oath. Once probate issues he must administer the estate, pay the debts, give Siripala the house devised to him and file a final account within twelve months, failing which he risks personal liability for interest.

answer_claims.claim_text: After the testator's death the will must be duly proved and recorded in the District Court empowered to grant probate or administration.

The person who held or who finds the will after the death must produce it, as soon as reasonably may be, to the District Court of the district in which he resides or in which the testator died, with an affidavit verifying the time and place of death and the property left.

The executor named in the will may apply to the District Court of the district of his residence, of the testator's residence at death, or where land of the estate lies, in the manner and within the time specified in section 524, to have the will proved and probate granted to him; and if no one applies the court itself proceeds to grant probate to the named executor.

The application must be made within three months of the finding of the will, by petition and affidavit setting out in numbered paragraphs the making of the will, the details and situation of the property, the heirs to the best of the petitioner's knowledge, the grounds of entitlement and the character claimed, with the will produced, proof of due execution and the charges for publication.
Notice of the application is published by the Probate Officer calling on persons with objections to file them in writing supported by affidavit before the date stated in the notice.

Where no objection is filed and the court is satisfied of prima facie proof of the due making of the will and the character of the petitioner, it declares the will proved, declares the applicant executor and directs the grant of probate to him; where objections are filed, probate is granted after the final hearing unless the prima facie proof is rebutted.

The executor in whose favour the order is made must take the executor's oath within fifteen days of the order and file an inventory of the property with a valuation within one month of the oath, whereupon the court grants probate.

An unlimited grant of probate carries power over every portion of the deceased's movable and immovable property in Sri Lanka until the administration is complete, and the executor must file a true and final account verified on oath within twelve months of the grant or such further time as the court allows.
An executor who fails within one year of the grant to pay over the sums due to creditors, heirs or legatees is liable to pay interest out of his own funds unless he shows good and sufficient cause.

Nihal, having found the original will in Martin's safe on 17 February 2026, must produce it with the verifying affidavit to the District Court of Colombo, which is both the district where Martin died and the district where Nihal resides.

As the executor named in the will Nihal must petition that court to have the will proved and probate granted to him by 17 May 2026, within three months of finding the will, naming Anusha and Dinesh as heirs and Siripala as legatee and describing the house and the savings account.
Martin's children may use the published notice to object, in which case the application proceeds to a final hearing on framed issues rather than being allowed on the papers.

On the order declaring the will proved Nihal must take the executor's oath within fifteen days and file within a month of the oath an inventory and valuation covering the house at No. 47/3, the savings account and the debts.

Under the grant Nihal must get in the assets, pay the funeral expenses and the hospital bill, transfer the house to Siripala in terms of the will, and file his final account within twelve months of the grant.

Nihal's required steps are therefore production of the will with an affidavit, a petition within three months for proof of the will and probate, publication and disposal of objections, the executor's oath within fifteen days of the order and the inventory within a month of the oath, then administration of the estate and a final account within twelve months of the grant.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: In relation to a transfer deed - (a) both the transferor and the transferee shall affix their signatures and thumb impressions as required by subsection (1): Provided however, where the transferee is unable to be present and execute the deed or instrument, he shall authorise in writing, any other person to sign such deed or instrument on his behalf, who shall comply with the requirements set out in subsection (1)
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the subsection inserted by the latest amendment (Act No. 4 of 2024). It is the provision the question turns on: it now requires the transferee, as well as the transferor, to sign and place a thumb impression on a transfer deed, and it gives the transferee who cannot be present the one statutory escape route - a written authorisation to another person to sign on her behalf. Wimala is the transferee and cannot be present.

legal_issues.issue: Whether, after the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 4 of 2024, a transferee (purchaser) must herself sign and place a thumb impression on the deed of transfer.
What a transferee who is unable to be present in Sri Lanka must do so that the deed of transfer is nevertheless in force and avails in law.
How a written authorisation granted from abroad for such a transaction must be executed, what it must contain, and whether and when it must be registered.
What the attesting notary must verify and record when a deed of transfer is signed by an authorised person rather than by the transferee.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Wimala is the purchaser, and therefore the transferee, under a proposed deed of transfer of land at Galle. She cannot be in Sri Lanka when the deed is executed. The issues are whether a transferee must now sign the deed at all, what she must do if she cannot be present, how the instrument by which she authorises another person must be executed abroad and what it must contain, whether that instrument must be registered, and what the attesting notary must satisfy himself of.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1) requires that no sale, purchase or transfer of immovable property is in force or avails in law unless the deed is in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and by the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary public, all present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and attested by that notary, and unless the thumb impression of every executant is affixed beside the signature on the original, duplicate and protocol in the presence of the notary and the witnesses. Section 2(2), added by the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 4 of 2024, provides that in relation to a transfer deed both the transferor and the transferee must affix their signatures and thumb impressions as required by subsection (1), but that where the transferee is unable to be present and execute the deed she shall authorise in writing any other person to sign on her behalf, that person complying with the requirements of subsection (1). Where such an authorisation is granted for a transaction within s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.3A(1) requires it to be executed subject to s.3A(2) or (3). If it is executed outside Sri Lanka, s.3A(3) requires that it be executed before a person authorised under s.2 of that Ordinance, that it describe the land by metes and bounds and extent, that it refer to the volume and folio of any prior registration, and that it be accompanied by a copy of the bio page of the grantor's passport signed by the grantor and by notarially certified identity documents of the attorney. Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.2 defines a power of attorney executed outside Sri Lanka as one executed before an Ambassador, a High Commissioner, a Diplomatic Officer or a Consular Officer within the meaning of the Consular Functions Act, or a person authorised to attest such an instrument under the law of that country. Section 3 requires every power of attorney to be registered with the Registrar-General, the holder submitting it within three months of execution where it was executed outside Sri Lanka, with a notarially certified copy and the affidavit in Schedule I. Section 3C limits validity to five years from execution unless the instrument states its own period or it is earlier revoked. Section 3B requires the notary attesting the deed to examine the relevant volumes and folios at the Registrar-General's department, to satisfy himself that the power has not been revoked or cancelled and to state that in his attestation. Notaries Ordinance s.31, rule (16)(c), requires the attorney signing a deed to give the notary an affidavit that the power of attorney is genuine and in force and that the grantor is alive at execution, and rule (30) requires the notary to keep a true copy of the power with his protocol and to forward a copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands.
gold_answer_draft.application: Wimala's purchase of the Galle land is a purchase and transfer of immovable property and so falls squarely within Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1). Since the 2024 amendment she cannot simply leave the deed to the vendor: s.2(2)(a) makes her, as transferee, a signatory who must also place a thumb impression, and the vendor Nihal Weerakoon, being in Sri Lanka, can attend and comply for his part. Because her employment prevents her from travelling before March 2026, she is a transferee 'unable to be present and execute the deed' and the proviso to s.2(2)(a) applies: she must authorise her brother Sunil in writing to sign for her, and it will be Sunil who signs, gives his thumb impression and appears before the notary and the two witnesses as s.2(1) requires. That written authority is a power of attorney granted for a s.2 transaction, so s.3A(1) of the Powers of Attorney Ordinance applies, and because she will sign it in Canberra, s.3A(3) governs. Signing at the Sri Lanka High Commission before a consular officer satisfies s.3A(3)(a) read with s.2(b). The instrument must set out Kahatagahawatta by its four boundaries and its extent of eighteen decimal five perches, must refer to Volume 214 Folio 85 of the Galle Land Registry as the prior registration, and must be accompanied by the bio page of her passport signed by her and by a notarially certified copy of Sunil's identity document. Once executed on 12 November 2025 it must be lodged by Sunil with the Registrar-General within three months, that is by 12 February 2026, together with a certified true copy and the Schedule I affidavit; since the deed is to be executed in the first week of December 2025 the authority should in practice be registered before then, because the notary must be able to examine the volumes and folios and certify under s.3B that it has not been revoked. The authority will still be current at that date, being well within the five-year period allowed by s.3C. At execution Sunil must give the notary the affidavit required by Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (16)(c) confirming that the power is genuine and in force and that Wimala is alive, and the notary will keep a true copy of the power with his protocol and send a copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands under rule (30). Wimala being a citizen of Sri Lanka, nothing in Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2(1) stands in the way of the transfer.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Wimala can complete the purchase without travelling. She should execute, before a consular officer at the Sri Lanka High Commission in Canberra, a written power of attorney appointing her brother Sunil to sign the deed of transfer for her, drawn so as to describe the Galle land by metes and bounds and extent and to refer to Volume 214 Folio 85, and accompanied by her signed passport bio page and Sunil's certified identity document. Sunil must register it with the Registrar-General within three months of execution, and in practice before the deed is executed, and must then sign the deed, affix his thumb impression and appear with the two witnesses before the notary, giving the notary the affidavit that the power is genuine, in force and that Wimala is alive. A deed executed in that way is in force and avails in law under Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 as amended by Act No. 4 of 2024. If instead she simply stays away and lets the vendor alone sign, the deed will not satisfy s.2(2)(a) and will not avail in law. The precise date of operation of the 2024 amendment should be confirmed before the advice is acted on.

answer_claims.claim_text: A purchase or transfer of immovable property is not in force and does not avail in law unless the deed is in writing, signed by every executant or by a person duly authorised by the executant and by the witnesses before a licensed notary all present together, attested by that notary, and bearing the thumb impression of every executant on the original, duplicate and protocol.

Since the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 4 of 2024, section 2(2)(a) requires both the transferor and the transferee of a transfer deed to affix their signatures and thumb impressions as required by section 2(1).

Where the transferee is unable to be present and execute the deed, she must authorise another person in writing to sign on her behalf, and that person must comply with the requirements of section 2(1).

A power of attorney granted for a transaction within section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance must be executed subject to section 3A(2) or (3) of the Powers of Attorney Ordinance, according to whether it is executed in or outside Sri Lanka.

A power of attorney executed outside Sri Lanka must be executed before an Ambassador, High Commissioner, Diplomatic Officer or Consular Officer, or a person authorised to attest it under the law of that country.

Such a power of attorney executed outside Sri Lanka must describe the land by metes and bounds and extent, refer to the volume and folio of any prior registration, and be accompanied by the grantor's signed passport bio page and notarially certified identity documents of the attorney.

Every power of attorney must be registered with the Registrar-General, and one executed outside Sri Lanka must be submitted for registration within three months of execution with a notarially certified copy and the affidavit in Schedule I.

The notary attesting the deed must examine the relevant volumes and folios at the Registrar-General's department, satisfy himself that the power of attorney has not been revoked or cancelled, and state that in his attestation.

An attorney signing a deed must give the notary an affidavit that the power of attorney is genuine and in force and that the grantor is alive at execution, and the notary must keep a true copy of the power with his protocol and forward a copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands.
A power of attorney is valid for only five years from execution unless it states its own period or is earlier revoked or cancelled.
Wimala's purchase of the Galle land is a purchase and transfer of immovable property within section 2(1), so the section 2 formalities govern her deed.

As transferee Wimala is now required to sign and place her thumb impression on the deed, and because her employment prevents her from travelling before March 2026 she is a transferee unable to be present within the proviso to section 2(2)(a).
Wimala must therefore authorise her brother Sunil in writing to sign the deed for her, and it is Sunil who must sign, give his thumb impression and appear before the notary and the two witnesses.

Signing the instrument at the Sri Lanka High Commission in Canberra before a consular officer satisfies the requirement of execution before an authorised person for a power of attorney executed outside Sri Lanka.

The instrument must set out Kahatagahawatta by its four boundaries and its extent of eighteen decimal five perches and refer to Volume 214 Folio 85 of the Galle Land Registry, and be accompanied by Wimala's signed passport bio page and a certified copy of Sunil's identity document.

Executed on 12 November 2025, the instrument must be lodged with the Registrar-General by 12 February 2026, and in practice before the deed is executed in the first week of December 2025 so that the notary can examine the volumes and folios and certify that it is unrevoked; it remains within the five-year validity period at that date.
Wimala being a citizen of Sri Lanka, the prohibition on transfers of land to a foreigner does not apply to this purchase.

A deed of transfer signed by Sunil under a power of attorney executed and registered as described, with the affidavit given to the notary, is in force and avails in law under section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance as amended by Act No. 4 of 2024.
If Wimala neither attends nor authorises anyone in writing and the vendor alone signs, the deed will not satisfy section 2(2)(a) and will not avail in law.

enrichment.original_background: Wimala intends to purchase a land in Galle. However, Wimala is unable to come to Sri Lanka to sign the Deed of Transfer.
enrichment.enriched_background: Wimala Gunasekara is a citizen of Sri Lanka who holds a Sri Lankan passport and has lived and worked in Melbourne, Australia for the past nine years. She has agreed to buy from Nihal Weerakoon an allotment of land called Kahatagahawatta, in extent eighteen decimal five perches, situated at Dangedara in the Municipal Council limits of Galle, in the District of Galle, bounded on the North by Lot 3 in Plan No. 2114, on the East by the property of D. Somapala, on the South by Dangedara Road and on the West by a drain, the whole of which was last registered in Volume 214 Folio 85 of the Galle Land Registry. The agreed price is Rs. 14,500,000, and the parties have fixed the first week of December 2025 for the execution of the deed. Wimala's employment contract does not allow her to take leave before March 2026, so she cannot be in Sri Lanka on the execution date. Her brother, Sunil Gunasekara, who lives at Dangedara, Galle, is willing to act for her. On 12 November 2025 Wimala proposes to sign, at the Sri Lanka High Commission in Canberra and before a consular officer there, a written instrument appointing Sunil to act for her in the purchase. She has asked a notary practising in Galle what she must do so that the deed she cannot sign will still be good in law.

added_facts.fact: Wimala Gunasekara is a citizen of Sri Lanka holding a Sri Lankan passport, resident and employed in Melbourne, Australia.
added_facts.reason: The original background gives no party identity and does not say whether the absent purchaser is a foreigner. Fixing her as a Sri Lankan citizen keeps the answer on the execution formalities and stops the scenario collapsing into a prohibited-transfer question.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If Wimala were a foreigner, the transfer of title would be prohibited under Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2(1)(a) unless an exemption applied, and the advice would be that no amount of correct execution can save the deed.

added_facts.fact: The property is an allotment called Kahatagahawatta, eighteen decimal five perches in extent, at Dangedara within the Galle Municipal Council limits, with stated boundaries on all four sides, last registered in Volume 214 Folio 85 of the Galle Land Registry.
added_facts.reason: The original says only 'a land in Galle'. A metes-and-bounds description and a prior registration reference are conditions the written authorisation must satisfy, so without them it cannot be tested against the statute.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Without an identified land and volume and folio, the instrument would fail Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.3A(3)(b) and (d) and the notary could not act on it.

added_facts.fact: Wimala's brother, Sunil Gunasekara, of Dangedara, Galle, is willing to act for her in the purchase, and she proposes to appoint him in writing.
added_facts.reason: Section 2(2) of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance requires the absent transferee to authorise 'any other person' in writing. The scenario is indeterminate until there is a person available in Sri Lanka to be authorised.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If nobody could be authorised, Wimala would have no way of completing the purchase in her absence and the deed could not be validly executed at all.

added_facts.fact: Wimala proposes to sign the instrument of authority on 12 November 2025 at the Sri Lanka High Commission in Canberra, before a consular officer there.
added_facts.reason: The place and the attesting officer are what determine which limb of the Powers of Attorney Ordinance applies. Signing abroad before a consular officer engages s.2(b) and s.3A(3) rather than the domestic notarial route.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If she signed abroad before an ordinary local witness with no authority to attest under the law of that country or under s.2(b), the instrument would not be a power of attorney for the purposes of the Ordinance and the deed signed on its strength would not avail in law.

added_facts.fact: The deed of transfer is to be executed in Galle in the first week of December 2025, and the agreed price is Rs. 14,500,000 payable by the purchaser.
added_facts.reason: Dates are needed to test the registration window that runs from the date of execution of the authority, and to show the authority is still current when the deed is signed.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the deed were executed more than three months after the authority without it having been lodged for registration, or after the authority had lapsed, the attorney's signature would be open to challenge.

added_facts.fact: The vendor is Nihal Weerakoon, who is in Sri Lanka and able to attend before the notary.
added_facts.reason: Section 2(2)(a) now requires signatures and thumb impressions from both transferor and transferee. Naming an available vendor confines the difficulty to the transferee's side.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the vendor were also absent, the same written-authorisation requirement would have to be satisfied for him, since the proviso in s.2(2)(a) is expressed only for the transferee.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: A person (hereinafter referred to as the "caveator") who (i) has a right, title or interest; or (ii) claims to have a right, title or interest, to a land, an undivided land, a land parcel or a condominium parcel (hereinafter in this section referred to as the "land") may present for registration a caveat substantially in Form VIII of the Second Schedule hereto requiring him to be served a notice of the presentation for registration of any instrument affecting such land.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The operative substituted section 32(1)(a). It states who may present a caveat: a person who has, or claims to have, a right, title or interest in the land. Romani's entitlement stands or falls on this provision.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Act No. 32 of 2022 was enacted in 2022 and is in force at the matter reference date 2025-10. Corpus in_force_from_year = 2022; no later amendment to section 32 appears in the corpus (Act No. 18 of 2024 does not touch section 32).

indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Standing alone is not enough: the substituted section makes the caveat conditional on duplicate lodgement, an affidavit and an attorney-at-law's certificate substantiating the claimed right, title or interest. Removing it would leave the answer stating an unconditional right.

legal_issues.issue: Whether Romani, as the owner of the Battaramulla land who is about to leave the country, is a person entitled to present a caveat for registration, and what she must lodge with it.
Who may file a caveat under the Registration of Documents Ordinance as amended by Act No. 32 of 2022, and how that differs from the pre-amendment position.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Romani, the owner of a Battaramulla land who is leaving for New Zealand, may present a caveat for registration in respect of that land, and who is entitled to file a caveat under the Registration of Documents Ordinance as amended by Act No. 32 of 2022.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Section 32 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance (Chapter 117) provides for caveats. Its subsection (1) was repealed and substituted by section 2(1) of the Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act No. 32 of 2022. Before that amendment section 32(1) allowed any person to present a caveat for registration. Under the substituted section 32(1)(a) a person who has, or who claims to have, a right, title or interest to a land, an undivided land, a land parcel or a condominium parcel may present for registration a caveat substantially in Form VIII of the Second Schedule, requiring to be served with notice of the presentation for registration of any instrument affecting that land. Section 32(1)(c)(i) extends the term caveator to a body of persons, a beneficiary under any trust affecting a land, the lawful guardian or next friend of a minor or of a person of unsound mind or mentally deficient person, an attorney of a person, a judgement creditor, an executor or administrator of the estate of a deceased, a legal heir, and an intended purchaser who has entered into an agreement with the owner or a developer of a land. Section 32(1)(c)(iii) extends the term interest to interests arising from an unregistered deed incapable of immediate registration, a trust, testate or intestate inheritance, instruments relating to a mortgage or an agreement to sell, co-ownership, condominium ownership and the estate of a minor or of a person of unsound mind. Land itself is defined in section 3 of the Ordinance to include things attached to the earth and any estate or interest in land. Standing is not sufficient on its own: section 32(1)(b)(i) requires the caveat to be in duplicate with an affidavit of the caveator and a certificate of an Attorney-at-law substantiating the right, title or interest; section 32(1)(b)(iii) requires a certified copy of a duly registered power of attorney where the caveator is an attorney; and section 32(1)(b)(iv) requires the caveat to contain the caveator's name, signature, identity card, passport or driving licence number, an address of the caveator in Sri Lanka for service, the right, title or interest claimed, the grounds of the claim and the description of the land. Section 32(2) obliges the Registrar to register a caveat received and to retain it, and section 32(3) as substituted by section 2(3) of the 2022 Act limits a caveat to a maximum of two years. Section 2(5) of the 2022 Act substituted sixty days for thirty days in section 32(5), so a caveator served with notice of a competing instrument has sixty days from posting of the notice to sue. A power of attorney relied on must be registered with the Registrar-General under section 3 of the Powers of Attorney Ordinance, and by section 26(1)(d) of the Ordinance a notary may present an instrument for registration on behalf of an entitled person. Section 33(1)(a), inserted by section 3(2) of the 2022 Act, allows the caveator or an attorney to withdraw the caveat in writing.
gold_answer_draft.application: Romani is the sole owner of the Battaramulla allotment under registered Deed of Transfer No. 4821, so she has a right and title to a land within the meaning of the substituted section 32(1)(a), and the allotment with the house on it is land under section 3. She therefore does not need to rely on the extended meaning of interest in section 32(1)(c)(iii) or on any of the derivative classes of caveator in section 32(1)(c)(i). She can satisfy section 32(1)(b)(i), since she is ready to lodge in duplicate with her affidavit and an attorney-at-law's certificate substantiating her ownership. Her impending departure engages section 32(1)(b)(iv): the caveat must state an address in Sri Lanka at which notices are to be served, and her sister's Rajagiriya address answers that requirement, whereas a New Zealand address alone would not. Because she is the owner, the Form X notices to other owners under section 32(1)(b)(ii) do not arise. As the notary consulted, you may present the caveat on her behalf under section 26(1)(d). Two matters should be pointed out to her. First, under section 32(3) the caveat lasts a maximum of two years, which is shorter than her intended three-year absence, so it will have to be renewed. Second, if an instrument affecting the land is presented while the caveat is in force, notice will go to her Sri Lanka address and she must commence action in a competent court within sixty days under section 32(5) as amended; the registered power of attorney in favour of her brother would let him receive the notice and act, and under section 32(1)(b)(iii) a certified copy of that registered power of attorney must accompany any caveat he lodges as attorney, the registration being required by section 3 of the Powers of Attorney Ordinance.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Yes. Romani may file a caveat. As owner holding title under a registered deed she has a right, title and interest to the land and so falls squarely within section 32(1)(a) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance as substituted by section 2(1) of Act No. 32 of 2022, provided she lodges it in Form VIII in duplicate with her affidavit and an attorney-at-law's certificate under section 32(1)(b)(i) and gives an address in Sri Lanka for service under section 32(1)(b)(iv). More generally, a caveat may now be filed only by a person who has or claims to have a right, title or interest in the land, and not by any person at large as the section read before the amendment; by section 32(1)(c)(i) that includes a body of persons, a beneficiary under a trust affecting the land, the guardian or next friend of a minor or of a person of unsound mind or mentally deficient person, an attorney, a judgement creditor, an executor, administrator or legal heir of a deceased, and an intended purchaser under an agreement with the owner or developer. She should be advised that the caveat lasts a maximum of two years under section 32(3) and will need renewal during a three-year absence.

answer_claims.claim_text: Under section 32(1)(a) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance as substituted by section 2(1) of Act No. 32 of 2022, a person who has, or claims to have, a right, title or interest to a land, undivided land, land parcel or condominium parcel may present a caveat for registration in Form VIII of the Second Schedule.
Before that substitution section 32(1) permitted any person to present a caveat, so the amendment narrowed standing to persons with, or claiming, a right, title or interest.

Section 32(1)(c)(i) extends the term caveator to a body of persons, a beneficiary under a trust affecting land, the lawful guardian or next friend of a minor or of a person of unsound mind or mentally deficient person, an attorney of a person, a judgement creditor, an executor or administrator of a deceased's estate, a legal heir, and an intended purchaser who has entered into an agreement with the owner or a developer.

Section 32(1)(c)(iii) extends the term interest to interests under an unregistered deed incapable of immediate registration, a trust, testate or intestate inheritance, mortgage or agreement-to-sell instruments, co-ownership, condominium ownership and the estate of a minor or person of unsound mind.
A caveat must be lodged in duplicate with an affidavit of the caveator and a certificate of an Attorney-at-law substantiating the right, title or interest claimed.

The caveat must contain the caveator's name, signature, identity card, passport or driving licence number and an address of the caveator in Sri Lanka at which notices relating to the caveat are to be served, together with the interest claimed, the grounds and the description of the land.

Where the caveator is the holder of a power of attorney, a certified copy of the power of attorney duly registered with the Registrar-General or the relevant Registrar must accompany the caveat, and every power of attorney must be registered with the Registrar-General.

A caveat is in force for a maximum period of two years, the Registrar must register and retain a caveat received, and a caveator served with notice of a competing instrument must commence action in a competent court within sixty days of the posting of that notice.

Romani holds title to the Battaramulla allotment under a registered deed of transfer, so she has a right, title and interest to land and meets the standing test in section 32(1)(a); the allotment and the house on it are land under section 3 of the Ordinance.
Because she is ready to lodge in duplicate with her affidavit and her attorney-at-law's certificate of title, she can satisfy section 32(1)(b)(i).
Her departure for New Zealand does not disqualify her, but she must give an address in Sri Lanka for service; her sister's Rajagiriya address satisfies section 32(1)(b)(iv).

As she is the owner, she need not rely on the extended classes of caveator or the extended meaning of interest, and the notices to other owners required where the caveator is not the owner do not arise.

The notary consulted by Romani may present the caveat papers for registration on her behalf, and her brother, once his power of attorney is registered, may act for her as an attorney in relation to the caveat.
Since the caveat expires after two years and her absence is expected to last about three, it will have to be renewed during that period.

Romani can file a caveat in respect of her Battaramulla property, provided the caveat is in the prescribed form with the affidavit, the attorney-at-law's certificate and an address in Sri Lanka for service.

Under the Ordinance as amended a caveat may be filed only by a person who has or claims to have a right, title or interest in the land, including the classes listed in the inclusive definition of caveator, and no longer by any person at large.

enrichment.original_background: Romani who intends to go to New Zealand wants to file a caveat to her property situated in Battaramulla and meets you who are a Notary practising in Colombo.
enrichment.enriched_background: Romani, aged forty-one, is the sole owner of a fifteen-perch allotment of land with a two-storey house standing on it at No. 47/3, Pahalawela Road, Battaramulla, being Lot 12B in Plan No. 3126 dated 8 January 2016 made by K. Amarasiri, Licensed Surveyor. She bought the land from her uncle on Deed of Transfer No. 4821 dated 12 March 2016, attested by W. D. Silva, Notary Public of Colombo, and that deed is registered in Volume/Folio B 218/94 at the Delkanda-Nugegoda Land Registry. She holds the original deed and has obtained a certified copy of the folio; her attorney-at-law is willing to give a written certificate confirming her ownership, and she is ready to swear an affidavit and to lodge her papers in duplicate. Romani leaves for New Zealand on 20 November 2025 to work there for about three years, and no relative will be living in the house; she is afraid that someone may present a forged transfer of the land for registration while she is away. She has given her sister's address at No. 12, Kalapaluwawa Road, Rajagiriya as an address in Sri Lanka at which any notices about her land may be served on her. Before she leaves she also proposes to execute a power of attorney in favour of her brother Nihal, to be registered with the Registrar-General, so that he can act for her in matters concerning the land. Romani, who intends to go to New Zealand, wants to file a caveat to her property situated in Battaramulla and meets you who are a Notary practising in Colombo.

added_facts.fact: Romani is the sole owner of the Battaramulla land (Lot 12B in Plan No. 3126 of 8 January 2016, fifteen perches with a two-storey house, No. 47/3 Pahalawela Road), having bought it on Deed of Transfer No. 4821 dated 12 March 2016, registered in Volume/Folio B 218/94 at the Delkanda-Nugegoda Land Registry.
added_facts.reason: The substituted standing test turns on whether the applicant has, or claims to have, a right, title or interest in the land. The original background only says the property is hers, which is too loose to decide the point.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If Romani were only a person in occupation with no deed and no claim of title, she would fall outside the standing test and could not lodge a caveat.

added_facts.fact: She holds the original deed and a certified copy of the folio, her attorney-at-law will issue a written certificate substantiating her ownership, and she is ready to swear an affidavit and lodge the caveat in duplicate.
added_facts.reason: The amended section makes the caveat conditional on duplicate lodgement, an affidavit and an attorney-at-law's certificate; without these facts the scenario cannot be said to comply.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Without the attorney-at-law's certificate and affidavit the Registrar could not be satisfied that the required documents had been provided, and the caveat would not be accepted.

added_facts.fact: Romani leaves for New Zealand on 20 November 2025 for about three years and nominates her sister's address at No. 12, Kalapaluwawa Road, Rajagiriya as the address in Sri Lanka at which notices about the caveat may be served on her.
added_facts.reason: The prescribed contents require an address of the caveator in Sri Lanka for service. Departure abroad is the one fact the original background gives, and it makes this requirement the live issue.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If she gave only a New Zealand address, the caveat would not contain the address in Sri Lanka the section requires and notice of a competing instrument could not be served on her there.

added_facts.fact: Before leaving she proposes to execute a power of attorney in favour of her brother Nihal and to have it registered with the Registrar-General so that he can act for her in matters concerning the land.
added_facts.reason: Makes concrete the alternative route of lodging or maintaining a caveat through an attorney, which the amended definition of caveator expressly allows.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the power of attorney were left unregistered, the attorney could not supply the certified copy of a duly registered power of attorney that must accompany a caveat lodged by an attorney.

added_facts.fact: Romani's concern is that a forged transfer of the land may be presented for registration while she is out of the country and the house is unoccupied.
added_facts.reason: Supplies the purpose the caveat serves and connects the facts to the notice-and-action machinery of the section.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Without any apprehension of a competing instrument the caveat would serve no protective purpose and could expose the caveator to a damages claim for registration without reasonable cause.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: If, while a caveat is in force, an instrument affecting the land described in the caveat is presented for registration, and in an action commenced by the caveator in a competent court within thirty days from posting of the notice required by subsection (4) it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that the instrument presented for registration is or was at the time of registration void or voidable by the caveator or fraudulent as against him or in derogation of his lawful rights the court may order the instrument to be rectified or cancelled
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the provision that fixes the time limit the question asks about: the caveator must commence the action in a competent court within the stated number of days from the posting of the notice of presentation.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force since 1927. The corpus text is the 1990 consolidation and still reads 'thirty days'; that figure was replaced by 'sixty days' by Act No. 32 of 2022, s.2(5), so at the matter date (2025-10) subsection (5) must be read with sixty days substituted. The rest of the subsection is unchanged.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act No. 32 of 2022
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (5) in subsection (5) thereof, by the substitution for the words "a competent court within thirty days" of the words "a competent court within sixty days".
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Supplies the number the question asks for. It substitutes sixty days for thirty days in section 32(5) of the Ordinance, so a caveator notified in 2025 has sixty days, not thirty.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Enacted 2022, before the October 2025 matter date. The corpus copy carries no commencement section (32-2022/s1 is the short title only), so the amendment is taken to operate from certification in 2022; see corpus_gaps.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim in 32-2022/s2 and the substitution of sixty for thirty days is exactly as stated, but the corpus copy of Act No. 32 of 2022 has no date-of-operation clause (s 1 is short title only, unlike 21-2013/s1 and 18-2024/s1 which are headed 'Short title and date of operation'), so operation before June 2025 is inferred from the absence of a deferred-commencement clause and the corpus in_force_from_year of 2022, not proved from the corpus.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (4) The notice to be given to the caveator shall be in the prescribed form and shall be sent by registered letter to the address mentioned in the caveat.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Identifies the notice from whose posting the period runs. Without it the time limit in subsection (5) has no starting point, so the answer cannot be stated without it.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force since 1927; the opening words were replaced by Act No. 32 of 2022, s.2(4), which changed the description of the notice but not the fact that a notice is given to the caveator and posted to the address in the caveat.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim in the 1990 consolidation but is the pre-2022 text: 32-2022/s2(4) replaced the opening words 'The notice to be given to the caveator shall be in the prescribed form', so only the surviving tail 'and shall be sent by registered letter to the address mentioned in the caveat' is the operative support at the matter date.

legal_issues.issue: Within what period, and from what event, must a caveator commence an action in a competent court after being notified that an instrument affecting the land described in the caveat has been presented for registration?
Which version of section 32(5) applies to a caveator notified in 2025, given the 2022 substitution of sixty days for thirty days?

gold_answer_draft.issue: How long does Romani, as a registered caveator who has been notified that an instrument affecting the land described in her caveat has been presented for registration, have to commence her action in a competent court, and from what date does that period run?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Under section 32(5) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, where an instrument affecting the land described in a caveat is presented for registration while the caveat is in force, the caveator's remedy is an action commenced in a competent court within the period fixed by that subsection, running from the posting of the notice required by section 32(4). Section 32(4) is the notice given to the caveator when an instrument affecting the same land is subsequently presented, sent by registered letter to the address given in the caveat; the Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act No. 32 of 2022 s.2(4) recast it as a notice in Form XI of the Second Schedule. As originally enacted section 32(5) allowed thirty days, but s.2(5) of the same 2022 Act substituted 'a competent court within sixty days' for 'a competent court within thirty days'. In that action the caveator must prove that the instrument presented is or was void or voidable by her, or fraudulent as against her, or in derogation of her lawful rights, and the court may then order it to be rectified or cancelled and the register corrected. A caveat itself lasts a maximum of two years under section 32(3) as substituted by s.2(3) of the 2022 Act.
gold_answer_draft.application: Romani's caveat over the Battaramulla land was registered on 3 March 2025 and was still current in June 2025, so the caveat was in force. The document presented is a deed of transfer of the same allotment of land by a stranger, which is an instrument affecting the land described in her caveat, so section 32(5) is engaged. The Registrar posted the notice by registered letter to the Colombo address given in the caveat on 12 June 2025, and it is that posting, not Romani's receipt of the letter in New Zealand, that starts the period. Because the notice was posted in 2025, well after the 2022 amendment, the applicable period is sixty days and not the original thirty. Whether Romani can in fact obtain rectification or cancellation depends on proof that the transfer is void, voidable or fraudulent as against her, which the facts do not settle; the time limit applies regardless.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Romani must commence her action in a competent court within sixty days from the posting of the Registrar's notice, that is by about 11 August 2025 on a notice posted on 12 June 2025. She should be advised to instruct an attorney in Sri Lanka before she leaves, since the period runs from posting and not from her actual receipt of the letter abroad.

answer_claims.claim_text: Where an instrument affecting the land described in a caveat is presented for registration while the caveat is in force, the caveator's statutory remedy is an action commenced in a competent court within the period fixed by section 32(5) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance.
That period runs from the posting of the notice required by section 32(4), which is sent to the caveator by registered letter at the address given in the caveat.

As originally enacted section 32(5) required the action to be commenced within thirty days, but the Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act No. 32 of 2022 s.2(5) substituted sixty days for thirty days, so the current period is sixty days.

The notice under section 32(4) is the notice given to the caveator when an instrument affecting the same land described in the caveat is subsequently presented for registration, now in Form XI of the Second Schedule.
A caveat is in force for a maximum of two years, so Romani's caveat registered on 3 March 2025 was still in force when the deed of transfer was presented in June 2025.
The deed of transfer of the same allotment of land executed by a stranger is an instrument affecting the land described in Romani's caveat, so section 32(5) is engaged.
Time began to run when the Registrar posted the notice by registered letter to the Colombo address in the caveat on 12 June 2025, not when Romani received it abroad.
Because the notice was posted in 2025, after the 2022 amendment, the sixty-day period applies rather than the original thirty days.
Romani must commence her action in a competent court within sixty days from the posting of the notice.
On a notice posted on 12 June 2025 that gives her until about 11 August 2025, counting sixty days from the day after posting.

The document is a deed of transfer of the same allotment of land, executed by a person other than Romani in favour of a purchaser. added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the land in the caveat were a different land from the one affected by the presented instrument, subsection (5) would not be engaged at all and no time limit would run.

added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the caveat had lapsed before the document was presented, no notice would be due and the sixty-day period would never begin.

added_facts.fact: The document presented for registration is a deed of transfer of the same allotment of land, executed by a person other than Romani in favour of a purchaser.
added_facts.reason: The original background says only 'a document affecting the land'. Identifying it as a deed of transfer of the same land by a stranger makes it an instrument affecting the land described in the caveat and one Romani would say is in derogation of her rights.

added_facts.fact: The Registrar posted the notice to Romani by registered letter to the Colombo address given in her caveat on 12 June 2025.
added_facts.reason: The original background gives no date and no mode of notice. The period runs from the posting of the notice, so a posting date is needed to make the answer determinate, and a 2025 date places the matter under the amended text.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Without a posting date the period has no starting point; had the notice been posted before the 2022 amendment came into operation, the period would have been thirty days rather than sixty.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: It shall be lawful for any person who has reached the age of eighteen years and residing within or outside Sri Lanka to execute a will bequeathing and disposing any movable and immovable property
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the operative age rule. As substituted in 2022 it fixes eighteen completed years as the age at which a person becomes competent to execute a will, and it covers persons residing within or outside Sri Lanka and both movable and immovable property.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1844; the present text was substituted by Act No. 29 of 2022 (latest_change_year 2022), so it was in force well before the matter reference date of October 2025.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Section 2 of the Wills Ordinance (Chapter 60) (hereinafter referred to as the "principal enactment") is hereby repealed and the following section is substituted therefor
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The question asks for the age limit according to the latest amendments. This is the amending provision that repealed and replaced section 2 of the Wills Ordinance with the present eighteen-year rule, and Act No. 29 of 2022 is the most recent amendment to that Ordinance in the corpus.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Enacted in 2022, before the October 2025 matter reference date. No later amendment to the Wills Ordinance appears in the corpus.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: No will, testament, or codicil containing any devise of land or other immovable property, or any bequest of movable property, or for any other purpose whatsoever, shall be valid unless it shall be in writing and executed subject to the provisions specified in subsection (2); (2) The testator shall - (a) sign; and (b) affix his left or right thumb impression, at the foot or end of the will, testament or codicil referred to in subsection (1), before a notary public and two witnesses who shall be present at the same time
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the core of the procedure the testator must follow. The will must be in writing; the testator must sign and affix his thumb impression at the foot or end of the instrument, and must do so before a notary public and two witnesses all present at the same time. The proviso allows another finger impression or a toe impression where the thumb impression cannot be obtained.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section 4 was renumbered and expanded by the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 (latest_change_year 2022), so this text was in force before October 2025.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Wording and role are right, but the proviso permitting another finger impression or a toe impression, which the gold answer and CL-M021-Q01-005 rely on, sits in 7-1840/s4 outside the recorded relevant_excerpt; the excerpt should be extended to the end of subsection (2) so the quoted text carries the whole rule relied on.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: in the case of a will- (i) set out in the attestation of the will that the testator was in good and sound mind to execute the will; and (ii) enter in the deed register maintained by him, the number assigned to such will, the date and the name of the testator.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the will-specific notarial duty and the point at which the chronic illness in the scenario bites procedurally: the attesting notary must state in the attestation that the testator was of good and sound mind when he executed the will, and must enter the will's number, its date and the testator's name in his deed register.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (20)(h) was added to section 31 by the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022; section 31 was further amended by Act No. 6 of 2024, which did not disturb paragraph (h). Both changes precede October 2025.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Rule (20)(h) confirmed as inserted by 31-2022 s.16(11)(d) and untouched by 6-2024 s.3(7), which reached only paragraph (g).

legal_issues.issue: What is the minimum age at which a person may lawfully execute a last will under the Wills Ordinance as most recently amended, and is a person of twenty competent?
What formalities must be observed for the will to be valid: writing, signature, thumb impression, and the presence of a notary public and two witnesses at the same time.
What duties fall on the attesting notary in the case of a will, in particular the statement of the testator's sound mind in the attestation, the deed register entry and the protocol requirements.
What practical constraints govern the choice of attesting witnesses and the number of copies to be executed.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Two issues arise. First, what is the minimum age for executing a last will under the Wills Ordinance as most recently amended, and whether Sunil, who is 20, meets it. Second, what procedure Sunil must follow to execute a valid last will, given that he is seriously ill and wishes to dispose of both a house and a fixed deposit.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The latest amendment to the Wills Ordinance is the Wills Ordinance (Amendment) Act No. 29 of 2022. Section 2 of that Act repealed section 2 of the Ordinance and substituted a new section under which it is lawful for any person who has reached the age of eighteen years, residing within or outside Sri Lanka, to execute a will disposing of movable and immovable property (Wills Ordinance s.2(1)). Section 3 of the amending Act repealed section 3 of the Ordinance, the provision that had invalidated wills made below the prescribed age and that had earlier been amended by Act No. 5 of 1993 to replace twenty-one years for males and eighteen years for females with a uniform eighteen years. The age limit is therefore eighteen completed years. The word will in the Ordinance extends to a testament, a codicil and any other testamentary disposition (Wills Ordinance s.9). As to form, no will is valid unless it is in writing and executed as prescribed, and the testator must sign and affix his left or right thumb impression at the foot or end of the will before a notary public and two witnesses who are present at the same time; if the thumb impression cannot be obtained, another finger impression or the toe impression is to be affixed (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4(1) and (2), as amended by Act No. 30 of 2022). The notary must not attest unless at least two witnesses have subscribed their signatures in letters (Notaries Ordinance s.31(8)) and unless the executant and the witnesses have signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, he himself signing in their presence (Notaries Ordinance s.31(12)). In the case of a will the notary must set out in the attestation that the testator was in good and sound mind to execute the will, and must enter in his deed register the number assigned to the will, its date and the name of the testator (Notaries Ordinance s.31(20)(h)). For a will the notary must also affix to the protocol a sealed passport size photograph of the signatory and keep a copy of his identity document with the protocol (Notaries Ordinance s.31(17)(b)(iii)). A will is excepted from the requirement that notarial instruments be executed in triplicate (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.16). A benefit given by the will to an attesting witness or to that witness's spouse is void so far as that witness is concerned, though the witness remains competent to prove the will (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11). A will duly executed needs no other publication; it is proved in the District Court after the testator's death (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.9).
gold_answer_draft.application: Sunil was born on 14 March 2005 and is 20 years old at the intended date of execution, so he has reached the age of eighteen years and is competent under Wills Ordinance s.2(1) as substituted in 2022. His estate consists of an immovable property held on a deed of gift and a fixed deposit, both of which fall within the movable and immovable property that s.2(1) permits him to dispose of, and s.9 of the Ordinance means the same rule would govern any codicil he later makes. His illness does not by itself affect competence under the Ordinance; his physician's record that he remains lucid and able to sign and place a thumb impression means the notary can properly make the statement of good and sound mind that Notaries Ordinance s.31(20)(h) requires, and that the signature and thumb impression required by Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4(2) can be obtained. Had the thumb impression been unobtainable, the proviso permitting another finger impression or a toe impression would apply. The procedure he should follow is therefore to have the notary draw the will in writing; to assemble the notary and his two neighbours as witnesses at his residence at the one time; to sign and affix his thumb impression at the foot or end of the will in the presence of all of them, with the two witnesses subscribing their signatures in letters in his presence and in the presence of one another and of the notary, and the notary signing in their presence, as s.4(2) and Notaries Ordinance s.31(8) and (12) require; and to allow the notary to complete the attestation stating the sound mind of the testator, to make the deed register entry, and to attach the photograph and the copy of the identity document to the protocol. Because his chosen witnesses take no benefit under the will, Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11 does not cut down any of the gifts. Only one instrument need be executed, s.16 excepting wills from the triplicate rule, and no publication is needed during his lifetime, the will being proved in the District Court after his death under s.9.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The age limit for executing a last will is eighteen years, fixed by Wills Ordinance s.2(1) as substituted by the Wills Ordinance (Amendment) Act No. 29 of 2022, the former section 3 having been repealed by the same Act. Sunil, at 20, is competent to make a will disposing of both his house and his fixed deposit. To make it valid he must execute it in writing and sign it, together with his thumb impression, at the foot or end of the will before a notary public and two witnesses all present at the same time, the notary attesting it, stating in the attestation that Sunil was of good and sound mind, entering the will in his deed register and attaching Sunil's photograph and a copy of his identity document to the protocol. His illness is no bar so long as he is of sound mind at execution, and if his thumb impression cannot be taken another finger impression or a toe impression may be used instead.

answer_claims.claim_text: The most recent amendment to the Wills Ordinance is the Wills Ordinance (Amendment) Act No. 29 of 2022, which repealed and substituted section 2 of the Ordinance.

Under the substituted section 2(1) it is lawful for any person who has reached the age of eighteen years, residing within or outside Sri Lanka, to execute a will disposing of movable and immovable property, so the age limit is eighteen completed years.

Section 3 of the Wills Ordinance, which formerly invalidated wills made below the prescribed age and had been amended in 1993 to set a uniform age of eighteen years for males and females, was repealed by the 2022 amending Act, so the age question is now answered solely by section 2.
The word will in the Wills Ordinance extends to a testament, a codicil and any other testamentary disposition.

A will is not valid unless it is in writing and the testator signs and affixes his left or right thumb impression at the foot or end of the will before a notary public and two witnesses who are present at the same time, another finger impression or the toe impression being permitted where the thumb impression cannot be obtained.

The notary may not attest unless at least two witnesses have subscribed their signatures in letters and unless the executant and the witnesses have signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, the notary signing in their presence.

In the case of a will the notary must state in the attestation that the testator was in good and sound mind to execute the will and must enter the number assigned to the will, its date and the testator's name in his deed register.

For a will the notary must also affix to the protocol a sealed passport size photograph of the signatory and keep a copy of his national identity card, passport or driving licence attached to the protocol.
A benefit given by the will to an attesting witness or to that witness's spouse is void so far as that witness is concerned, although the witness remains competent to prove the will.

A will is excepted from the rule that notarially attested instruments be executed in triplicate, and once duly executed it needs no other publication, being proved in the District Court after the testator's death.
Sunil, born on 14 March 2005 and aged 20 at the intended date of execution, has reached the age of eighteen years and is competent to execute a will.
The house held on the deed of gift and the fixed deposit are respectively immovable and movable property within what section 2(1) permits a testator to dispose of.

Sunil's chronic illness does not affect his competence under the Ordinance, and because he remains lucid and able to sign and place a thumb impression, the notary can properly certify his good and sound mind and the signature and thumb impression required at execution can be obtained.

The steps Sunil should follow are to have the will drawn in writing, to sign it and affix his thumb impression at its foot or end before the notary and his two witnesses all present at the same time, with the witnesses subscribing in letters in the presence of each other and of the notary, and to let the notary complete the attestation, the deed register entry and the protocol requirements.
Because the two proposed witnesses and their spouses take no benefit under the will, no gift in the will is cut down on account of the attestation.
Only one instrument need be executed and no publication is required during Sunil's lifetime.
The age limit is eighteen years and Sunil, at 20, may lawfully execute a last will disposing of his house and his fixed deposit.

To be valid the will must be in writing and signed by Sunil, with his thumb impression, at the foot or end before a notary public and two witnesses present at the same time, the notary attesting it, stating his good and sound mind, entering it in the deed register and attaching his photograph and a copy of his identity document to the protocol.

enrichment.original_background: Sunil who is a 20 year old boy is suffering from a non-curable chronic disease and intends to execute a Last Will.
enrichment.enriched_background: Sunil Bandara Weerakoon, who was born on 14 March 2005 and is therefore 20 years old, lives at No. 27/3, Temple Lane, Nugegoda. He is suffering from a non-curable chronic disease and intends to execute a Last Will. He is unmarried and has no children. His treating consultant physician recorded on 2 September 2025 that although his physical condition is deteriorating he remains fully lucid, understands his affairs, and is able to sign his name and to place a thumb impression without assistance. Sunil wishes to dispose of two assets: a two-storey house standing on the land called Millagahawatta, Lot B in Survey Plan No. 4521 dated 12 June 2018 made by S. Ranaweera, Licensed Surveyor, situated at Pelawatta in the District of Colombo, which came to him under Deed of Gift No. 1120 dated 3 May 2019 from his grandmother; and a fixed deposit of Rs. 2,500,000 held in his own name. He wishes to leave the house to his sister Nayana and the deposit to his mother, and to appoint his uncle Mr. D. B. Weerakoon as executor. He has instructed Mr. K. Perera, a notary public practising in the Colombo District in the Sinhala language, to draw a last will for him alone and not a joint will, and Mr. Perera proposes to attend at Sunil's residence on 20 October 2025 for the execution. The two persons Sunil proposes to have as witnesses are his neighbours Mr. A. Silva and Mrs. R. Fernando, neither of whom, nor either of their spouses, takes any benefit under the intended will.

added_facts.fact: Sunil's full name is Sunil Bandara Weerakoon, he was born on 14 March 2005, he lives at No. 27/3, Temple Lane, Nugegoda, and he is unmarried with no children.
added_facts.reason: The background gives an age but no date of birth or identity. Fixing the date of birth makes it determinate that he had completed eighteen years before the intended execution date, which is the condition in the age provision.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If his date of birth put him under eighteen years at the date of execution he would not be competent to execute a will and the will would be invalid.

added_facts.fact: A consultant physician recorded on 2 September 2025 that Sunil remains fully lucid, understands his affairs, and can sign his name and place a thumb impression without assistance despite his deteriorating physical condition.
