legal_issues.issue: The shares taken by Champa and by each of Kapila's four children on his intestate death on 24 January 2011.
The devolution of Anusha's 1/8 share on her death issueless on 15 June 2012, between her surviving husband and her three half-sisters on the father's side.
The devolution of Prema's share on her death unmarried and issueless on 4 September 2015, between her surviving mother and her two full sisters.
The resulting present fractional shares of each heir in Lot 1.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What fractional shares in Lot 1 are presently held by each heir, after the intestate deaths of Kapila on 24 January 2011, of Anusha on 15 June 2012 and of Prema on 4 September 2015.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Intestate succession to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance (s.21(1)), which applies to the estate of any person dying after its proclamation (s.20). A surviving spouse first takes one-half of the intestate's property (s.22). Subject to that, inheritance passes in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals (s.23), children taking equally per capita and the issue of a deceased child taking per stirpes (s.24). If descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half and the full brothers and sisters, together with half-brothers and sisters related through the deceased parent, take the other half (s.25). If both parents have failed, the estate goes to the brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or half blood (s.26); where all the half-siblings are related on one side only they take the whole, unless an ascendant on the other side survives (s.29). Heirs equally near in degree take per capita (s.30). The word 'unmarried' means not having a husband or wife living (s.3).
gold_answer_draft.application: Kapila held the entirety of Lot 1 under Deed of Gift No 925 once his father's reserved life interest ended on Mahesh's death on 24 April 2008. On Kapila's intestate death on 24 January 2011 his widow Champa took one-half (s.22) and his four surviving children Anusha, Prema, Rupa and Seetha took the remaining half equally per capita under s.24, that is 1/8 each. Anusha died on 15 June 2012 issueless, leaving her husband Hasitha Perera, who took one-half of her 1/8, that is 1/16 (s.22). Her descendants having failed and both her parents Kapila and Sandya having predeceased her, the balance 1/16 passed to her siblings under s.26; her only siblings were the three half-sisters Prema, Rupa and Seetha, all related to her on her father's side alone, and no ascendant on her mother's side is shown to survive, so under s.29 they took the whole 1/16, per capita under s.30, that is 1/48 each. Each of Prema, Rupa and Seetha then held 1/8 + 1/48 = 7/48. Prema died on 4 September 2015 unmarried (s.3) and issueless, so no spouse's half is deducted under s.22 and no descendant takes under s.24. Her father Kapila had predeceased her and her mother Champa survived, so under s.25 Champa took half of 7/48, that is 7/96, and the other 7/96 went to her sisters. Her only surviving siblings were her full sisters Rupa and Seetha, Anusha having already died issueless, so they took 7/192 each under s.25 read with s.30. Section 27 does not alter Anusha's devolution because she left no full siblings, so the half-blood division there is governed by s.29.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The present shares in Lot 1 are: Champa Gunesekera 55/96 (that is 110/192), being 1/2 inherited from Kapila plus 7/96 inherited from Prema; Rupa Gunesekera 35/192; Seetha Gunesekera 35/192; and Hasitha Perera 12/192, that is 1/16, as the widower of Anusha. These fractions total 192/192. The computation assumes, as the facts do not state otherwise, that Anusha and Prema each died intestate and that no ascendant on Sandya's side survived Anusha. Malani and Mithila take nothing in this land because Mahesh had already gifted the entirety away in 2006.

answer_claims.claim_text: Intestate succession to the immovable property Lot 1 is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, which applies to the estate of any person dying after its proclamation.
A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of a person who dies intestate.
Subject to the spouse's half, children are preferent to all others and take equally per capita, the issue of a deceased child taking by representation.
Where descendants fail and both parents have predeceased the intestate, the estate passes to the brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or half blood, and their issue by representation.
Where all the surviving half-siblings are related to the intestate on one side only, they take the whole inheritance unless a grandparent or higher ascendant related on the other side survives.

Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half and the full brothers and sisters, together with half-siblings related through the deceased parent, take the other half.
Heirs who are equally near in degree to the intestate take per capita and not per stirpes.
A person who dies unmarried leaves no husband or wife living, so no spouse's half falls to be deducted from that estate.
On Kapila's intestate death on 24 January 2011 his widow Champa took one-half of Lot 1 and his four surviving children Anusha, Prema, Rupa and Seetha took 1/8 each.
Anusha's husband Hasitha Perera took one-half of her 1/8 share, that is 1/16.

The balance 1/16 of Anusha's share passed to her three half-sisters Prema, Rupa and Seetha, who took 1/48 each, both her parents having predeceased her and all her siblings being related to her on her father's side only.
After Anusha's death each of Prema, Rupa and Seetha held 7/48 of Lot 1.
On Prema's death unmarried and issueless on 4 September 2015 her surviving mother Champa took half of her 7/48, that is 7/96, and her full sisters Rupa and Seetha took 7/192 each.
The present shares are Champa 55/96, Rupa 35/192, Seetha 35/192 and Hasitha Perera 1/16.
Malani and Mithila hold no share in Lot 1, because Mahesh had gifted the entirety to Kapila before his death.

gold_answer_draft.issue: The question asks for the pedigree, that is the chain of devolution of title to the land and premises bearing Assessment No.45, Colombo Road, Pugoda (Lot 1 in Plan No.173, in extent 38 perches), from Gamini Jayasinghe to the persons who own it today. The chain runs through two inter vivos notarial dispositions, an administration of an intestate estate, and three intestate deaths, so the issues are the effect of the Deed of Gift on Kamala Silva's own estate, and then the devolution of the land on the successive intestacies of Kasun, Thilak and Sarathi.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance (s.21(1)), which applies to the estate of any person dying after the proclamation of the Ordinance (s.20) and does not apply to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils of the Northern Province subject to the Thesawalamai (s.2). A surviving spouse inherits one-half (s.22); subject to that, inheritance passes in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals (s.23). Children and remoter descendants are preferent to all others and take equally per capita, the issue of a deceased child taking by representation (s.24). Where descendants fail, the estate goes to both parents if both are alive; if only one parent is alive, that parent takes half and the other half goes to the brothers and sisters of the full blood, the issue of deceased full-blood siblings by representation, and the brothers and sisters of the half-blood who are related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent (s.25). A person is "unmarried" for the purposes of the Ordinance when he has no husband or wife living (s.3). Where those who succeed are equally near in degree they take per capita (s.30). Dispositions of immovable property must be by notarially attested writing (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2), and on an intestacy the District Court identifies the heirs and their shares in a testamentary proceeding (Civil Procedure Code s.531) and discharges the administrator once the estate has been duly administered and distributed (Civil Procedure Code s.724B).
gold_answer_draft.application: Gamini Jayasinghe held the entirety under the final decree of 25 October 2010 in Partition Case No. 582/P. By Deed of Transfer No.2778 of 10 March 2011 he conveyed the entirety to Kamala Silva, and by Deed of Gift No.5634 of 18 April 2011 Kamala gifted the entirety to her only son Kasun. Kamala therefore held no interest in this land when she died on 7 July 2011, and nothing in it passed to her surviving husband Namal Silva or to her children Sarathi and Amal at that point. Kasun died on 3 May 2013 intestate and unmarried, that is without a spouse living within the meaning of s.3, and without issue, so no half share arises under s.22 and the descendant class in s.23 is empty. Under s.25 his mother Kamala had predeceased him and his father Thilak survived: Thilak took one-half, and the other half went to the brothers and sisters of the half-blood related to Kasun by the side of his deceased parent, namely his mother's other children Sarathi and Amal, who being equally near in degree took that half per capita under s.30, one-quarter each. Sunil and Lalith, Thilak's children by Sumana, are half-blood siblings on the side of the surviving parent and so take nothing out of Kasun's estate. That devolution was carried into effect in Testamentary Proceeding No.1589/2013/T, in which the heirs and their shares were determined (Civil Procedure Code s.531), and by the notarially attested Administrator's Conveyance No.6231 of 21 March 2014 executed by Thilak as administrator on the termination of the proceeding (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2; Civil Procedure Code s.724B). Thilak then died intestate on 3 March 2017. No surviving spouse is disclosed, so s.22 is not engaged and under s.24 his children are preferent and take equally per capita; Kasun had predeceased him in 2013 without issue, so only Sunil and Lalith take, and Thilak's one-half share passed to them in equal parts. Sarathi died intestate and issueless on 8 August 2018 leaving her husband Sena. Under s.22 Sena took one-half of her one-quarter share. As to the balance, her descendants fail, so s.25 applies: her mother Kamala had predeceased her in 2011 and, on the footing that her father is Namal Silva and that he survives her, the surviving parent takes half of that balance and the other half goes to her full-blood brother Amal, her half-brother Kasun on the mother's side having predeceased her without issue.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The pedigree runs: Gamini Jayasinghe (entirety under the final decree of 25 October 2010) to Kamala Silva (Deed of Transfer No.2778 of 10 March 2011) to Kasun (Deed of Gift No.5634 of 18 April 2011). On Kasun's intestate death on 3 May 2013 the land devolved on his father Thilak as to one-half and on his half-brother and half-sister on the mother's side, Amal and Sarathi, as to one-quarter each, which is what Administrator's Conveyance No.6231 of 21 March 2014 gave effect to. On Thilak's intestate death on 3 March 2017 his one-half devolved on his surviving children Sunil and Lalith in equal shares, one-quarter of the land each. On Sarathi's intestate death on 8 August 2018 her one-quarter devolved as to one-half on her husband Sena and, on the footing stated above, as to one-quarter on her surviving father Namal Silva and as to one-quarter on her brother Amal. The present owners are therefore Amal, Sunil, Lalith, Sena and Namal Silva. Two facts are open on the background as given: it does not name the grantees in Administrator's Conveyance No.6231, and it does not state in terms that Namal Silva is the father of Sarathi and Amal or that he is still living. The pedigree above reads the conveyance as a distribution to Kasun's heirs and treats Namal Silva as the surviving father; if instead both of Sarathi's parents were dead at her death, her non-spousal half would pass wholly to Amal under s.26 of the Ordinance.

answer_claims.claim_text: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, whatever the domicile of the deceased.
Subject to the surviving spouse's one-half under s.22, the right of inheritance is divided in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals.

Where a person dies intestate leaving no descendants and only one parent alive, that surviving parent takes one-half and the other half goes to the full-blood brothers and sisters and to the half-blood brothers and sisters related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent.
A person is unmarried for the purposes of the Ordinance when he has no husband or wife living, so an intestate who dies unmarried leaves no spouse to take a half share under s.22.
Children and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of a parent and take equally per capita, the issue of a deceased child taking by representation.
Persons equally near in degree to the intestate take per capita and not per stirpes.

Having conveyed the entirety to Kasun by Deed of Gift No.5634 of 18 April 2011, Kamala Silva held no interest in this land at her death on 7 July 2011, so nothing in it passed to Namal Silva, Sarathi or Amal on her death.

Kasun died intestate, unmarried and without issue on 3 May 2013, so no spousal half arose and the descendant class was empty; his mother Kamala had predeceased him and his father Thilak survived, so Thilak took one-half of the land.

The other half of Kasun's estate went to Sarathi and Amal as the half-blood brother and sister related to him by the side of his deceased mother, in equal shares, while Sunil and Lalith, related through his surviving father, took nothing.

That devolution was carried into effect in Testamentary Proceeding No.1589/2013/T and by the notarially attested Administrator's Conveyance No.6231 of 21 March 2014 executed by Thilak as administrator on the termination of the proceeding.
On Thilak's intestate death on 3 March 2017 with no surviving spouse disclosed, his surviving children Sunil and Lalith took his one-half in equal shares, Kasun having predeceased him without issue.

On Sarathi's intestate and issueless death on 8 August 2018 her husband Sena took one-half of her share, and the balance devolved under s.25 on her surviving parent and her brother Amal, her mother having predeceased her and her half-brother Kasun having predeceased her without issue.

The pedigree is Gamini Jayasinghe to Kamala Silva by Deed of Transfer No.2778, to Kasun by Deed of Gift No.5634, then on Kasun's intestacy to Thilak, Sarathi and Amal, then on Thilak's intestacy to Sunil and Lalith, and then on Sarathi's intestacy to Sena, Namal Silva and Amal, so that the present owners are Amal, Sunil, Lalith, Sena and Namal Silva.

The pedigree rests on two facts that the background leaves open: the grantees named in Administrator's Conveyance No.6231, and whether Namal Silva is the father of Sarathi and Amal and survives Sarathi.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Inheritance ab interstate to the immovable property in Sri Lanka of a person deceased shall be governed and regulated by the following provisions of this Ordinance wherever such person may have or have had his actual or matrimonial domicile.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The subject matter is immovable property in Sri Lanka (the land and premises bearing Assessment No.45, Colombo Road, Pugoda). This subsection is the gateway provision: it makes Part III of the Ordinance the governing law for every intestate devolution in the chain, irrespective of the domicile of Kasun, Thilak or Sarathi.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; the corpus records no amendment event for this section, so the same text governed the deaths in 2013, 2017 and 2018 and is in force at 2024-10.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: When any person shall die intestate as to any of his or her property, leaving a spouse surviving, the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property of such person.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Governs the share of Sena, the surviving husband of Sarathi, who died intestate on 8 August 2018. It also explains why nothing passes to a spouse out of the estates of Kasun (who died unmarried) and Thilak (no surviving spouse disclosed).
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so the same text applied at Sarathi's death in 2018 and at 2024-10.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Subject to the right of the surviving spouse in the preceding section mentioned, the right of inheritance is divided in the following order as respects (a) descendants, (b) ascendants, (c) collaterals.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Sets the order in which the remaining half (or the whole, where there is no surviving spouse) is taken, and makes clear that the spouse's half under s.22 is carved out first. It is the ordering rule that sends each of the three intestate estates in this matter past the descendant class, which is empty in every case.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of the parents; all the children take equally per capita, but the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Governs the devolution of Thilak's half share on his intestate death on 3 March 2017: his surviving children Sunil and Lalith are preferent to all others and take equally per capita. It also shows that Kasun, who predeceased his father in 2013 without issue, leaves nobody to take by representation.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so the same text applied at Thilak's death in 2017 and at 2024-10.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: The children and remoter descendants failing, the inheritance of the deceased goes to his father and mother in case they are both alive; but if only one of the parents be alive, the surviving parent takes half, and the brothers and sisters of the deceased of the full blood, and the issue of any deceased brother or sister of the full blood, by representation, and the brothers and sisters of the half-blood who are related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent, and the issue of any such deceased brother or sister of the half-blood, by representation, take the other half.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The central operative rule. It governs Kasun's estate (no descendants; mother Kamala predeceased in 2011, father Thilak surviving, so Thilak takes half and the half-blood brothers and sisters on the deceased mother's side take the other half) and, on the footing that Namal Silva is Sarathi's father and survives her, the non-spousal half of Sarathi's estate. Its restriction of half-blood siblings to those related through the deceased parent is what excludes Sunil and Lalith, who are related to Kasun through his surviving father.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so the same text applied at Kasun's death in 2013, at Sarathi's death in 2018 and at 2024-10.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Wording is verbatim and the reading of "by the side of the deceased parent" is right, but the excerpt stops before the second sentence of s.25 ("In case there is no full or half-brother or sister alive at the death of the deceased, the surviving parent inherits the whole, although there may be children or other issue of deceased brothers or sisters"), which has to be read with the first: it is only because Sarathi and Amal were alive at Kasun's death that Thilak took a half and not the whole.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Except when otherwise expressly provided, if all those who succeed to the inheritance are equally near in degree to the intestate, they take per capita, and not per stirpes.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Supplies the mode of division within the sibling half of Kasun's estate: Sarathi and Amal are equally near in degree to Kasun (both half-sisters and half-brothers on the mother's side), so they take that half per capita, one-quarter of the land each.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt verbatim, but s.30 opens "Except when otherwise expressly provided" and s.27 (added as PROV-M025-901) is the express provision on dividing among half-blood brothers and sisters; s.30 supplies the per capita division here only because s.25 confines the takers of the sibling half to the deceased mother's side, so no father's-side against mother's-side split under s.27 arises.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: means not having a husband or wife living
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Defines "unmarried" for the purposes of the Ordinance. The background records that Kasun died "intestate and unmarried", which on this definition means he left no surviving spouse, so s.22 gives no half share out of his estate and the whole of it falls to be divided under s.25.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus. The corpus text of this interpretation section has lost its defined-term lead-ins in extraction, so the excerpt reads as a bare definition body; the corpus row records "unmarried" among the section's defined terms.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: The excerpt is a verbatim substring of s.3 but the corpus extraction has dropped the defined-term lead-ins, so the words "means not having a husband or wife living" cannot be tied to "unmarried" from the excerpt alone; defs 15-1876 unmarried confirms s.3 defines that term, and the provision should be cited as s.3 sv "unmarried".

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: The division however in the case of half-brothers and sisters is as follows: - The inheritance is divided into two parts ; the one-half the full brothers and sisters and the issue of such as are deceased by representation divide with the half-brothers and sisters of the father's side and the issue of such as are deceased by representation ; and the other half they divide with those of the mother's side and the issue of such as are deceased by representation
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Added by the verifier. Section 27 is the express provision on how an inheritance is divided where half-blood brothers and sisters take, and s.30 applies only "Except when otherwise expressly provided", so s.27 has to be checked before s.30 is used on the sibling half of Kasun's estate. It does not change the result: s.25 admits only the half-blood brothers and sisters related to Kasun through his deceased mother, so there is no father's-side share to set against a mother's-side share and no full brother or sister to take a preferential half. supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; the corpus records no amendment event for this section, so the same text applied at Kasun's death in 2013 and is in force at 2024-10.

legal_issues.issue: What undivided share of the land each surviving heir now holds, after the successive intestacies of Kasun, Thilak and Sarathi.
Whether the surviving husband of Sarathi takes a half of her share to the exclusion of her parent and sibling, or shares with them.

gold_answer_draft.issue: The question asks what undivided share of the land and premises bearing Assessment No.45, Colombo Road, Pugoda each heir now holds. This turns on quantifying the three successive intestate devolutions: Kasun's estate in 2013, Thilak's share on his death in 2017, and Sarathi's share on her death in 2018.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the intestate's property (Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.22), and the remainder passes in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals (s.23). Children take equally per capita and are preferent to all others (s.24). Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes one-half and the other half goes to full-blood brothers and sisters and to half-blood brothers and sisters related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent (s.25). Heirs equally near in degree take per capita (s.30). An intestate who dies unmarried, that is with no husband or wife living (s.3), leaves no spouse to take under s.22. The Ordinance governs inheritance to immovable property in Sri Lanka (s.21(1)).
gold_answer_draft.application: Kasun held the entirety when he died intestate, unmarried and issueless on 3 May 2013. No share passed under s.22. Under s.25 his surviving father Thilak took one-half, and Sarathi and Amal, the half-blood sister and brother related to him through his deceased mother Kamala, took the other half per capita under s.30, that is one-quarter of the land each. Thilak died intestate on 3 March 2017 with no surviving spouse disclosed; under s.24 his one-half passed equally to his surviving children Sunil and Lalith, giving each one-quarter of the land. Sarathi died intestate and issueless on 8 August 2018 holding one-quarter. Under s.22 her husband Sena took one-half of that quarter, namely one-eighth of the land. The remaining one-eighth fell under s.25: her descendants failed, her mother Kamala had predeceased her in 2011, and on the footing that her father is Namal Silva and that he survives her, he takes one-half of that eighth, namely one-sixteenth, while the other one-sixteenth goes to her full-blood brother Amal, her half-brother Kasun having predeceased her without issue. Amal therefore adds one-sixteenth to the one-quarter he took from Kasun's estate, giving him five-sixteenths.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: On the footing set out above the present shares in the land and premises bearing Assessment No.45, Colombo Road, Pugoda are: Amal five-sixteenths; Sunil one-quarter (four-sixteenths); Lalith one-quarter (four-sixteenths); Sena one-eighth (two-sixteenths); and Namal Silva one-sixteenth. These add up to the entirety. The one-sixteenth attributed to Namal Silva depends on the reading that he is the father of Sarathi and Amal and was living at Sarathi's death, neither of which the background states in terms; if both of Sarathi's parents were dead when she died, her non-spousal one-eighth would pass wholly to Amal under s.26 of the Ordinance, giving Amal three-eighths and leaving Namal Silva with nothing.

answer_claims.claim_text: A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of a person who dies intestate.
Subject to the spouse's half, inheritance passes in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals, and children take equally per capita in preference to all others.

Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes one-half and the other half goes to the full-blood siblings and to the half-blood siblings related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent, those equally near in degree taking per capita.
The Ordinance governs inheritance to immovable property in Sri Lanka, and a person who dies unmarried has no husband or wife living and so leaves no spouse to take a half share.
On Kasun's intestate death Thilak took one-half of the land and Sarathi and Amal took one-quarter each.
On Thilak's intestate death his one-half passed equally to Sunil and Lalith, giving each one-quarter of the land.
On Sarathi's intestate death her husband Sena took one-half of her one-quarter, that is one-eighth of the land.

The remaining one-eighth of Sarathi's share went one-sixteenth to her surviving father Namal Silva and one-sixteenth to her brother Amal, her mother having predeceased her and her half-brother Kasun having predeceased her without issue.
The present shares are Amal five-sixteenths, Sunil one-quarter, Lalith one-quarter, Sena one-eighth and Namal Silva one-sixteenth, together making up the entirety.
The one-sixteenth attributed to Namal Silva depends on him being the father of Sarathi and Amal and being alive at Sarathi's death, neither of which the background states in terms.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: shall be in force or avail in law unless - (a) the relevant deed or instrument shall be in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and the same shall be attested by such notary;
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: A lease of an apartment for three years is an agreement affecting immovable property outside the 'lease at will or for any period not exceeding one month' exclusion, so it is of no force in law unless it is in writing, signed by every executant or by a person duly authorised by the executant, together with the witnesses, in the presence of a licenced notary and attested by that notary. This both compels notarial execution and supplies the route by which Shantha may sign through an authorised person.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section 2 was last amended in 2024 (Act No. 4 of 2024) and in 2022 (Act No. 30 of 2022); the corpus text is the consolidated version. Commencement dates are not in the corpus.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (12) He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same and the witnesses shall have signed the same in his presence and in the presence of one another, and unless he shall have signed the same in the presence of the executant and of the attesting witnesses.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the core execution requirement: the executant and the witnesses must sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another. This is why Shantha cannot simply post a signed agreement to Kanthi.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section in the consolidated Notaries Ordinance text; the corpus records the latest change as 2024 (Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 6 of 2024). indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (22) He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice nor authenticate or attest any deed or instrument drawn in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: A notary may not attest a deed in any area other than the area in which she is authorised to practise. Kanthi practises in Colombo, so if the Negombo area lies outside her authorised area she cannot travel to Negombo and attest Shantha's signature there.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (25) Where any deed or instrument is executed or acknowledged before more than one notary- (a) the notary who first attests such deed or instrument shall comply with all the requirements of rule (20), and every other notary attesting such deed or instrument shall comply with the requirements of paragraphs (a) to (e) of the aforesaid rule

legal_issues.issue: Whether a three-year lease of an apartment must be executed notarially, and in whose presence the lessor and lessee must sign.

How the agreement can be validly signed when the lessor cannot attend before the Colombo notary - execution before more than one notary at different times and places, or execution by a duly authorised attorney under a registered power of attorney.
What registration steps the notary must take for a lease of land situated in a district other than the one in which she resides and practises, and within what time.

gold_answer_draft.issue: How a three-year lease of a Negombo apartment at Rs.120,000 a month can be signed by a lessor who cannot come to Colombo and by a lessee who can, and what a Colombo notary must then do to register the instrument.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A lease of immovable property for a period exceeding one month is of no force in law unless it is in writing, signed by every executant, or by a person duly authorised by the executant, and by the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and attested by that notary (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)(a)). The notary may not attest unless the executant and the witnesses signed in her presence and in the presence of one another (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (12)), and she may not attest in any area other than the area in which she is authorised to practise (s.31 rule (22)). The Ordinance nevertheless contemplates a deed executed or acknowledged before more than one notary and divides the attestation duties between the first attesting notary and every other attesting notary (s.31 rule (25)), and s.32(2) provides for parties who do not sign at the same time and place, deeming the instrument executed for the purposes of rules (6), (7), (23) and (25) when it is first signed. Alternatively the lessor may authorise an attorney: a power of attorney executed in Sri Lanka must be executed before two witnesses and attested by a notary (Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.2), must meet the additional requirements of s.3A where the transaction falls within s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, must be submitted for registration with the Registrar-General within one month (s.3(1)(b)), and the attesting notary must check the Registrar-General's volumes and folios and state in her attestation that it has not been revoked (s.3B), keep a true copy with her protocol and forward a copy with the duplicate (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (30)), and take the attorney's affidavit that the power is genuine, in force and the grantor alive. As to registration, an instrument creating an interest in land is deemed to affect land and so is registrable (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.8(b)), an unregistered instrument is void against a subsequent duly registered instrument taken for value (s.7(1)), registration must be effected in the book allotted to the division in which the land is situated (s.14(1)), and the notary acting for a party may present it (s.26(1)(d)). The notary must submit the deed for registration within thirty days of attestation, or sixty days where it is to be registered outside the jurisdiction in which she practises (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (30A)), send the duplicate and Form F1 list to the Registrar of Lands of her own district by the fifteenth of the following month (rule (26)), send a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the district where the land lies (rule (29)), and use due diligence in registering where she has instructions and funds (s.37).
gold_answer_draft.application: The lease is for three years, well outside the one-month exclusion, so notarial execution is compulsory and Shantha cannot simply sign at home and send the paper to Colombo. Kanthi practises in Colombo and the apartment and Shantha are in Negombo, so rule (22) prevents her attesting Shantha's signature outside the area she is authorised for. Two lawful routes remain. First, execution before more than one notary under rule (25): Ananda Gamage signs the agreement before Kanthi in Colombo with two witnesses, and Shantha signs the same instrument before a notary authorised to practise where he is, each notary attesting the signatures taken before her or him, each numbering the instrument in his or her own protocol register, and s.32(2) accommodating the fact that the parties sign at different times and places. Second, Shantha grants a power of attorney, attested by a notary before two witnesses and complying with s.3A because the lease falls within s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, registers it with the Registrar-General within one month, and his attorney then signs before Kanthi in Colombo along with Ananda; Kanthi must satisfy herself from the Registrar-General's volumes and folios that the power stands unrevoked and say so in her attestation, take the attorney's affidavit, and keep and forward copies of the power. Either way she must have an assurance that the stamp duty is provided before attesting. On registration, the lease creates an interest in land and is registrable; it must go to the land registry for the division in which the Negombo apartment is situated, not Colombo. Because that registration is outside the jurisdiction in which Kanthi practises, she has sixty days from attestation to submit it, she must transmit the duplicate and Form F1 list to the Registrar of Lands of her own district by the fifteenth of the following month, and she must send a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the apartment lies. If the apartment forms part of a registered Condominium Property, she should also check whether the interest has to be registered under the Registration of Title Act rather than in the ordinary land register. The scenario does not state Shantha's judicial zone, whether the apartment is registered condominium property, or whether the parties have instructed and funded Kanthi to register, so those points are stated conditionally.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The agreement can be signed either before two notaries at different times and places, Ananda before Kanthi in Colombo and Shantha before a notary where he is, or by an attorney holding a duly attested and registered power of attorney signing for Shantha before Kanthi. Kanthi must then have the duty stamped, submit the instrument for registration in the land registry division covering the Negombo apartment within sixty days of attestation, transmit the duplicate with the Form F1 list to the Registrar of Lands of her own district by the fifteenth of the following month, and send a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the district where the apartment is situated.

answer_claims.claim_text: A lease of immovable property for a period exceeding one month is of no force in law unless it is in writing, signed by every executant or a person duly authorised by the executant and by the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary, and attested by that notary.
A notary may not attest a deed unless the executant and the witnesses signed it in her presence and in the presence of one another.
A notary may not attest a deed in any area other than the area in which she is authorised to practise.

The Notaries Ordinance permits a deed to be executed or acknowledged before more than one notary and allocates the attestation duties between the first attesting notary and every other attesting notary, and it provides for parties who do not sign at the same time and place.

An executant may instead sign through a duly authorised attorney under a power of attorney attested by a notary before two witnesses, which for a transaction within section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance must comply with section 3A and be submitted for registration within one month, and the attesting notary must verify from the Registrar-General's records that the power is unrevoked, state that in her attestation, take the attorney's affidavit and keep and forward copies of the power.
An instrument that creates an interest in land is deemed to affect land and is registrable, and an unregistered instrument is void against a subsequent duly registered instrument taken for value.
Registration must be effected in the book allotted to the division in which the land affected is situated, and the notary acting on behalf of a party may present the instrument.

A notary must submit a deed she has attested for registration within thirty days of attestation, or within sixty days where it is to be registered outside the jurisdiction in which she practises, must transmit the duplicate and the Form F1 list to the Registrar of Lands of her own district by the fifteenth of the following month, must send a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated, and is liable to a fine if, having instructions and funds, she fails to use due diligence in registering.

Because the lease runs for three years it is outside the one-month exclusion, so notarial execution before Kanthi or another notary is compulsory and Shantha cannot sign it in Negombo and send it to Colombo.

Since Kanthi is authorised to practise in Colombo and Shantha is in Negombo, she cannot attest his signature there, so the agreement must be executed either before two notaries or through an attorney who signs before her in Colombo.
The fact that the lessor is Kanthi's brother-in-law does not disqualify her, because the rule bars only the attestation of a deed to which the notary herself is a party.

Because the apartment is in Negombo while Kanthi practises and resides in Colombo, the lease must be registered in the land registry division covering the apartment, the sixty-day limb of the registration deadline applies, and a certified copy must go to the Registrar of Lands of the district where the apartment lies.
Kanthi must not attest the agreement until she has an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided.

If the apartment forms part of a registered Condominium Property, Kanthi must also check whether the lessee's interest has to be registered under the Registration of Title Act rather than in the ordinary land register.

The agreement can therefore be signed either before two notaries at different times and places or by an attorney holding a duly attested and registered power of attorney signing for Shantha before Kanthi in Colombo.

Kanthi must then have the duty stamped, submit the instrument for registration in the land registry division covering the Negombo apartment within sixty days of attestation, transmit the duplicate with the Form F1 list to the Registrar of Lands of her own district by the fifteenth of the following month, and send a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the district where the apartment is situated.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What liability a notary incurs by attesting a lease agreement in a year for which she did not obtain the yearly certificate from the Registrar of the High Court.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The certificate that a person is a notary duly authorised to practise is issued yearly by the Registrar of the High Court; it must be applied for and granted on or before 1 April in every year and is in force for one year and no longer (Notaries Ordinance s.27(2)). Where the certificate was not applied for within that time, the High Court Judge may, if satisfied that the delay was due to accident, misfortune or other unavoidable cause, direct the Registrar to issue it notwithstanding the delay (s.27(2), proviso). A person who acts as a notary without having obtained such a certificate is guilty of an offence for or in respect of every deed executed or acknowledged before him while he was without it, and is liable to a fine of not less than five thousand rupees and not exceeding twenty five thousand rupees (s.30). The Registrar-General may, instead of prosecuting, accept from the notary such sum as he considers proper in composition of a section 30 offence (s.35(1)). Separately, on a High Court Judge's report of an offence or of misconduct, the Minister may cancel the notary's warrant or suspend her from office for such period as appears just (s.21(2)).
gold_answer_draft.application: Kanthi attested the lease agreement in a year for which she had not obtained the yearly certificate, so at the moment of attestation she was acting as a notary without the certificate required by s.27. That engages s.30 directly, and because the offence is framed 'for or in respect of every deed executed or acknowledged before him', her exposure is counted per deed: the lease agreement is one such deed, and any other deed she attested while uncertificated attracts its own fine of between Rs.5,000 and Rs.25,000. The Registrar-General may take the matter administratively and accept a composition sum instead of prosecuting her. Beyond the fine, a conviction or a finding of misconduct reported by the High Court Judge exposes her to cancellation of her warrant or to suspension. She should apply at once for the certificate and, since the 1 April date has passed, ask the High Court Judge to direct the Registrar to issue it on the ground that the delay was due to accident, misfortune or other unavoidable cause, but that relief operates on the issue of the certificate and does not erase the attestation already made without one. Whether the lease agreement itself is invalid is not settled by these provisions: s.33 saves an instrument only from a notary's failure in a matter of form under a s.31 rule and expressly does not validate an instrument invalid under any other written law, and s.30 is not a s.31 rule.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Kanthi is criminally liable under s.30 of the Notaries Ordinance for having acted as a notary without the yearly certificate, to a fine of not less than Rs.5,000 and not more than Rs.25,000 in respect of every deed she attested while uncertificated, including this lease agreement; the Registrar-General may compound the offence instead of prosecuting; and she is additionally exposed to suspension or cancellation of her warrant by the Minister on a report by the High Court Judge. She should immediately seek the certificate, relying on the proviso to s.27(2) if the delay was due to accident, misfortune or other unavoidable cause.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary's yearly certificate must be applied for and granted on or before 1 April in every year and is in force for one year and no longer.

A person who acts as a notary without having obtained the certificate is guilty of an offence in respect of every deed executed or acknowledged before him while he was without it, and is liable to a fine of not less than five thousand rupees and not exceeding twenty five thousand rupees.
The Registrar-General may accept a sum of money in composition of a section 30 offence instead of instituting criminal proceedings.
On a High Court Judge's report of an offence or misconduct the Minister may cancel the notary's warrant or suspend her from office for such period as appears just.
A late application for the certificate may still be allowed if the High Court Judge is satisfied that the delay was due to accident, misfortune or other unavoidable cause.
Kanthi attested the lease agreement without having obtained the yearly certificate for the current year, so she acted as a notary while uncertificated.

Because the offence is framed in respect of every deed executed or acknowledged before her while uncertificated, her fine exposure runs per deed and covers this lease agreement and any other deed she attested in the same period.

She should apply at once for the certificate and, the 1 April date having passed, ask the High Court Judge to direct its issue on the ground of accident, misfortune or other unavoidable cause, which does not undo the attestation already made.

Whether the lease agreement itself is invalidated is not resolved by these provisions, because section 33 saves an instrument only from a failure in a matter of form under a section 31 rule and section 30 is not a section 31 rule.

Kanthi is liable under section 30 of the Notaries Ordinance to a fine of not less than Rs.5,000 and not more than Rs.25,000 in respect of every deed attested while uncertificated, including this lease agreement, subject to the Registrar-General's power to compound, and is additionally exposed to suspension or cancellation of her warrant.

legal_issues.issue: What the notary must do before drawing the deed: verify his own competence for the area, call for the vendor's title deeds and search the land registry for the state of the title and registered encumbrances.
How the disclosed mortgage over the estate must be dealt with, and how the purchaser's priority is protected between search and registration.
What the deed itself must contain: an accurate description of the thirty-acre estate and bungalow by boundaries, extent and administrative situation, and the true and full consideration.
Whether any statutory ceiling or consent regime applies to the purchase of a thirty-acre coconut estate.
What the notary must do at and after execution: identification, witnesses, attestation, stamp duty and registration within the statutory period.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What steps the notary retained by the intending purchaser of a thirty-acre coconut estate with a bungalow in Kurunegala must take before, at and after the execution of the conveyance.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A sale of land is of no force in law unless the deed is in writing and signed by every executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary who attests it (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)(a)). A notary may act only in the area and language for which he is authorised (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule 22). Before drawing a deed affecting an interest in land he must search the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered (s.31 rule 17(a)) and must obtain from the Registrar the certified extract of the folio showing ownership and registered encumbrances (s.31 rule 17(b)(i)); the registry books may be searched and certified extracts obtained by a person interested or his agent (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.42). The search matters because an unregistered instrument is void against a party claiming adversely for value under a later duly registered instrument (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7(1)), and a transferee for value may lodge a priority notice which holds for six weeks and back-dates registration (s.30(5)). On a transfer the notary must use his best endeavours to obtain the vendor's title deed and endorse the new deed's particulars on it (s.31 rule 33). The deed must carry an accurate description of the land by boundaries, extent and situation with the district, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division and Grama Niladhari Division (s.31 rule 16(a)), and the true and full consideration must be ascertained and set out (Notaries Ordinance s.38(1)). The notary may not attest without an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided (s.31 rule 6), duty being payable by him (s.31 rule 7A(a)) and charged on every specified instrument (Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.3(1)). He must identify the executants from personal knowledge or their identity documents (s.31 rule 9), attest without delay under his signature and seal recording execution, identification, date, place, reading over, consideration paid in his presence and stamps (s.31 rule 20), and submit the deed for registration within thirty days of attestation (s.31 rule 30A). Two statutory restrictions must be excluded: agricultural land other than paddy may not be owned above fifty acres (Land Reform Law s.3(1)(b)), and land held on a state grant cannot be disposed of without the prior approval of the Government Agent (Land Development Ordinance s.19(6)); a consent certificate of the Board is required only for tea or rubber estates (Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act s.3(1)).
gold_answer_draft.application: The estate lies at Wariyapola in the Kurunegala District and the notary is authorised to practise in Sinhala in that district, so he may accept the retainer and attest the deed. He should take full instructions, call for and examine the vendor's prior deeds, beginning with Deed of Transfer No. 1032 of 1998 and tracing back through the 1979 partition decree, and search the Kurunegala land registry folio in which that deed is registered, taking a certified folio extract. That extract should disclose Bond No. 2210 of 2021 in favour of the bank, and the notary must arrange for a registered discharge, or for the bank's release to be executed and registered simultaneously with the conveyance out of the purchase money; otherwise the client would take subject to that earlier registered interest. Because execution is not to take place until 20 May 2024, a priority notice should be considered so that no instrument executed by the vendor in the interval gains priority. The thirty-acre extent and the boundaries of Lot 1 in Survey Plan No. 4127 must be checked on the ground against the folio description and reproduced in the schedule with the village, Divisional Secretary's Division and district, the bungalow being described with the land. The whole thirty acres is coconut and the client owns no other agricultural land, so the purchase leaves him below the fifty-acre ceiling; coconut is neither tea nor rubber, so no consent certificate is needed; and as the chain shows private freehold with no state permit or grant, no approval of the Government Agent is called for. The full price of Rs. 42,000,000, including the Rs. 4,200,000 advance paid under the agreement of 10 January 2024, must be set out as the consideration, and the balance paid at execution recorded in the attestation with the details of any cheque or draft. Stamp duty on that value must be provided for and paid before attestation. At execution the notary must identify both parties from their national identity cards, have two witnesses of good repute sign, read over and explain the deed, then attest, sign and seal it without delay, endorse the particulars on the vendor's title deed, and lodge the deed for registration by 19 June 2024.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary's steps are, in sequence: confirm his competence for the area and take instructions; call for and examine the vendor's title deeds; search the Kurunegala land registry and obtain a certified folio extract; deal with the disclosed mortgage and consider a priority notice; verify extent and boundaries against the survey plan; satisfy himself that no ceiling or consent regime bars the purchase; draw the deed with an accurate schedule and the true and full consideration; provide for and pay stamp duty; execute and attest the deed with identified parties and two witnesses; and submit it for registration within thirty days of attestation. On these facts nothing in the statutory material bars the purchase, provided the bond is discharged and the deed is properly drawn, attested and registered in time.

answer_claims.claim_text: A sale of land has no force in law unless the deed is in writing, signed by every executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary who attests it, so the transaction has to be carried through by a notary.
A notary may only attest a deed in the area and language in which he is authorised to practise.

Before drawing any deed affecting an interest in land the notary must search, or cause to be searched, the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed affecting the land has been registered.

The notary must obtain from the Registrar of the relevant Land Registry a certified extract of the folio containing the last entry showing the ownership of and the registered encumbrances on the land.
The registry duplicates, books and indexes may be searched by a person interested or by his agent duly authorised in writing, and certified extracts obtained.

An instrument that is not duly registered is void against a party claiming an adverse interest for valuable consideration under a later instrument that is duly registered, so priority depends on registration.

A person acquiring an interest in land for valuable consideration may lodge a priority notice, which remains in force for six weeks and back-dates the registration of the instrument to the date of the notice.
The notary must use his best endeavours to obtain the vendor's title deed on a transfer and endorse on it the number and date of the new deed and the nature of the transaction.

The deed must embody, in itself or in an annexed schedule, an accurate and clear description of the land showing its boundaries, extent and situation, specifying the district, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division and Grama Niladhari Division.
The notary must endeavour to ascertain the true and full consideration and set it out in the deed.

The notary may not attest unless he has an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided, and stamp duty on the instrument is payable by the notary, duty being charged on every specified instrument at the rate the Minister determines.
The notary must establish the identity of the executants, either by personal knowledge or by inspecting the national identity card, passport bio-page or driving licence.

The notary must without delay attest the deed and sign and seal an attestation recording, among other things, execution in his presence and in the presence of one another, how the executants were identified, the date and place, the reading over, the consideration actually paid in his presence and the stamps.
The attested deed must be submitted for registration within thirty days of attestation.
A person may not own more than fifty acres of agricultural land where the land is not exclusively paddy, and land owned in excess of that ceiling vests in the Commission.
Land alienated on a state grant may not be disposed of except with the prior approval of the Government Agent, and not in portions below the minimum specified in the grant.
Prior consent of the Board, evidenced by a certificate attached to the deed, is required only for the transfer of a tea or rubber estate.

The notary should also satisfy himself that an out-and-out purchase is the transaction the parties actually intend and explain the deed to them before signature, although this express duty was introduced by an amendment of 2024 whose commencement relative to April 2024 is not established on the corpus.
Because the estate lies at Wariyapola in the Kurunegala District and the notary is authorised to practise in Sinhala in that district, he may accept the retainer and attest the deed himself.

The vendor's assertion that he owns on Deed of Transfer No. 1032 of 1998, traced back to the 1979 partition decree, must be tested by searching the Kurunegala land registry folio in which that deed is registered and by obtaining the certified folio extract, and the notary should call for and examine the prior deeds themselves.

The search and folio extract should disclose Bond No. 2210 of 2021 in favour of the bank, so the notary must arrange for a registered discharge or for the release to be executed and registered together with the conveyance, since otherwise the buyer takes subject to that earlier registered interest.

Because the bond is outstanding and execution is not to take place until 20 May 2024, the notary should consider lodging a priority notice so that an instrument executed by the vendor in the interval cannot gain priority over the client's conveyance.

The schedule to the deed must reproduce the thirty-acre extent and the boundaries of Lot 1 in Survey Plan No. 4127 with the village, Divisional Secretary's Division and district, and the notary should have the plan checked on the ground against the folio description before drawing the deed.

Since the whole thirty acres is coconut land and the client owns no other agricultural land, the purchase leaves his holding well below the fifty-acre ceiling, but the notary should record that check.
Coconut is neither tea nor rubber, so no consent certificate of the Board needs to be obtained or attached to this deed.
The chain shows private freehold and no state permit or grant, so no prior approval of the Government Agent has to be obtained before the vendor conveys.

The full price of Rs. 42,000,000, including the Rs. 4,200,000 advance already paid under the agreement of 10 January 2024, must be set out in the deed as the consideration, and the balance paid at execution must be recorded in the attestation with the details of any cheque or bank draft.
Stamp duty on that consideration must be worked out, provided for and paid by the notary before he attests, and the receipt or stamps dealt with as the rules require.

At execution the notary must identify Mr. Ranasinghe and the vendor from their national identity cards, have two witnesses of good repute sign, read over and explain the deed, and then attest, sign and seal it without delay.

If the deed is executed on 20 May 2024 it must be lodged for registration in the Kurunegala land registry by 19 June 2024, and the notary should also endorse the particulars of the new deed on the vendor's title deed.

The notary's steps therefore run in sequence: confirm his own competence for the area, call for and examine the vendor's title deeds, search the land registry and take a certified folio extract, deal with the disclosed mortgage and consider a priority notice, verify the extent and boundaries against the survey plan, check that no statutory ceiling or consent regime bites, draw the deed with an accurate schedule and the true consideration, provide for stamp duty, execute and attest it with identified parties and two witnesses, and lodge it for registration within thirty days.
On the enriched facts nothing in the frozen statutory material bars the purchase, provided the bank's bond is discharged and the deed is properly drawn, attested and registered in time.

enrichment.original_background: Mr. Ranasinghe is your client and he intends to buy a coconut estate with a bungalow situated in Kurunegala thirty acres (A30, RO, PO) in extent.
enrichment.enriched_background: Mr. Ranasinghe is your client and he intends to buy a coconut estate with a bungalow situated in Kurunegala thirty acres (A30, RO, PO) in extent. He is a citizen of Sri Lanka, resident in Colombo 5, and he owns no other agricultural land. The property is known as Pinnaduwa Watta, depicted as Lot 1 in Survey Plan No. 4127 dated 12 June 2019 made by K. Amarasekara, Licensed Surveyor, and lies in the village of Kadigawa, Wariyapola Divisional Secretary's Division, Dewamedi Hatpattu, Kurunegala District; the whole thirty acres is under mature coconut and carries one two-storeyed bungalow. The intended vendor is Mr. K. B. Wijesundara Bandara of Wariyapola, who says he became owner on Deed of Transfer No. 1032 attested on 4 March 1998 by Mr. S. Herath, Notary Public of Kurunegala, and that the land was allotted to his predecessor by a partition decree entered in 1979 in the District Court of Kurunegala. He holds no state permit or grant in respect of the land, and there is no tea or rubber on it. The vendor has disclosed that the estate stands mortgaged to a licensed commercial bank on Bond No. 2210 dated 8 July 2021, with about Rs. 8,500,000 outstanding. The parties signed an agreement to sell on 10 January 2024 at a price of Rs. 42,000,000, of which Rs. 4,200,000 has been paid as an advance and the balance is to be paid on execution of the conveyance, which they wish to have executed on 20 May 2024. You are authorised to practise in Sinhala in the Kurunegala district and your office is at Kurunegala.

added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If he were a foreign transferee, or already held agricultural land close to the ceiling, additional statutory restrictions would come into play and the advice would change.

added_facts.fact: The property is known as Pinnaduwa Watta, depicted as Lot 1 in Survey Plan No. 4127 dated 12 June 2019 made by K. Amarasekara, Licensed Surveyor, lying in the village of Kadigawa, Wariyapola Divisional Secretary's Division, Dewamedi Hatpattu, Kurunegala District; the whole thirty acres is under mature coconut and carries one two-storeyed bungalow.
added_facts.reason: Without an identified plan, boundaries and administrative divisions the description requirement for the schedule to the deed cannot be applied to the facts.

added_facts.fact: The intended vendor is Mr. K. B. Wijesundara Bandara of Wariyapola, who says he became owner on Deed of Transfer No. 1032 attested on 4 March 1998 by Mr. S. Herath, Notary Public of Kurunegala, and that the land was allotted to his predecessor by a partition decree entered in 1979 in the District Court of Kurunegala.

added_facts.reason: Supplies the consideration figure the notary must state in the deed and record in the attestation, and the value on which stamp duty is worked out.

added_facts.reason: Excludes the statutory consent regimes that would otherwise have to be cleared before the transfer.
