indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Revocation of Irrevocable Deeds of Gift on the Ground of Gross Ingratitude Act
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: An irrevocable deed of gift may be revoked on the ground of gross ingratitude, only on an Order made by a competent court, in an action filed by the donor of such deed against the donee to have the said deed revoked.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Directly answers the question. It establishes that a deed of gift expressed to be irrevocable is nevertheless capable of revocation, and fixes the only ground (gross ingratitude), the only mode (an order of a competent court) and the only parties (donor as plaintiff, donee as defendant). The word "only" also excludes unilateral revocation by the donor's own act or deed.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 2017 per the corpus (in_force_from_year 2017); no amendment events recorded. In force at 2023-10.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Revocation of Irrevocable Deeds of Gift on the Ground of Gross Ingratitude Act
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Court shall not entertain an action referred to in section 2, unless it is filed within a period of ten years from the date of the execution of such deed of gift and within two years from the date on which the cause of action arose.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: A necessary statutory condition on the section 2 remedy. Even where the ground exists, the court cannot entertain the action outside the two cumulative time limits, so whether the deed could be revoked on the facts turns on the date of execution of the deed and the date the cause of action arose.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 2017 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded. In force at 2023-10.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Revocation of Irrevocable Deeds of Gift on the Ground of Gross Ingratitude Act
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: The plaintiff in an action instituted under the provisions of this Act shall file or cause to be filed in court with the plaint, an application for registration of lis pendens
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Explains what the donor must do when instituting the action. It is a filing requirement rather than a condition of the right, so it supports the practical answer without changing whether revocation is available.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 2017 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded. In force at 2023-10.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Wording confirmed verbatim and the supporting role is right, but the excerpt stops at "an application for registration of lis pendens" and omits paragraphs (a) and (b) of section 4(1), which are the words the answer actually relies on for addressing the application to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the deed is registered (or, if unregistered, in which the land lies); the full section text supports the claim.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Revocation of Irrevocable Deeds of Gift on the Ground of Gross Ingratitude Act
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Every action filed under the provisions of this Act shall be proceeded with and regulated by the procedure provided for in the Civil Procedure Code (Chapter 101).
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Identifies the procedure the revocation action follows. Supporting context for the mode of revocation; it does not affect whether the deed can be revoked.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 2017 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded. In force at 2023-10.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a deed of gift that declares itself absolute and irrevocable can be revoked at all, notwithstanding those words.
If it can be revoked, on what ground, by whom, against whom and by what mode revocation must be effected, and whether the donor can revoke by his own act.
Whether the statutory time limits for filing the revocation action are satisfied on the date of execution of the deed and the date the cause of action arose.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether a deed of gift which states on its face that it is absolute and irrevocable can nevertheless be revoked, and if so on what ground, by whom and in what manner; and whether the donor here is within the time allowed for seeking revocation of the 2019 deed after the donee's conduct in June 2023.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The words "absolute and irrevocable" in the deed do not put the gift beyond recall. Section 2 of the Revocation of Irrevocable Deeds of Gift on the Ground of Gross Ingratitude Act, No. 5 of 2017 provides that an irrevocable deed of gift may be revoked on the ground of gross ingratitude, only on an order made by a competent court, in an action filed by the donor against the donee. Three limits follow from the section itself: gross ingratitude is the only ground; an order of a competent court is the only mode, so the donor cannot revoke by his own act or by executing a deed of revocation; and the action lies at the suit of the donor against the donee. Section 3 adds that the court shall not entertain such an action unless it is filed within ten years from the date of execution of the deed of gift and within two years from the date on which the cause of action arose, and both limits must be satisfied. Under section 4(1) the plaintiff must file with the plaint an application for registration of the action as a lis pendens, addressed to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the deed is registered or, where it is unregistered, in which the land lies. Under section 5 the action is proceeded with and regulated by the procedure of the Civil Procedure Code. The Act does not define gross ingratitude, so whether particular conduct amounts to it is for the court to decide on the evidence.
gold_answer_draft.application: The deed of gift of Kahatagahawatta was executed on 12 March 2019 and declares the gift absolute and irrevocable. That wording is no answer to a claim under section 2. The donor, Wimalasena Perera, is the proper plaintiff and the donee, his nephew Chaminda Perera, the proper defendant. The conduct relied on is the assault in June 2023 and the donor's eviction from the annexe of the very house he gave away, neither of which the donee denies; that is the material the donor would place before the court as gross ingratitude, though the finding is for the court and cannot be assumed. On the dates, an action filed in or shortly after October 2023 is within ten years of 12 March 2019 and within two years of the June 2023 conduct, so section 3 does not shut the donor out. Because the land is registered in the Kalutara land registry, the lis pendens application under section 4(1) goes to the Registrar of Lands of that district and must be filed with the plaint, and the action proceeds under the Civil Procedure Code. What the donor cannot do is execute a deed cancelling the gift and treat the property as his own again; nothing short of a court order will undo the gift.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Yes, it could be revoked, but only in one way. Despite the recital that it is absolute and irrevocable, the deed can be revoked on the ground of gross ingratitude by order of a competent court in an action filed by the donor against the donee under section 2 of Act No. 5 of 2017, and on these dates such an action is within both the ten-year and the two-year limits in section 3. The donor should be advised to sue promptly, filing the lis pendens application with the plaint; whether the donee's conduct amounts to gross ingratitude is a matter for the court on the evidence, and the donor has no power to revoke the deed himself.

answer_claims.claim_text: A recital that a deed of gift is absolute and irrevocable does not prevent its revocation; an irrevocable deed of gift may be revoked on the ground of gross ingratitude.
Revocation may be effected only on an order made by a competent court, in an action filed by the donor against the donee, so the donor cannot revoke the gift by his own act or deed.
Gross ingratitude is the only ground on which such an action may be founded, and the Act does not define the term, so whether given conduct amounts to gross ingratitude is for the court to decide.
The court shall not entertain the action unless it is filed within ten years from the date of execution of the deed of gift and within two years from the date on which the cause of action arose.
The plaintiff must file with the plaint an application for registration of the action as a lis pendens, addressed to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the deed is registered.
The revocation action is proceeded with and regulated by the procedure of the Civil Procedure Code.
The donor is the proper plaintiff and the donee, his nephew, the proper defendant in the revocation action.

The assault in June 2023 and the eviction of the donor from the annexe, neither of which the donee denies, are the matters the donor would place before the court as gross ingratitude; the finding remains for the court.

An action filed in or shortly after October 2023 is within ten years of the execution of the deed on 12 March 2019 and within two years of the June 2023 cause of action, so the time limits do not bar the donor.
Because the land is registered in the Kalutara land registry, the lis pendens application is addressed to the Registrar of Lands of that district and must be filed with the plaint.

The deed can be revoked, but only by order of a competent court on the ground of gross ingratitude in an action by the donor against the donee, and on these dates such an action is within both statutory time limits.
The donor cannot undo the gift by executing a deed of revocation himself; without a court order the gift stands.

enrichment.original_background: A deed of gift states that it is absolute and irrevocable.
enrichment.enriched_background: Wimalasena Perera, aged 74, a retired schoolmaster of Panadura, gifted the land called Kahatagahawatta, thirty-two perches in extent with the house standing on it, at Panadura in the District of Kalutara, to his nephew Chaminda Perera. The parties are low-country Sinhalese governed by the general law. The gift was made by deed No. 4417 dated 12 March 2019, attested by a notary public and registered in the Kalutara land registry, and the deed states that the gift is absolute and irrevocable. The donee took possession, and the donor went on living in an annexe of the same house as the deed allowed him to. In June 2023 the donee assaulted the donor during a quarrel over the property, causing injuries for which the donor was treated in hospital, and then locked the annexe and put the donor out of the premises; the donor has since been living with a daughter. The donee does not deny the assault or the eviction and refuses to reconvey the property. The donor consults you in October 2023 and asks whether he can get the property back.

added_facts.fact: The donor is Wimalasena Perera, aged 74, of Panadura, and the donee is his nephew Chaminda Perera; the parties are low-country Sinhalese governed by the general law.
added_facts.reason: The question gives no party identity or relationship. The remedy works through the donor and donee as plaintiff and defendant, so both must be identified. Stating that the general law applies keeps the special personal laws out of the scenario.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the parties were Kandyan, a further question about the revocability of a Kandyan deed of gift would arise under legislation that is not in this corpus, and the answer could not rest on this Act alone.

added_facts.fact: The subject matter is the land called Kahatagahawatta, thirty-two perches with the house on it, at Panadura in the District of Kalutara, registered in the Kalutara land registry; the donee took possession and the donor retained the right to live in an annexe.
added_facts.reason: The question names no property. Immovable property in an identified district is needed to work out the lis pendens step, which is addressed to the Registrar of Lands of the district where the deed is registered.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the subject of the gift were movable property, or the district unknown, the lis pendens step could not be worked out on the facts.

added_facts.fact: The gift was made by deed No. 4417 dated 12 March 2019, attested by a notary public and registered.
added_facts.reason: The question gives no instrument date. The ten-year limit runs from the date of execution of the deed, and a date after the commencement of the Act avoids any question whether the Act reaches deeds executed before it.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the deed had been executed more than ten years before the action, the court could not entertain it and the answer would be that revocation is time barred. If it had been executed before 2017, the separate and unresolved question whether the Act applies to earlier deeds would arise.

added_facts.fact: In June 2023 the donee assaulted the donor, causing injuries for which the donor was treated in hospital, and then locked the annexe and put the donor out of the premises; the donee does not deny the assault or the eviction.
added_facts.reason: The question states no default or misconduct. Revocation lies on one ground only, so conduct capable of being put to the court as gross ingratitude, and a date from which the cause of action runs, are needed for the scenario to be determinate.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Without misconduct by the donee there is no ground on which the action could be founded, and the answer would be that the deed stands.

added_facts.fact: The donor consults his lawyer in October 2023, wishing to recover the property; the donee refuses to reconvey it.
added_facts.reason: Fixes the date from which the two-year limit is measured against the June 2023 cause of action, and shows that the donor, not a third party, is the person seeking revocation.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the donor delayed beyond two years from June 2023, the court could not entertain the action even though the ten-year limit was still open.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: There shall be charged on- (a) every instrument relating to a transfer of situated in the immovable property Western Province;
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Provincial charging section. A Deed of Gift of a house and land at Maharagama is an instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province, so it is chargeable with stamp duty at the prescribed rate. The word order as printed in the corpus is transposed by OCR, but the sense is plain.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force long before the October 2022 matter date; the corpus records no amendment event on this section.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim in 6-1990/s37 and the section charges stamp duty at the prescribed rate on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property in the Western Province; the corpus text transposes the words 'situated in the immovable property Western Province' as OCR damage, and the reading relied on is the only sensible one.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: means a sale and shall include a gift or exchange or a conveyance, without consideration, by an executor or administrators of an estate of a deceased to a person beneficially entitled to such property
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The charge in s.37 bites on a transfer. The interpretation section defines Transfer to include a gift, so a Deed of Gift is within the charge even though no money passes. Without this definition the gratuitous deed would not obviously be dutiable.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force long before the October 2022 matter date; the corpus records no amendment event on this section.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (1) Where any property is conveyed by an instrument, the stamp duty with which such instrument is chargeable shall be calculated on the value of the property conveyed.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the base of the charge: duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, not on any consideration recited. This is what makes the value figure entered in the deed the operative amount.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force long before the October 2022 matter date; the corpus records no amendment event on this section.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (c) any immovable property which is gifted, being immovable property which was acquired by the donor after March 31, 1977 means - the price which, in the opinion ofthe Assessor, such property would have fetched if sold in the open market on the date which such on property was acquired by the donor, increased by an amount equal to the cost of the improvements, alterations and additions, if any, made to such property after the date on which the property was acquired by the donor,
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Definitive on the first limb of the statutory value of gifted immovable property acquired after 31 March 1977: the open market price at the date the donor acquired it, increased by the cost of improvements made after acquisition. The donor bought in December 1977, so paragraph (c), not paragraph (b), governs.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force long before the October 2022 matter date; the corpus records no amendment event on this section.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Verbatim; the corpus text of paragraph (c) has lost the '(i)' marker of the first limb through OCR, and the clean parallel in 43-1982/s71(c)(i) confirms the limb structure.

indispensable_provisions.subsection: definition of "value", paragraph (c), second limb and the lower-of rule
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: or (ii) the price which, in the opinion of the assessor, that property would have: fetched, if sold in the open market on the date of the instrument by which such property was gifted. whichever price is the lower.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Supplies the second limb (open market price at the date of the deed) and the decisive instruction that the lower of the two limbs is the statutory value. Without it the present valuation would be assumed to govern.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force long before the October 2022 matter date; the corpus records no amendment event on this section.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (2) Every notary public who attests an instrument of conveyance shall before doing SO take all reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the value on which the stamp duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Directly addresses what the attesting notary must do about the value figure: satisfy himself that the value on which duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed. Section 78(1) of the same section requires all facts affecting chargeability, and the amount of duty, to be set out in the instrument.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force long before the October 2022 matter date; the corpus records no amendment event on this section.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: includes conveyance on sale and every instrument by which property, or any interest in any property is transferred
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Added by the verifier. Section 48(1), which fixes the base of the charge, applies where property is 'conveyed by an instrument', while the charging section and the definition relied on by the researcher speak of a 'transfer'. The interpretation section defines conveyance to include every instrument by which property or an interest in property is transferred, which is what brings a Deed of Gift within s.48(1) and lets the statutory value operate as the base. Without it the step from the charge to the valuation rule is unbridged.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a Deed of Gift of a house and land in the Western Province is an instrument chargeable with stamp duty, a gift being gratuitous.
On what amount stamp duty on that deed is calculated: the price paid in 1977, that price plus the cost of improvements, or the present market value.
Which paragraph of the statutory definition of value applies where the donor acquired the property in December 1977, and how the two limbs of that paragraph are compared.
What figure the attesting notary must therefore set out in the deed.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What value should be stated in the Deed of Gift by which Rohan Perera gifts his Maharagama house and land to his son Wasantha, for the purpose of stamp duty, given that he bought the property in December 1977 for Rs.250,000/-, improved it at a cost of Rs.800,000/- and it is now worth Rs.6,500,000/-.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp duty is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province (Western Province Financial Statute s.37), and Transfer is defined by s.106 of that Statute to mean a sale and to include a gift, so a Deed of Gift is chargeable although nothing is paid for it. Section 48(1) provides that where property is conveyed by an instrument, the duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, so the operative figure is a statutory value and not the consideration. For gifted immovable property, value is defined in s.106. Where the donor acquired the property after 31 March 1977, paragraph (c) of that definition applies: value means the lower of (i) the price the property would have fetched in the open market on the date the donor acquired it, increased by the cost of improvements, alterations and additions made after acquisition and before the date of the gift instrument, and (ii) the price it would fetch in the open market on the date of that instrument. The national Act states the same rule for gifted land in Stamp Duty Act s.71, which continues to speak to instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property because Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.13 excepts such instruments from the displacement of the 1982 Act. Section 78(2) of the Western Province Financial Statute requires the attesting notary to take all reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the value on which the duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed, and s.78(1) requires the facts affecting chargeability and the amount of duty to be set out in the instrument.
gold_answer_draft.application: The land is at Maharagama in the Western Province and the instrument is a Deed of Gift, so s.37 read with the definition of Transfer in s.106 brings it into charge; no exemption in s.39 covers a gift from a father to his son. Duty is therefore calculated under s.48(1) on the value of the property conveyed. Rohan Perera acquired the property in December 1977, which is after 31 March 1977, so paragraph (c) of the definition of value applies and paragraph (b), which is pegged to a 31 March 1977 open market price, does not. The first limb is the open market price on the date he acquired the property, which on the facts given is the Rs.250,000/- he paid at arm's length in December 1977, increased by the Rs.800,000/- spent on the upper floor, garage and boundary wall, all of which were built after he acquired the property and before the proposed deed. That limb comes to Rs.1,050,000/-. The second limb is the open market price on the date of the instrument, which the valuation as at October 2022 puts at Rs.6,500,000/-. Paragraph (c) directs that whichever price is the lower is the value, and Rs.1,050,000/- is the lower of the two.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The value to be mentioned in the Deed of Gift for stamp duty purposes is Rs.1,050,000/-, being the Rs.250,000/- open market price at which Rohan Perera acquired the property in December 1977 together with the Rs.800,000/- cost of improvements made before the gift, that sum being lower than the present open market value of Rs.6,500,000/-. The attesting notary should satisfy himself that this figure represents the statutory value and set it out in the deed, and the figure remains open to the Assessor's own opinion of the open market prices at the two relevant dates.

answer_claims.claim_text: A Deed of Gift of immovable property situated in the Western Province is an instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property and is chargeable with stamp duty.
Transfer is defined to mean a sale and to include a gift, so the absence of consideration does not take a Deed of Gift out of the charge.
Where property is conveyed by an instrument, the stamp duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, not on any consideration recited.

For immovable property that is gifted and was acquired by the donor after 31 March 1977, value means the lower of (i) the open market price on the date of acquisition increased by the cost of improvements made after acquisition and before the date of the gift instrument, and (ii) the open market price on the date of that instrument.

The valuation rules of the Stamp Duty Act of 1982 continue to speak to instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property, because those instruments are excepted from the displacement of that Act by the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act.
No exemption covers a gift of land between a father and his son, so the deed is not exempt.
The property is at Maharagama in the Western Province, so the provincial charging and valuation provisions apply to the proposed deed.
Rohan Perera acquired the property in December 1977, which is after 31 March 1977, so paragraph (c) of the definition of value governs and paragraph (b) does not.
The first limb is Rs.250,000/- as the open market price at acquisition plus Rs.800,000/- for improvements made after acquisition and before the deed, that is Rs.1,050,000/-.
The second limb is Rs.6,500,000/-, the open market price of the property at the date of the deed.
Rs.1,050,000/- is the lower of the two limbs and is therefore the statutory value of the property gifted.

The value to be mentioned in the Deed of Gift for stamp duty purposes is Rs.1,050,000/-, and the attesting notary must take reasonable steps to satisfy himself that this figure represents the value of the property conveyed and must set out in the deed the facts affecting chargeability and the amount of duty.

enrichment.original_background: Rohan Perera purchased a house and property in December 1977 for Rs.250,000/-, and done improvements to the house to the value of Rs.800,000/-. The property is presently valued at Rs.6,500,000/-. He wishes to gift the said property to his son Wasantha.
enrichment.enriched_background:
Rohan Perera purchased a house and property in December 1977 for Rs.250,000/-, and done improvements to the house to the value of Rs.800,000/-. The property is presently valued at Rs.6,500,000/-. He wishes to gift the said property to his son Wasantha.

The property is Lot 12 depicted in Plan No. 2456 dated 3 March 1974 made by K. B. Wijesinghe, Licensed Surveyor, in extent fifteen decimal five perches, together with the two storeyed dwelling house bearing Assessment No. 47/3, Pathiragoda Road, Maharagama, within the Divisional Secretary's Division of Maharagama in the District of Colombo, Western Province. Rohan Perera bought it outright and at arm's length from an unrelated seller by Deed of Transfer No. 1187 dated 12 December 1977 attested by S. A. Dissanayake, Notary Public, and the Rs.250,000/- he paid was the open market price of the land and house on that date. The improvements costing Rs.800,000/- were an additional upper floor, a garage and a boundary wall, all built between 1996 and 1999, that is after he bought the property and before the deed he now proposes. He is the sole owner, the property is free of any mortgage or lease, and he intends an outright gift, keeping no life interest or other reservation for himself or anyone else. The Deed of Gift in favour of his son Wasantha Perera is to be executed at Colombo on 14 October 2022, and a valuation report dated 1 October 2022 by a chartered valuer puts the open market price of the property on that date at Rs.6,500,000/-.

added_facts.fact: The subject property is Lot 12 in Plan No. 2456 dated 3 March 1974, in extent fifteen decimal five perches, with the two storeyed dwelling house bearing Assessment No. 47/3, Pathiragoda Road, Maharagama, and Rohan Perera is its sole owner, the land being free of any mortgage or lease.
added_facts.reason: The question names no land at all. A definite lot, extent and assessment number make the subject of the deed identifiable without changing any element of the charge or the valuation.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: None on the outcome. A different lot number, extent or assessment number would not alter either the charge or the statutory value.

added_facts.fact: The property is situated at Maharagama in the District of Colombo, in the Western Province, and the Deed of Gift is to be executed at Colombo.
added_facts.reason: Stamp duty on the transfer of immovable property is levied province by province. Without a province the applicable charging statute is indeterminate; placing the land in the Western Province makes the governing enactment one that is present in the corpus.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the land lay in another province, the corresponding provincial statute would govern and the provincial provisions relied on here would not apply to it.

added_facts.fact: Rohan Perera acquired the property by Deed of Transfer No. 1187 dated 12 December 1977, bought outright and at arm's length from an unrelated seller, and the Rs.250,000/- he paid was the open market price of the land and house on that date.
added_facts.reason: The first limb of the statutory value is the open market price at the date of acquisition, not the price paid. Recording that the December 1977 purchase was at arm's length lets the Rs.250,000/- stand as the open market price on that date and makes the first limb computable.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the purchase had been at an undervalue between related parties, the open market price at acquisition would have to be assessed separately and the first limb would exceed Rs.250,000/- plus improvements.

added_facts.fact: The improvements costing Rs.800,000/- were an additional upper floor, a garage and a boundary wall, all built between 1996 and 1999, that is after the December 1977 purchase and before the proposed deed.
added_facts.reason: The first limb only admits improvements made after the donor acquired the property and before the date of the gift instrument. The original text does not date the improvements, so without this the Rs.800,000/- could not be added.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Had the improvements been made before Rohan Perera acquired the property, or after the date of the deed, the Rs.800,000/- could not be added to the first limb and that limb would be Rs.250,000/-.

added_facts.fact: The Deed of Gift in favour of Wasantha Perera is to be executed on 14 October 2022, and a valuation report dated 1 October 2022 puts the open market price of the property on that date at Rs.6,500,000/-.
added_facts.reason: The second limb is the open market price at the date of the gift instrument. Fixing the date of execution and tying the Rs.6,500,000/- to a valuation as at that date makes the second limb determinate and fixes the law to be applied.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the present valuation were as at some earlier date, the open market price at the date of the deed would have to be assessed afresh and the comparison between the two limbs could change.

added_facts.fact: The gift is outright: Rohan Perera reserves no life interest, no right of habitation and no other benefit for himself or for any other person, and imposes no fideicommissum.
added_facts.reason: Removes an open question about reservations. It is neutral because gifted property subject to a reservation is in any event valued as if gifted without the reservation.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: None on the value. A reserved life interest would not reduce the value on which duty is calculated.

legal_issues.issue: Whether ten years' undisturbed and uninterrupted adverse possession would satisfy the statutory conditions for prescriptive title to land.
Whether the Prescription Ordinance applies at all to a land parcel registered under the Registration of Title Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership.

Whether a person not named in the Title Register can assert an unregistered title against the registered owner, and whether the ten-year conversion route under the Registration of Title Act is open to such a person.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Nimal, a stranger in undisturbed and uninterrupted possession for more than ten years of a land parcel registered under the Registration of Title Act No. 21 of 1998 in another person's name with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, can claim prescriptive title to that parcel.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Prescriptive title to land rests on Prescription Ordinance s.3, which entitles a person to a decree on proof of ten years' undisturbed and uninterrupted possession by a title adverse to or independent of the owner's, unaccompanied by payment of rent or produce or by any act from which an acknowledgment of another's right would fairly be inferred. That Ordinance is withdrawn from land brought on to the Title Register: Registration of Title Act s.57 provides that the Prescription Ordinance shall not apply to lands or interests in land registered under that Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership or a Second Class Title of Ownership, and s.14 shows that these are the classes with which a claimant is declared eligible to be registered on initial compilation. Registration of Title Act s.73 gives that Act effect notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other written law, so the Prescription Ordinance cannot survive s.57 in this field. Alongside the exclusion, Registration of Title Act s.33(1) makes entries in the Title Register conclusive evidence of the ownership recorded and provides that they shall not be questioned in a court of law except as the Act provides, and s.38 denies entitlement to any title or interest in a registered land parcel unless that title or interest is itself registered. The only route by which ten years' possession improves a position under the Act is s.31(1), and it belongs to a person already registered with a Second Class Title of Ownership, who becomes eligible at the end of ten years from registration, absent an action under s.29, for conversion to a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership.
gold_answer_draft.application: The parcel Nimal occupies lies in a declared area and is registered under the Registration of Title Act, with Somapala entered in the Title Register as owner with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership since March 2009. Nimal's occupation from January 2011 to October 2021 is continuous, unaccompanied by rent or produce and free of any act of acknowledgment, so on its own terms it would answer the description in Prescription Ordinance s.3 and exceed the ten-year term. That does not assist him, because the parcel is land registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership and Registration of Title Act s.57 makes the Prescription Ordinance inapplicable to it; the rule he would invoke is simply not available for this land. Nor can he reach the same result by another statutory route. He is not named in the Title Register in any capacity, so under s.38 he is not entitled to any title or interest in the parcel, and under s.33(1) Somapala's registered ownership is conclusive and cannot be questioned in court except as the Act allows, which does not extend to a claim founded on adverse possession. The conversion right in s.31(1) is closed to him as well, since it presupposes registration with a Second Class Title of Ownership and Nimal has no registration at all.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: No. Nimal cannot claim prescriptive title. Because the parcel is registered under the Registration of Title Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, s.57 puts the Prescription Ordinance out of play, so no period of adverse possession, however long or however undisturbed, can ripen into title to it, and s.38 leaves him without entitlement while he remains off the register. This assumes the parcel was on the Title Register throughout the period relied on; if part of that possession ran before the land was brought under the Act, the position for that earlier period would need separate consideration.

answer_claims.claim_text: Section 3 of the Prescription Ordinance entitles a person to a decree on proof of ten years' undisturbed and uninterrupted possession of land by a title adverse to or independent of the owner's, unaccompanied by rent, produce, service or any act from which an acknowledgment of another's right would fairly be inferred.

On initial compilation under the Registration of Title Act a claimant is declared eligible for registration either with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership or, where he does not so qualify but is in bonafide possession, with a Second Class Title of Ownership.

Registration of Title Act s.57 provides that the Prescription Ordinance shall not apply to lands or interests in land registered under that Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership or a Second Class Title of Ownership.
The Registration of Title Act has effect notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other written law, so the Prescription Ordinance cannot operate against s.57.
Entries in the Title Register are conclusive evidence of the ownership specified in them and shall not be questioned in a court of law except as provided for in the Registration of Title Act.
No person acquiring an interest in a land parcel registered under the Registration of Title Act is entitled to that title or interest unless it is itself registered under the Act.

A person registered with a Second Class Title of Ownership becomes eligible, at the end of ten years from that registration and absent an action under s.29, for conversion of his registration to a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership.

Nimal's occupation from January 2011 to October 2021 was continuous, without payment of rent or produce and without any act of acknowledgment, so it would answer the description of adverse possession in Prescription Ordinance s.3 and exceed the ten-year term.

The parcel is land registered under the Registration of Title Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership in Somapala's name, so it falls within the exclusion in s.57 and the Prescription Ordinance does not apply to it.

Because Nimal is not named in the Title Register in any capacity, he is not entitled to any title or interest in the parcel, and Somapala's registered ownership is conclusive and not open to challenge in court on a ground the Act does not provide for.
The ten-year conversion right is not open to Nimal, because it presupposes an existing registration with a Second Class Title of Ownership and he holds no registration at all.

Nimal cannot claim prescriptive title to the parcel; no length of adverse possession of land registered under the Registration of Title Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership can ripen into title, and he remains without entitlement while he is off the register.

The conclusion assumes the parcel was on the Title Register throughout the period of possession relied on; possession running before the land was brought under the Act would need separate consideration.

enrichment.original_background: Nimal has been in possession of a land registered under Registration of Title Act for more than 10 years.
enrichment.enriched_background: Nimal, a retired schoolteacher of Pelawatta, has been in possession of a land registered under Registration of Title Act for more than 10 years. The land is Land Parcel No. 214 delineated on Cadastral Map No. 520150 for the village of Pelawatta in the Homagama Divisional Secretary's Division, an area the Minister declared by Order published in the Gazette to be an area to which the Registration of Title Act applies. The Title Register for that parcel records Somapala as the registered owner, registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership on 3 March 2009. Nimal's name appears nowhere in the Title Register, either as owner or under any registered interest, and he holds no deed, lease or grant in respect of the parcel. He entered into occupation of the parcel in January 2011 and has occupied it continuously and without interruption since then, paying no rent or produce to Somapala and doing nothing from which an acknowledgment of a right in Somapala could fairly be inferred. In October 2021 he wishes to assert ownership of the parcel against Somapala.

added_facts.fact: The land is Land Parcel No. 214 delineated on Cadastral Map No. 520150 for the village of Pelawatta in the Homagama Divisional Secretary's Division, an area declared by Order of the Minister published in the Gazette to be an area to which the Registration of Title Act applies.

added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the land lay outside any declared area it could not be registered under the Act at all, section 57 would not be engaged, and the ordinary ten-year prescription rule would govern.

added_facts.fact: The Title Register records Somapala as the registered owner of the parcel, registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership on 3 March 2009, and Nimal's name appears nowhere in the Title Register as owner or as the holder of any registered interest.

added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Were Nimal himself the person registered with a Second Class Title of Ownership, he would not need prescription at all: after ten years he would be eligible for conversion to a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership under section 31.

added_facts.fact: Nimal entered into occupation of the parcel in January 2011 and has occupied it continuously and without interruption to October 2021, paying no rent or produce to Somapala and doing nothing from which an acknowledgment of a right in Somapala could fairly be inferred.
added_facts.reason: Fixes the missing applicable time and makes the possession answer the description in section 3 of the Prescription Ordinance, so the question is squarely whether that section is available rather than whether its conditions are met.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the possession had been permissive, or accompanied by payment of rent or any acknowledgment, it would fail section 3 on its own terms and the section 57 point would never be reached.

added_facts.fact: Nimal is a retired schoolteacher of Pelawatta who is not a co-owner, lessee, manager or beneficiary in respect of the parcel and holds no deed, lease or grant to it.
added_facts.reason: Supplies the missing party identity and rules out the alternative capacities in which a person may appear on the Title Register, so his position is that of a stranger in possession.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If he held a registered interest such as a lease or a servitude, his rights would flow from that registered interest and the prescription question would not arise in this form.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (1) Where any property is conveyed by an instrument, the stamp duty with which such instrument is chargeable shall be calculated on the value of the property conveyed.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the base on which duty is calculated: the 'value' of the property conveyed. This is what sends the Assessor to the statutory definition of 'value' rather than to the consideration, the cost of construction or the current market price.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1990; corpus records no later change. In force at 2021-10.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (c) any immovable property which is gifted, being immovable property which was acquired by the donor after March 31, 1977 means - the price which, in the opinion ofthe Assessor, such property would have fetched if sold in the open market on the date which such on property was acquired by the donor, increased by an amount equal to the cost of the improvements, alterations and additions, if any, made to such property after the date on which the property was acquired by the donor, and prior to the date of the instrument by which such property is gifted ; or (ii) the price which, in the opinion of the assessor, that property would have: fetched, if sold in the open market on the date of the instrument by which such property was gifted. whichever price is the lower.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The operative definition. The donor acquired the Pannipitiya land in January 1978, that is after March 31, 1977, so paragraph (c) governs: the Assessor takes the lower of (i) the open-market price at the date of acquisition plus the cost of improvements made before the gift, and (ii) the open-market price at the date of the Deed of Gift. Paragraphs (a) and (b) are displaced - (a) excludes gifted immovable property, (b) applies only to property acquired on or before March 31, 1977.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Interpretation section in force from 1990; corpus records no later change. In force at 2021-10. The March 31, 1977 cut-off inside the definition is a fixed statutory date, not a commencement issue.
