legal_issues.issue: Whether a notary who does not himself know the executant may attest the deed when only one of the two attesting witnesses is well acquainted with the executant.
Whether an attesting witness who is the notary's own brother is disqualified from attesting, or bars the notary from attesting the deed.
Which text of rule (9) of section 31 governs a deed attested in October 2019, given the substitutions made in 2022 and 2024.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the notary may attest this deed of transfer when he does not himself know the executant, when only one of the two attesting witnesses is well acquainted with the executant, and when that witness is the notary's own brother.
gold_answer_draft.rule: At October 2019 rule (9) of section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance provided that a notary shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same be known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses thereto; those words are recited as the words replaced by section 16(6) of the Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 31 of 2022, and the replacing words, which allow identification by inspection of a national identity card, passport bio-page or driving licence, took effect only in 2022 and do not govern this deed. Where the notary relies on the witnesses rather than on his own knowledge, the same rule (9) requires him to satisfy himself, before accepting them as witnesses, that they are persons of good repute and that they are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation and residence, and requires the witnesses to sign a declaration at the foot of the deed to that effect; the requirement is stated of the witnesses in the plural, and rule (8) of section 31 requires at least two witnesses to subscribe their signatures in letters. Section 31 imposes only one personal bar on the notary himself: by rule (13) he shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which he is a party. No rule in section 31 disqualifies an attesting witness by reason of his relationship to the notary.
gold_answer_draft.application: The notary does not know Mr. Rajapaksha, so he can proceed only on the witness limb of rule (9), which needs the executant to be known to at least two of the attesting witnesses. Only the brother, Mr. P. A. Dharmasena, is well acquainted with Mr. Rajapaksha and able to state his proper name, occupation and residence; the second witness had never met him before that morning and cannot state his occupation or residence. The executant is therefore known to one attesting witness only, the notary cannot satisfy himself of the matters rule (9) requires as to both witnesses, and both witnesses cannot honestly sign the declaration at the foot of the deed. The identity-document route was not open in October 2019 and in any event no such document was produced. The brother relationship is a separate point and does not add a bar: rule (13) prevents the notary attesting only where he is a party, and he is not a party to or interested in this deed, while nothing in section 31 excludes a relative of the notary from signing as an attesting witness. The weight later given to his evidence is another matter, but the rules do not disqualify him.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary could not properly attest this deed as the facts stand, and the reason is the identification requirement rather than the family connection. The executant was neither known to the notary nor known to at least two of the attesting witnesses. The brother is not disqualified by being the notary's brother, so the defect is cured if a second witness who is of good repute and well acquainted with the executant, and able to state his proper name, occupation and residence, is brought in and both witnesses sign the required declaration at the foot of the deed; the notary may then attest.

answer_claims.claim_text: At the matter reference date a notary was forbidden to authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing it was known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses.

Identification of an executant by inspection of a national identity card, passport bio-page or driving licence was introduced into rule (9) only in 2022 and was not an available route in October 2019.

Where the notary relies on the attesting witnesses instead of his own knowledge, he must satisfy himself before accepting them that they are persons of good repute and are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation and residence, and the witnesses must sign a declaration at the foot of the deed to that effect.
At least two witnesses must subscribe their signatures in letters to the deed, so the acquaintance and declaration requirement applies to two or more attesting witnesses and not to one.

The only personal bar section 31 places on the notary is that he shall not authenticate or attest a deed or instrument to which he is a party, and no rule in section 31 disqualifies an attesting witness because he is related to the notary.
Because the notary does not know the executant, he can attest only on the footing that the executant is known to at least two of the attesting witnesses.

Only one of the two attesting witnesses, the notary's brother, is well acquainted with the executant and able to state his proper name, occupation and residence; the second witness had never met the executant and cannot state his occupation or residence.

The executant is therefore not known to at least two of the attesting witnesses, and the two witnesses cannot both sign the declaration that they are well acquainted with him and know his proper name, occupation and residence.
No identity document was produced, so even on the text that came into force after the matter reference date the identification limb would not be satisfied by inspection.

The notary is not a party to this deed and has no interest in the land, so the single personal bar in rule (13) is not engaged, and the brother is not disqualified from acting as an attesting witness by his relationship to the notary.
On these facts the notary could not properly attest the deed, because the executant was neither known to him nor known to at least two of the attesting witnesses.

The bar arises from the identification requirement and not from the fact that the acquainted witness is the notary's brother, so the notary may attest once a second witness of good repute who is well acquainted with the executant is brought in and both witnesses sign the required declaration.

enrichment.original_background: The Notary does not know the executant but he is well known to one of the witnesses. This witness is the Notary's own brother.
enrichment.enriched_background: Mr. K. A. Dharmasena is a notary public authorised to practise in Sinhala in the Colombo judicial zone. On 12 October 2019 Mr. Sunil Rajapaksha comes to his office and asks him to attest a deed of transfer, drawn by the notary himself, by which Mr. Rajapaksha transfers to Ms. Nirmali Fernando an allotment of land at Maharagama; Mr. Rajapaksha produces the title deed by which he bought the land. He brings two persons with him to sign as attesting witnesses. The Notary does not know the executant but he is well known to one of the witnesses. This witness is the Notary's own brother, Mr. P. A. Dharmasena, a retired schoolmaster of good repute who has lived next door to Mr. Rajapaksha for many years and can state his full name, his occupation and his address. The second witness is a clerk from the shop next to the notary's office who had never met Mr. Rajapaksha before that morning and cannot say what his occupation or his residence is. Mr. Rajapaksha produces no identity card, passport or driving licence. The notary is not a party to the deed and has no interest in the land.

added_facts.fact: The notary is Mr. K. A. Dharmasena, practising in Sinhala in the Colombo judicial zone; the executant is Mr. Sunil Rajapaksha; the transferee is Ms. Nirmali Fernando; the instrument is a deed of transfer of an allotment of land at Maharagama, presented for attestation on 12 October 2019, and the executant produces the title deed under which he bought the land.
added_facts.reason: The original scenario names no party, no instrument and no document, which are the three missing fact types recorded for this question. Naming them makes the scenario determinate without changing the legal question.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Without an identified deed and identified parties the attestation rules cannot be applied to a concrete instrument; the answer would be a statement of the rules in the abstract.

added_facts.fact: The witness who is the notary's brother, Mr. P. A. Dharmasena, is a retired schoolmaster of good repute, has lived next door to the executant for many years, and can state the executant's proper name, occupation and residence.
added_facts.reason: Makes the phrase well known to one of the witnesses precise in the terms the rule uses, so that this witness plainly satisfies the acquaintance requirement and the analysis turns on the second witness rather than on an ambiguity about the first.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If this witness were not of good repute or could not state the executant's name, occupation and residence, the deed would fail the acquaintance requirement on both witnesses rather than on one, and the reasoning would be shorter.

The rule turns on whether the executant is known to at least two attesting witnesses, so the standing of the second witness has to be settled for the question to have a determinate answer.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the second witness were also well acquainted with the executant and could state his name, occupation and residence, the identification requirement would be satisfied and the notary could attest.

added_facts.fact: The executant produces no national identity card, passport or driving licence to the notary.
added_facts.reason: Closes an alternative route that exists only under the text of rule (9) substituted in 2022. At the matter reference date of October 2019 identification by inspecting an identity document was not an available route, so the fact does not change the answer for this matter; it is added so that a reader working from the current consolidated text cannot mistake the scenario.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Under the rule as it stands after 2022 the production of an identity card would satisfy the identification limb; at the matter reference date it would make no difference.

added_facts.fact: The notary is not a party to the deed and has no interest in the land transferred.
added_facts.reason: The only personal bar the rules place on the notary is that he must not attest a deed to which he is a party. Stating that he is not a party keeps the brother point on its own footing instead of leaving that bar open.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the notary were a party to the deed he would be barred from attesting outright, and the identification point would not need to be reached.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Inheritance ab interstate to the immovable property in Sri Lanka of a person deceased shall be governed and regulated by the following provisions of this Ordinance wherever such person may have or have had his actual or matrimonial domicile.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The matter concerns immovable property in Colombo devolving on two intestacies. This is the gateway provision that makes Part III of the Ordinance the governing law for that devolution.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text applies to the deaths in 2014 and to the reference date 2019-04.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: When any person shall die intestate as to any of his or her property, leaving a spouse surviving, the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property of such person.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the half share of Kamal De Silva on Kanthi Perera's intestacy and the half share of Anura Fernando on Amali Perera's intestacy. Both deceased left a surviving spouse.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus. Applies to both deaths in 2014.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of the parents; all the children take equally per capita, but the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Gives Kanthi Perera's three surviving children, Amali, Anusha and Anuk, the half not taken by the surviving spouse, in equal per capita shares. It also confirms that a child of an earlier marriage takes equally with the children of the later marriage.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Father and mother both failing, the property of the intestate goes to his brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or balf-blood, and their children and other issue by representation.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Both of Amali Perera's parents predeceased her, so the half of her estate not taken by her surviving husband goes to her brothers and sisters. Anusha and Anuk are her half-blood siblings on the mother's side and are expressly included.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus. The corpus body carries the typographical error balf-blood for half-blood; the excerpt is reproduced exactly as it stands in the corpus.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: In case all the half-brothers and sisters, their children and remoter issue, are related to the intestate on one side only, they take the whole of the inheritance, unless there be a grandfather or grandmother or higher ascendant yet alive, related to the intestate on the other side
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Amali Perera left no full brother or sister; her only siblings were the two half-blood siblings on her mother's side. This section, not the split in s.27, governs and gives them the whole of the collateral half, subject to there being no surviving ascendant on her father's side.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Verbatim but the excerpt drops the opening qualifier 'Except when otherwise expressly provided,', which matters because ss.25, 26 and 27 expressly provide for taking by representation.

legal_issues.issue: What property formed part of Kanthi Perera's intestate estate at her death on 1st September 2014, given the 2005 gift of Lot 1 subject to a reserved life interest.
How Kanthi Perera's intestate estate devolves between her surviving husband Kamal De Silva and her three children Amali, Anusha and Anuk.
How Amali Perera's inherited share devolves on her death intestate and issueless about a month later, leaving a surviving husband, no living parent, and two half-blood siblings on her mother's side.
What effect the Administrator's Conveyance of 3rd December 2015 and Kamal De Silva's subsequent gift of his share to his two children have on the pedigree.

gold_answer_draft.issue: The pedigree has to trace the devolution of Kanthi Perera's intestate estate from her acquisition of the land in 1999 and 2000 down to the present owners. Three questions arise: what remained in her estate at her death on 1st September 2014, how that estate devolved on her surviving husband and her three children, and how Amali Perera's inherited share devolved when she died intestate and issueless about a month later.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance (s.21), which applies to the estate of a person who dies after the proclamation of the Ordinance and who was married after it (s.20), and which does not reach Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils subject to the Tesawalamai (s.2). A surviving spouse inherits one-half (s.22). Subject to that half, the inheritance passes first to descendants, then ascendants, then collaterals (s.23), and children are preferent to all others and take equally per capita (s.24). Where descendants fail, the estate goes to the parents, and only a surviving parent takes a half (s.25); where both parents have failed it goes to the brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or half blood (s.26). Where all the half-brothers and sisters are related to the intestate on one side only, they take the whole of that inheritance unless a grandparent or higher ascendant on the other side is alive (s.29), and persons equally near in degree take per capita (s.30).
gold_answer_draft.application: Kanthi Perera became entitled to Lot 3 of Plan No. 2131 by the Final Decree of 2nd December 1999 in DC Colombo case No. 523/P and to Lot 2 of the same plan by Deed of Transfer No. 456 of 6th February 2000, and she amalgamated and resubdivided the two into Lots 1, 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567 of 10th June 2001, each 20 perches. By Deed of Gift No. 1054 of 6th February 2005 she gifted Lot 1 to her daughter Amali Perera subject to her own life interest, so from 2005 Lot 1 no longer belonged to her and formed no part of her intestate estate, and her life interest in it ended at her death in any event. Her intestate estate on 1st September 2014 therefore consisted of Lots 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567. She left her husband Kamal De Silva surviving, so under s.22 he took one half. Under ss.23 and 24 the other half went in equal per capita shares to her three children, Amali of the earlier marriage and Anusha and Anuk of the marriage to Kamal De Silva, giving each of them one sixth. The Administrator's Conveyance of 3rd December 2015 in DC Colombo case No. 567/T conveyed the estate to those heirs and records, rather than creates, a devolution that took effect by operation of law at the death. Kamal De Silva then gifted his own one half to Anusha and Anuk, one quarter to each. Amali Perera died intestate and issueless about one month after her mother, leaving her husband Anura Fernando. Under s.22 he takes one half of her one sixth, that is one twelfth. Her descendants having failed and both her parents being dead, her mother on 1st September 2014 and her father after her marriage to Anura Fernando, s.25 gives nothing to a surviving parent and s.26 sends the other one twelfth to her brothers and sisters. Her only siblings are Anusha and Anuk, half blood on her mother's side, and on the footing that no grandparent or higher ascendant on her father's side survived her, s.29 gives them the whole of that share and s.30 divides it between them per capita, one twenty-fourth each.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The pedigree runs: Kanthi Perera, entitled under the Final Decree of 1999 and Deed of Transfer No. 456 of 2000 and holding Lots 1, 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567 from 2001, gifted Lot 1 away in 2005 by Deed of Gift No. 1054 and died intestate on 1st September 2014, whereupon Lots 2 and 3 devolved as to one half on Kamal De Silva and as to one sixth each on Amali Perera, Anusha and Anuk. Amali Perera then died intestate and issueless, her one sixth passing one twelfth to Anura Fernando and one twenty-fourth each to Anusha and Anuk. Kamal De Silva gifted his one half equally to Anusha and Anuk. The present owners are therefore Anusha and Anuk with eleven twenty-fourths each and Anura Fernando with two twenty-fourths, that is one twelfth. This is subject to the family being governed by the general law and to no ascendant of Amali Perera on her father's side having survived her; the scenario states neither expressly.

answer_claims.claim_text: Inheritance ab intestato to the immovable property in Sri Lanka of a deceased person is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, which applies to persons dying after its proclamation who were married after it and which does not extend to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils subject to the Tesawalamai.
A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of a person who dies intestate.
Subject to the surviving spouse's half, inheritance passes first to descendants, and children are preferent to all others and take equally per capita.
Where the descendants fail and both parents of the intestate are dead, the estate goes to the brothers and sisters of the intestate, whether of the whole or half blood.

Where all the half-brothers and sisters are related to the intestate on one side only they take the whole of that inheritance, unless a grandparent or higher ascendant on the other side is alive, and those equally near in degree take per capita.

Kanthi Perera's intestate estate consisted of Lots 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567, because Lot 1 had passed to Amali Perera by Deed of Gift No. 1054 of 2005 and Kanthi Perera's reserved life interest in it ended at her death.
On Kanthi Perera's death intestate on 1st September 2014 her surviving husband Kamal De Silva took one half of Lots 2 and 3.
The remaining half went in equal shares to Kanthi Perera's three children Amali, Anusha and Anuk, so each took one sixth of Lots 2 and 3.

The Administrator's Conveyance of 3rd December 2015 in DC Colombo case No. 567/T conveyed the estate to those heirs and records a devolution that had already taken effect by operation of law at the death.
Amali Perera died intestate and issueless about one month after her mother, leaving her husband Anura Fernando, who took one half of her one sixth, namely one twelfth of Lots 2 and 3.

Both of Amali Perera's parents having predeceased her and her only siblings being Anusha and Anuk of the half blood on her mother's side, and on the footing that no ascendant on her father's side survived her, the other one twelfth went to Anusha and Anuk per capita, one twenty-fourth each.
Kamal De Silva gifted the one half he had inherited to his two children Anusha and Anuk, giving each of them a further one quarter.
The pedigree ends with Anusha and Anuk holding eleven twenty-fourths each and Anura Fernando holding one twelfth of Lots 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567.

enrichment.original_background: By a Final Decree dated 2nd December 1999 entered in DC Colombo Partition case No. 523/P, premises bearing Assessment No. 35, Sarasavi Lane Colombo 3 depicted as Lot 3 in Plan No. 2131 dated 12th June 1998 made by Lal Peiris Licensed Surveyor in extent of 30 perches was allotted to Kanthi Perera. She purchased Lot 2 in extent of 30 perches of the said Plan from her brother Wimal Perera by Deed of Transfer 456 dated 6th February 2000 attested Sarath Wickremasinghe Notary Public Colombo. Kanthi Perera amalgamated the said 2 lots and caused to be subdivided into 3 lots depicted as Lot 1,2 and 3 (bearing Assessment Nos. 35/1, 35/2 and 35/3 respectively) in Plan No.567 dated 10th June 2001 made by the same surveyor each containing in extent 20 perches. Mrs Kanthi Perera gifted Lot 1 thereof to Amali Perera a minor who was 16 years old, her daughter from a previous marriage by Deed of Gift No. 1054 dated 6th February 2005 attested by Jagath Perera Notary Public subject to her life interest. In 2013 she sold this property. Mrs Kanthi Perera died intestate on 1st September 2014. Her estate was administered in DC Colombo case No. 567/T and her husband Kamal De Silva was appointed as Administrator. Proceedings of this case was terminated on 6th November 2015. Kanthi had two children out of her marriage to Kamal De Silva namely Anusha and Anuk. Kamal De silva wrote an Administrators Conveyance on 3rd December 2015 and passed the title of Kanthi Perera's intestate Estate to her heirs. Thereafter he gifted his share of the Estate to his two children. Amali Perea was living with his father and after her marriage to Anura Fernando he passed away. Amali met with an accident after one month of her mothers death and died intestate and issueless.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Inheritance ab interstate to the immovable property in Sri Lanka of a person deceased shall be governed and regulated by the following provisions of this Ordinance wherever such person may have or have had his actual or matrimonial domicile.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The matter concerns immovable property in Colombo devolving on two intestacies. This is the gateway provision that makes Part III of the Ordinance the governing law for that devolution.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text applies to the deaths in 2014 and to the reference date 2019-04.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: When any person shall die intestate as to any of his or her property, leaving a spouse surviving, the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property of such person.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the half share of Kamal De Silva on Kanthi Perera's intestacy and the half share of Anura Fernando on Amali Perera's intestacy. Both deceased left a surviving spouse.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus. Applies to both deaths in 2014.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of the parents; all the children take equally per capita, but the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Gives Kanthi Perera's three surviving children, Amali, Anusha and Anuk, the half not taken by the surviving spouse, in equal per capita shares. It also confirms that a child of an earlier marriage takes equally with the children of the later marriage.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Father and mother both failing, the property of the intestate goes to his brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or balf-blood, and their children and other issue by representation.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Both of Amali Perera's parents predeceased her, so the half of her estate not taken by her surviving husband goes to her brothers and sisters. Anusha and Anuk are her half-blood siblings on the mother's side and are expressly included.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus. The corpus body carries the typographical error balf-blood for half-blood; the excerpt is reproduced exactly as it stands in the corpus.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: In case all the half-brothers and sisters, their children and remoter issue, are related to the intestate on one side only, they take the whole of the inheritance, unless there be a grandfather or grandmother or higher ascendant yet alive, related to the intestate on the other side
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Amali Perera left no full brother or sister; her only siblings were the two half-blood siblings on her mother's side. This section, not the split in s.27, governs and gives them the whole of the collateral half, subject to there being no surviving ascendant on her father's side.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: if all those who succeed to the inheritance are equally near in degree to the intestate, they take per capita, and not per stirpes.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Anusha and Anuk are equally near in degree to Amali Perera, so the collateral half is divided between them per capita and not by representation.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Verbatim but the excerpt drops the opening qualifier 'Except when otherwise expressly provided,', which matters because ss.25, 26 and 27 expressly provide for taking by representation.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Subject to the right of the surviving spouse in the preceding section mentioned, the right of inheritance is divided in the following order as respects (a) descendants, (b) ascendants, (c) collaterals.

legal_issues.issue: What fractions of Lots 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567 each heir took on Kanthi Perera's intestacy.
How Amali Perera's one sixth was redistributed on her own intestacy between her surviving husband and her half-blood siblings.
What each heir owns today once Kamal De Silva's gift of his inherited half to Anusha and Anuk is taken into account.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What share of the property each heir presently owns. The property in question is Lots 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567, which is what remained of Kanthi Perera's holding after Lot 1 had been gifted away in 2005 and disposed of in 2013.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of an intestate (Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.22). Subject to that half, descendants come first and children take equally per capita (ss.23 and 24). Where descendants fail and both parents are dead, the estate goes to the brothers and sisters of the intestate whether of the whole or half blood (ss.25 and 26); where all the half-blood siblings are related on one side only they take the whole of that share unless an ascendant on the other side survives (s.29), and persons equally near in degree take per capita (s.30). Inheritance to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by these provisions (s.21), which apply to these estates (ss.2 and 20).
gold_answer_draft.application: On Kanthi Perera's death intestate on 1st September 2014, Kamal De Silva took one half of Lots 2 and 3 as surviving spouse, and Amali, Anusha and Anuk took the other half in equal shares, one sixth each. Amali Perera died about a month later, intestate and issueless, leaving her husband Anura Fernando; he took one half of her one sixth, that is one twelfth. Her descendants having failed and both her parents being dead, the other one twelfth passed to her brother and sister of the half blood on her mother's side, Anusha and Anuk, per capita, one twenty-fourth each, on the footing that no ascendant on her father's side survived her. Kamal De Silva then gifted the one half he had inherited to Anusha and Anuk, one quarter to each. Adding the three sources for each of them, Anusha holds one quarter by gift, one sixth by inheritance from her mother and one twenty-fourth from Amali Perera, that is six, four and one twenty-fourths, or eleven twenty-fourths; Anuk holds the same eleven twenty-fourths; and Anura Fernando holds two twenty-fourths. The three shares total twenty-four twenty-fourths.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Of Lots 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567, Anusha owns eleven twenty-fourths, Anuk owns eleven twenty-fourths and Anura Fernando owns one twelfth, that is two twenty-fourths. Kamal De Silva retains nothing, having gifted his half away. These shares assume the family is governed by the general law and that no ascendant of Amali Perera on her father's side survived her. Lot 1 is left out of account because it had been gifted to Amali Perera in 2005 and the scenario states that it was sold in 2013; the scenario does not make clear who sold it, and if only the reserved life interest was in fact sold, Lot 1 would have fallen into Amali Perera's estate and would now be held one half by Anura Fernando and one quarter each by Anusha and Anuk.

answer_claims.claim_text: A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of a person dying intestate.
Subject to the spouse's half, the children of the intestate are preferent to all others and take equally per capita.

Where descendants fail and both parents are dead the estate goes to the brothers and sisters of the whole or half blood, half-blood siblings related on one side only take the whole of that share absent an ascendant on the other side, and those equally near in degree take per capita.
On Kanthi Perera's intestacy Kamal De Silva took one half of Lots 2 and 3 and Amali, Anusha and Anuk took one sixth each.
Amali Perera's one sixth devolved one twelfth on her husband Anura Fernando and one twenty-fourth on each of Anusha and Anuk.
Kamal De Silva's gift of his inherited half to Anusha and Anuk added one quarter to each of them.
Anusha and Anuk each presently own eleven twenty-fourths of Lots 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567 and Anura Fernando owns one twelfth, Kamal De Silva retaining nothing.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Where it is shown to the satisfaction of the Registrar-General that any error or omission has been made in registering any instrument, whether before or after the commencement of this Ordinance, the Registrar-General shall issue notice in writing in the prescribed form (a) in the case of a deed to the parties thereto; or (b) in the case of a will to the executor or administrator, as the case may be; or (c) in the case of any other instrument to the person who presented it for registration, and order such error or omission to be corrected
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the operative correction power. It fixes the first three steps of the procedure: the error must be shown to the satisfaction of the Registrar-General, who then issues written notice in the prescribed form to the parties to the deed (Deed No. 351), and orders the correction. Registering the sub-divided Lot 3A in the parent folio Vol/Folio A 350/25 is an error or omission made in registering an instrument.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Subsection (1) was repealed and re-substituted by section 3 of the Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act, No. 50 of 1982; the consolidated corpus text is that substituted text and it is the text in force in October 2018. No later amendment in the corpus (Nos. 5 of 1990, 21 of 2013, 32 of 2022, 18 of 2024) touches section 35.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: and order such error or omission to be corrected and the correction shall then be made by the Registrar concerned in the prescribed manner, but shall not affect any priority accrued before the correction is made
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the last two steps: after the Registrar-General's order the correction is made by the Registrar concerned (here the Registrar of Lands, Homagama) in the prescribed manner, and it does not disturb any priority that accrued before it. Without this the procedure is incomplete and the effect of the correction on priority is unstated.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Same 1982 substituted text as PROV-M098-001; in force at the matter reference date of October 2018.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Every instrument presented for registration shall be registered in the book allotted to the division in which the land affected by the instrument is situated and in the folio in which 1974] the first registered instrument affecting the same land is registered, or in another folio (whether of the same volume or of another volume) bearing a separate number, opened in continuation thereof, cross reference being entered in the prescribed manner so as to connect the said folios
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Supplies the standard that was breached and so identifies what the error is. It is what makes the registration of the divided Lot 3A in the parent folio of Lot 3 wrong: the sub-divided lot should have been carried to a separate folio opened in continuation, connected by cross reference. Without it the assertion that there is an error in registering has no statutory support.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Amended by Act No. 14 of 1974; the corpus consolidated text carries the 1974 wording (the stray '1974]' marker is an artefact of the consolidated source). In force at October 2018.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Wording, role and 1974 dating confirmed, but the excerpt carries a stray '1974]' marker from the consolidated source that is absent from the substituting text in 14-1974/s.2, so the excerpt should not be reproduced as the clean statutory wording.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Provided that the Registrar-General may with like effect make such an order for the correction of any error or omission made in registering any such instrument if it is proved to his satisfaction by any person interested that by reason of the death or legal incapacity of any person or party to whom notice is required to be issued as aforesaid or for any other sufficient cause whatsoever, such notice cannot be issued.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Supplies the alternative route where notice to a party to Deed No. 351 cannot be issued. Supporting rather than indispensable, because the facts do not state that any party has died or is incapacitated, but a complete statement of the procedure should note it.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Same 1982 substituted text; in force at October 2018.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (a) an instrument may, if the Registrar thinks fit, be entered in a new folio, cross references being entered in the prescribed manner so as to connect the registration with any previous registration affecting the same land or any part thereof
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Shows the form the corrected registration should take: a new folio for Lot 3A with cross references back to Vol/Folio A 350/25. Supporting, because the corrective act itself is ordered under section 35.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Part of the section 14 text in force at October 2018.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: An instrument, whether registered before or after the commencement of this Ordinance, shall not be deemed to be duly registered under this Chapter unless it is registered in accordance with the foregoing provisions of this section.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Explains why the mis-folioed registration must be put right rather than left alone: registration otherwise than in accordance with section 14 is not due registration, so the chain of registration for Lot 3A is defective until corrected.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force at October 2018.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: The Registrar-General may, if he thinks fit. exercise all or any of the powers possessed by a Registrar.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Identifies the officers named in section 35, the Registrar-General of Lands and the Registrar of the division (Homagama), and confirms the Registrar-General's own competence over registration acts. Contextual support for who the application is addressed to.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force at October 2018; subsection (7) also permits a Deputy or Assistant Registrar-General to act.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Section 2(6) is verbatim and does allow the Registrar-General to exercise a Registrar's powers, but it is section 2(2), not 2(6), that constitutes the offices of Registrar-General and Registrar; the why_relevant over-reads the subsection.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: The Minister may make regulations, to be published in the Gazette, as to any matter which by this Ordinance may or is to be prescribed and generally for regulating the forms to be used and the procedure and practice to be observed in carrying this Ordinance into effect.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Section 35 twice defers to what is prescribed: the form of the notice and the manner of correction. This section is the source of that prescription, so it locates the detailed procedural steps outside the Ordinance itself.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force at October 2018. The regulations made under it are not in the frozen corpus.

legal_issues.issue: Whether registering the divided Lot 3A in Vol/Folio A 350/25, the folio of the parent Lot 3, is an error or omission made in registering an instrument within section 35(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance.
What steps the Registration of Documents Ordinance requires to have that registration corrected, and which officer takes each step.
What effect the correction has on priorities accrued before it, and what happens where notice to a party to Deed No. 351 cannot be issued.

gold_answer_draft.issue: By what procedure under the Registration of Documents Ordinance can the wrongful registration of the divided Lot 3A in Vol/Folio A 350/25, the folio of the parent Lot 3, be corrected, so that instruments affecting Lot 3A, including the lease to Nimal Fernando, can be duly registered?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Registration of Documents Ordinance s.14(1) requires every instrument to be registered in the book allotted to the division in which the land lies and in the folio in which the first registered instrument affecting the same land is registered, or in another folio bearing a separate number opened in continuation of it, with cross references entered in the prescribed manner to connect the folios; proviso (a) allows the Registrar, if he thinks fit, to enter an instrument in a new folio with cross references to any previous registration affecting the same land or any part of it. By s.14(2) an instrument is not deemed duly registered unless it is registered in accordance with s.14. Where it is shown to the satisfaction of the Registrar-General that any error or omission has been made in registering any instrument, s.35(1) requires the Registrar-General to issue notice in writing in the prescribed form, in the case of a deed to the parties to it, and to order the error or omission to be corrected; the correction is then made by the Registrar concerned in the prescribed manner, but does not affect any priority accrued before the correction is made. The proviso to s.35(1) allows the Registrar-General to make the same order on proof by any person interested where, by reason of death, legal incapacity or any other sufficient cause, that notice cannot be issued. The form of the notice and the manner of the correction are prescribed by regulation under s.49 and by the forms in the Second Schedule under s.50, and by s.2(6) the Registrar-General may himself exercise a Registrar's powers.
gold_answer_draft.application: Lot 3A is a divided and defined portion of Lot 3, carved out by Plan No. 255 of 8/12/2000 and conveyed to Dininda Perera by Deed No. 351. Under s.14(1) the registration of Deed No. 351 should have been carried to a folio bearing a separate number opened in continuation of Vol/Folio A 350/25 and connected to it by cross reference, or under proviso (a) to a new folio with cross references; entering it in the parent folio of Lot 3 itself is therefore not registration in accordance with s.14, and by s.14(2) it is not due registration. That is an error or omission made in registering an instrument for the purposes of s.35(1), and it is the reason the Land Registry says the lease cannot be registered. The procedure is administrative. A person interested, Dininda Perera as proprietor of Lot 3A or the party who presented the lease, applies in writing to the Registrar-General of Lands through the Homagama Land Registry, setting out the error and producing the material that shows it: Deed No. 351, Plan No. 251 and Plan No. 255, and a certified extract of Vol/Folio A 350/25. If the error is shown to the Registrar-General's satisfaction, s.35(1) obliges him to issue notice in writing in the prescribed form; because the instrument concerned is a deed, notice goes to the parties to Deed No. 351, that is the vendor and Dininda Perera, and he orders the error to be corrected. If a party cannot be noticed because of death, legal incapacity or any other sufficient cause, the proviso lets the Registrar-General make the order on proof to his satisfaction by any person interested. On that order the Registrar of Lands, Homagama, makes the correction in the prescribed manner, carrying the registration of Lot 3A to a separate folio opened in continuation of, and cross referenced to, Vol/Folio A 350/25. By the closing words of s.35(1) the correction does not affect any priority accrued before it is made, so it cannot prejudice interests already ranked in the old folio. Once the folio is corrected the lease to Nimal Fernando can be presented again for registration in the folio of Lot 3A. If instead the Registrar makes a formal order refusing registration, a separate route exists in s.38(1), an appeal to the Registrar-General within thirty days, but that addresses the refusal and not the folio error.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The error is corrected administratively under the Registration of Documents Ordinance and not by court order. An interested party applies to the Registrar-General of Lands showing the error; on being satisfied, the Registrar-General issues notice in the prescribed form to the parties to Deed No. 351 and orders the correction under s.35(1); the Registrar of Lands, Homagama, then makes the correction in the prescribed manner by carrying the registration of Lot 3A into a separate folio cross referenced to Vol/Folio A 350/25 as s.14(1) requires; and the correction leaves untouched any priority that accrued before it was made. The lease can then be presented for registration in the corrected folio.

answer_claims.claim_text: An instrument affecting land must be registered in the folio in which the first registered instrument affecting the same land is registered, or in another folio bearing a separate number opened in continuation of it, with cross references entered in the prescribed manner.
An instrument is not deemed duly registered unless it is registered in accordance with section 14.

Where an error or omission in registering an instrument is shown to the satisfaction of the Registrar-General, he must issue written notice in the prescribed form, in the case of a deed to the parties to the deed, and order the error to be corrected.
The correction is then made by the Registrar concerned in the prescribed manner and does not affect any priority accrued before the correction is made.

Where notice to a party cannot be issued because of death, legal incapacity or any other sufficient cause, the Registrar-General may make the same correction order on proof to his satisfaction by any person interested.
The prescribed form of the notice and the prescribed manner of correction are fixed by regulation and by the forms in the Second Schedule, not by section 35 itself.

Because Lot 3A is a divided portion of Lot 3 depicted in Plan No. 255, the registration of Deed No. 351 belonged in a separate folio opened in continuation of, and cross referenced to, Vol/Folio A 350/25 rather than in that folio itself.
Registering the sub division of Lot 3A in the parent folio Vol/Folio A 350/25 is therefore an error or omission made in registering an instrument for the purposes of section 35(1).

A person interested, such as Dininda Perera or the party who presented the lease, must first apply to the Registrar-General of Lands through the Homagama Land Registry and show the error to his satisfaction, producing Deed No. 351, Plan No. 251, Plan No. 255 and an extract of Vol/Folio A 350/25.
The Registrar-General, if satisfied, issues notice in the prescribed form to the parties to Deed No. 351, namely the vendor and Dininda Perera, and orders the correction.

The Registrar of Lands, Homagama, then carries the registration of Lot 3A into a separate folio cross referenced to Vol/Folio A 350/25, without disturbing priorities accrued before the correction, after which the lease to Nimal Fernando can be presented again for registration.

The correction is obtained administratively under section 35(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, by application to the Registrar-General, notice in the prescribed form to the parties to the deed, an order to correct, and correction by the Registrar concerned in the prescribed manner, and no court order is required.

enrichment.original_background: Lot 3 of the land called Mahatenna in extent of 30 perches in Plan No. 251 dated 5/7/1999 made by A.Samaranayaka Liscensed Surveyor is registered in the Homagama Land Registry under Vol/Folio A 350/25. The owner, sub divided Lot 3 into 2 lots namely Lots 34 and 3B as depicted in Plan No.255 dated 8/12/2000 made by the same Surveyor. legal_issues.issue: Which law governs the intestate devolution of Nimal's interest in the divided lots, and does it apply to this family?
What did Nimal own at his death, given the 1996 Final Decree allotment and the 1998 purchase of Aruni's share?
How is Nimal's estate split between his surviving spouse Nalini and his children, and does Achini, his daughter by a first wife, share in it?
Who inherits Nalini's estate, and is Achini included among her heirs?
How does the share of Bimal, who died issueless leaving a widow and with both parents predeceased, devolve between his widow, his full siblings and his half-sister?

gold_answer_draft.issue: How did Nimal's half share of divided lots 6 and 7 devolve on his intestate death and on the successive intestate deaths of his widow Nalini and his son Bimal, so that a pedigree from Nimal to the present owners can be drawn?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Intestate succession to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.21(1), the lots being immovable property within s.3. The Ordinance applies here because none of the exclusions in s.2 (Kandyan, Muslim, Thesawalamai) is disclosed, and the s.20 condition is met since every death and marriage in question post-dates the 1876 proclamation. On each intestacy the surviving spouse first takes one-half of the estate (s.22). Subject to that half, the right of inheritance runs in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals (s.23). Children take equally per capita and the issue of a deceased child take per stirpes (s.24), and heirs equally near in degree take per capita (s.30). Where descendants fail, the estate goes to the parents (s.25); where both parents have also failed, it goes to the brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or half blood (s.26). Where the half-siblings are on one side only, s.27 directs that the full siblings take one half of that portion first and divide the other half with the half-siblings.
gold_answer_draft.application: Step 1 - Nimal's holding. Under the Final Decree of 21 August 1996 Nimal was allotted 5/12 of lots 6 and 7, and by Deed of Transfer No. 346 of 6 June 1998 he bought Aruni's 1/12. At his death he therefore held 5/12 + 1/12 = 6/12, that is a half share of the land. Sunil's 5/12 and Kusum's 1/12 are untouched by the deaths and remain with them. Step 2 - Nimal's intestacy, 23 April 2008. He left his widow Nalini and four children: Achini (by his first wife Malini), Amal, Bimal and Krishni. Nalini takes one-half of his estate under s.22, which is 1/4 of the land. Under ss.23, 24 and 30 the other half, also 1/4 of the land, is shared equally per capita among the four children, giving each child 1/16 of the land. Step 3 - Nalini's intestacy, within a year of April 2008. Her estate is the 1/4 she took from Nimal. Nimal had predeceased her, so there is no surviving spouse to take under s.22, and the whole estate passes to her descendants under ss.23, 24 and 30. Her children are Amal, Bimal and Krishni only; Achini is Nimal's daughter by Malini and is not a descendant of Nalini, so she takes nothing from this estate. Each of the three takes 1/4 divided by 3, that is 1/12 of the land. Immediately after this Amal, Bimal and Krishni each hold 1/16 + 1/12 = 7/48 of the land and Achini holds 1/16. Step 4 - Bimal's death, 4 March 2010, married to Amali and issueless. On the footing that he too died intestate, his estate of 7/48 devolves as follows. Amali takes one-half under s.22, that is 7/96 of the land. The remaining 7/96 must pass down the s.23 order: Bimal left no descendants, and under s.25 it would go to his parents, but both Nimal and Nalini were already dead, so under s.26 it goes to his brothers and sisters of the whole and half blood. Amal and Krishni are of the full blood; Achini is a half-sister on the father's side and there is no half-sibling on the mother's side. Section 27 therefore applies in its final limb: Amal and Krishni first take one half of the 7/96, that is 7/192, in equal shares of 7/384 each, and the other 7/192 is divided per capita among Amal, Krishni and Achini under ss.27 and 30, giving each of them 7/576. So from Bimal's estate Amal takes 7/384 + 7/576 = 35/1152, Krishni takes the same 35/1152, Achini takes 7/576 = 14/1152 and Amali takes 7/96 = 84/1152.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The pedigree runs: Nimal (holder of 6/12 of lots 6 and 7, being 5/12 under the Final Decree of 1996 plus 1/12 bought from Aruni by Deed No. 346 of 1998) died intestate on 23 April 2008 leaving his widow Nalini and four children, Achini (by his first wife Malini), Amal, Bimal and Krishni; Nalini took one-half of his estate and the four children the other half in equal shares. Nalini then died intestate within a year, and her share passed in equal shares to her own three children Amal, Bimal and Krishni, Achini being excluded as not her descendant. Bimal, married to Amali, then died on 4 March 2010 issueless and, on the footing that he died intestate, his share passed one-half to Amali as surviving spouse and the other half to his siblings, both parents having predeceased him: his full siblings Amal and Krishni taking one half of that portion between them and sharing the remaining half with his paternal half-sister Achini. The present owners of Nimal's half share are therefore Amal, Krishni, Achini and Amali, alongside the original co-owners Sunil and Kusum who are unaffected.

answer_claims.claim_text: Intestate inheritance to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.21(1), whatever the deceased's domicile, and the divided lots are immovable property within s.3.

The Ordinance's inheritance sections do not apply to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils of the Northern Province subject to the Thesawalamai, and apply only to estates of persons dying after the 1876 proclamation who were then unmarried or married after it.
A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of a person who dies intestate.
Subject to the surviving spouse's half, the right of inheritance runs in the order descendants, then ascendants, then collaterals.
Children are preferent to all others in a parent's estate and take equally per capita, and heirs equally near in degree take per capita and not per stirpes.
Where an intestate leaves no descendants the estate goes to the parents, and where both parents have also failed it goes to the brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or half blood.
Where there are half-siblings on one side only, the full brothers and sisters take one half of the sibling portion in the first place and divide the other half with the half-siblings.
Nimal held 6/12 (a half share) of lots 6 and 7 at his death: 5/12 under the Final Decree of 21 August 1996 plus the 1/12 bought from Aruni by Deed of Transfer No. 346 of 6 June 1998.
On Nimal's intestate death on 23 April 2008 his widow Nalini took one-half of his estate and his four children Achini, Amal, Bimal and Krishni took the other half in equal shares.

On Nalini's intestate death within a year her share passed wholly to her descendants, namely her three children Amal, Bimal and Krishni in equal shares; Achini, being Nimal's daughter by Malini and not a descendant of Nalini, took nothing from Nalini's estate.

Bimal died on 4 March 2010 married to Amali and issueless, so his descendants failed; both his parents had already died, so no ascendant survived and his estate passed to his collaterals after his widow's half.

Bimal's siblings were his full brother Amal and full sister Krishni and his paternal half-sister Achini, with no half-sibling on the mother's side, so the full siblings took one half of the sibling portion first and shared the other half with Achini.

The pedigree of Nimal's half share is: Nimal, died intestate 23 April 2008, leaving widow Nalini (one-half) and children Achini, Amal, Bimal and Krishni (one-half between them); Nalini, died intestate within a year, leaving her share to Amal, Bimal and Krishni; Bimal, died 4 March 2010 issueless, leaving his share one-half to his widow Amali and one-half to his siblings Amal, Krishni and Achini in the proportions fixed by section 27.
The present owners of the land are Sunil and Kusum, whose original shares are unaffected, together with Amal, Krishni, Achini and Amali as the heirs in Nimal's line.
The final step of the pedigree assumes that Bimal died intestate, which the scenario does not state expressly, and that Achini was born of a lawful marriage between Nimal and Malini.

enrichment.original_background: By a Final Decree dated 21 August 1996 entered in District Court Galle in Partition case No.2367/P Nimal, Sunil, Aruni and Kusum were allotted with 5/12th,5/12th, 1/12th and 1/12th shares respectively from and out of divided and defined lots 6 and 7 in Partition Plan No.185 dated 23rd June 1995 made by J.W. de Silva Licensed Surveyor By Deed of Transfer. No.346 dated 6th June 1998 attested by Ranjith Perera Notary Public Nimal purchased the 1/12th share of Aruni. Nimal was married to Nalini and had 3 children namely Amal, Bimal and Krishni. Nimal had a daughter named Achini by his first wife Malini, Nimal died intestate on 23rd April 2008. Within a year thereafter Nalini too died intestate. Nimal's son Bimal who was married to Amali died on 4th of March 2010 having met with an accident and issueless.

Where the half-siblings are on one side only, s.27 directs that the full siblings take one half of that portion first and divide the other half with the half-siblings.
gold_answer_draft.application: Step 1 - Nimal's holding. Under the Final Decree of 21 August 1996 Nimal was allotted 5/12 of lots 6 and 7, and by Deed of Transfer No. 346 of 6 June 1998 he bought Aruni's 1/12. At his death he therefore held 5/12 + 1/12 = 6/12, that is a half share of the land. Sunil's 5/12 and Kusum's 1/12 are untouched by the deaths and remain with them. Step 2 - Nimal's intestacy, 23 April 2008. He left his widow Nalini and four children: Achini (by his first wife Malini), Amal, Bimal and Krishni. Nalini takes one-half of his estate under s.22, which is 1/4 of the land. Under ss.23, 24 and 30 the other half, also 1/4 of the land, is shared equally per capita among the four children, giving each child 1/16 of the land. Step 3 - Nalini's intestacy, within a year of April 2008. Her estate is the 1/4 she took from Nimal. Nimal had predeceased her, so there is no surviving spouse to take under s.22, and the whole estate passes to her descendants under ss.23, 24 and 30. Her children are Amal, Bimal and Krishni only; Achini is Nimal's daughter by Malini and is not a descendant of Nalini, so she takes nothing from this estate. Each of the three takes 1/4 divided by 3, that is 1/12 of the land. Immediately after this Amal, Bimal and Krishni each hold 1/16 + 1/12 = 7/48 of the land and Achini holds 1/16. Step 4 - Bimal's death, 4 March 2010, married to Amali and issueless. On the footing that he too died intestate, his estate of 7/48 devolves as follows. Amali takes one-half under s.22, that is 7/96 of the land. The remaining 7/96 must pass down the s.23 order: Bimal left no descendants, and under s.25 it would go to his parents, but both Nimal and Nalini were already dead, so under s.26 it goes to his brothers and sisters of the whole and half blood. Amal and Krishni are of the full blood; Achini is a half-sister on the father's side and there is no half-sibling on the mother's side. Section 27 therefore applies in its final limb: Amal and Krishni first take one half of the 7/96, that is 7/192, in equal shares of 7/384 each, and the other 7/192 is divided per capita among Amal, Krishni and Achini under ss.27 and 30, giving each of them 7/576. So from Bimal's estate Amal takes 7/384 + 7/576 = 35/1152, Krishni takes the same 35/1152, Achini takes 7/576 = 14/1152 and Amali takes 7/96 = 84/1152.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Taking lots 6 and 7 as a whole, the shares presently owned are: Sunil 5/12 and Kusum 1/12, both unaffected by the deaths; and out of Nimal's former half share, Amal 203/1152, Krishni 203/1152, Achini 86/1152 (that is 43/576) and Amali 84/1152 (that is 7/96). These six shares add up to 1152/1152, the whole of the land. Expressed as shares of Nimal's estate alone, Amal and Krishni take 203/576 each, Achini 86/576 and Amali 84/576. The figures assume that Bimal, like his father and mother, died intestate and that Achini was born of a lawful marriage between Nimal and Malini; if either assumption fails the last step of the calculation changes.

answer_claims.claim_text: Intestate inheritance to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.21(1), whatever the deceased's domicile, and the divided lots are immovable property within s.3.

The Ordinance's inheritance sections do not apply to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils of the Northern Province subject to the Thesawalamai, and apply only to estates of persons dying after the 1876 proclamation who were then unmarried or married after it.
A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of a person who dies intestate.
Subject to the surviving spouse's half, the right of inheritance runs in the order descendants, then ascendants, then collaterals.
Children are preferent to all others in a parent's estate and take equally per capita, and heirs equally near in degree take per capita and not per stirpes.
Where an intestate leaves no descendants the estate goes to the parents, and where both parents have also failed it goes to the brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or half blood.
Where there are half-siblings on one side only, the full brothers and sisters take one half of the sibling portion in the first place and divide the other half with the half-siblings.
Nimal held 6/12 (a half share) of lots 6 and 7 at his death: 5/12 under the Final Decree of 21 August 1996 plus the 1/12 bought from Aruni by Deed of Transfer No. 346 of 6 June 1998.
On Nimal's intestate death on 23 April 2008 his widow Nalini took one-half of his estate and his four children Achini, Amal, Bimal and Krishni took the other half in equal shares.

On Nalini's intestate death within a year her share passed wholly to her descendants, namely her three children Amal, Bimal and Krishni in equal shares; Achini, being Nimal's daughter by Malini and not a descendant of Nalini, took nothing from Nalini's estate.

Bimal died on 4 March 2010 married to Amali and issueless, so his descendants failed; both his parents had already died, so no ascendant survived and his estate passed to his collaterals after his widow's half.

Bimal's siblings were his full brother Amal and full sister Krishni and his paternal half-sister Achini, with no half-sibling on the mother's side, so the full siblings took one half of the sibling portion first and shared the other half with Achini.
Each of Nimal's four children took 1/16 of the land from his estate and Nalini took 1/4 of the land.
Nalini's 1/4 divided equally among Amal, Bimal and Krishni gave each of them a further 1/12, so that each held 7/48 of the land while Achini held 1/16.

Of Bimal's 7/48, Amali took 7/96 as surviving spouse and the remaining 7/96 went to the siblings, of which Amal and Krishni took 7/192 between them in equal shares of 7/384 each, and Amal, Krishni and Achini shared the other 7/192 equally at 7/576 each.
The shares presently owned in lots 6 and 7 are Sunil 5/12, Kusum 1/12, Amal 203/1152, Krishni 203/1152, Achini 86/1152 (43/576) and Amali 84/1152 (7/96), which together make up the whole land.
Expressed as fractions of Nimal's former half share alone, Amal and Krishni take 203/576 each, Achini 86/576 and Amali 84/576.
The arithmetic assumes that Bimal died intestate, which the scenario does not state expressly, and that Achini was born of a lawful marriage between Nimal and Malini.

enrichment.original_background: By a Final Decree dated 21 August 1996 entered in District Court Galle in Partition case No.2367/P Nimal, Sunil, Aruni and Kusum were allotted with 5/12th,5/12th, 1/12th and 1/12th shares respectively from and out of divided and defined lots 6 and 7 in Partition Plan No.185 dated 23rd June 1995 made by J.W. de Silva Licensed Surveyor By Deed of Transfer. No.346 dated 6th June 1998 attested by Ranjith Perera Notary Public Nimal purchased the 1/12th share of Aruni. Nimal was married to Nalini and had 3 children namely Amal, Bimal and Krishni. Nimal had a daughter named Achini by his first wife Malini, Nimal died intestate on 23rd April 2008. Within a year thereafter Nalini too died intestate. Nimal's son Bimal who was married to Amali died on 4th of March 2010 having met with an accident and issueless.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: the common elements shall be held by the owners of all the condominium parcels as tenants in common proportional to their respective share parcels
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Fixes who owns the land on which a registered condominium stands: once the Condominium Plan is registered the land parcel outside the condominium parcels becomes common elements held by the parcel owners as tenants in common in proportion to their share parcels. Gihan owns no condominium parcel, so he can hold no share in that land.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1973; last amended by Act No. 39 of 2003 s.13, some fifteen years before the matter reference date of 2018-04. The consolidated text used here is the text in force in April 2018.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim in 11-1973/s9(1) and states what why_relevant claims; the section is in force from 1973 with amendment events in 1982 and 2003 only, so the consolidated text is the text in force in April 2018.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: each condominium parcel depicted therein together with the common elements appurtenant thereto shall be deemed to be absolutely owned by the person or persons described in the relevant plan as the owner or owners of the Condominium Property
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Confirms that on registration of the Condominium Plan absolute ownership vests in the person described in the plan as owner. Rehan, being so described, is the absolute owner; a stranger's declaration cannot displace that deemed ownership.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1973; subsection (5) in its present form comes from Act No. 39 of 2003 s.13, well before 2018-04.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim in 11-1973/s9(5); the omitted tail, which saves the rights of mortgagees and compensation claimants, does not qualify the deeming of absolute ownership relied on here.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: No share in the common elements of a registered, Condominium Property or of a registered Semi Condominium Property shall be disposed of or otherwise dealt with except as appurtenant to a condominium parcel of such property
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The central prohibition. A Deed of Declaration claiming a half share of the land on which the condominium stands is a dealing with a share in the common elements otherwise than as appurtenant to a condominium parcel, which this section forbids outright.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1973; last amended by Act No. 39 of 2003 s.16, before the matter reference date.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Wording is verbatim and s.11 does bar a share in the common elements from being held otherwise than as appurtenant to a condominium parcel, but it regulates dealings with a share that exists, so on these facts it reinforces rather than supplies the answer, which turns first on s.9(1) and s.9(5) leaving Gihan with no share at all.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Registration of an instrument under this Chapter shall not cure any defect in the instrument or confer upon it any effect or validity which it would not otherwise have except the priority conferred on it by this section.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Answers the second half of the question. Even if the Registrar accepts the Deed of Declaration and enters it in the register, registration gives the deed no validity it does not already have; it cannot manufacture a half share for a person who has none.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1927 with no recorded amendment event in the corpus; applicable at 2018-04.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim in 23-1927/s7(4); the corpus edition is the 1990 consolidation, and the only pre-2018 amending Acts in the corpus, Nos. 48 of 2011 and 21 of 2013, amend ss.13, 22, 48 and the First Schedule rather than s.7, so the text is applicable at 2018-04.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: all instruments, including wills, decrees and orders of any court or authority, and awards, which purport or operate to create, confer, declare, limit, assign, transfer, charge, incumber, release, or extinguish any right, title, or interest, whether vested or contingent, past, present, or future, to, in or over land
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Shows that a Deed of Declaration asserting a half share is on its face an instrument affecting land, so it falls within the class of documents the Ordinance accepts for registration. This is why the deed can be lodged at all, and why the answer has to turn on effect rather than on registrability.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1927 with no recorded amendment event; applicable at 2018-04.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim in 23-1927/s8(b) and a deed declaring an interest in land falls within it; none of the eleven provisos to paragraph (b) excludes such a deed.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: any person executing the instrument; (b) any person claiming any interest or benefit thereunder; (c) any person having any interest in or charge on any property affected thereby
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Gihan, as executant of the deed and as a person claiming a benefit under it, is a person who may present it for registration. The Ordinance does not require the presenter to prove title first.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1927 with no recorded amendment event; applicable at 2018-04.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim in 23-1927/s26(1), whose paragraphs (a) and (b) cover an executant claiming a benefit under the instrument.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: A Registrar may, if he thinks fit, refuse to register an instrument- (a) where he has reason to suspect that the person presenting the instrument for registration is not a person who is authorized by this Ordinance to present it for registration
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Sets out the grounds on which a Registrar may refuse registration. They are directed at authority to present, form and mode of execution, stamp duty and fees, not at the truth of the claim of title asserted in the deed, which confirms that acceptance for registration says nothing about the deed's validity.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1927 with no recorded amendment event; applicable at 2018-04.

supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Gives the only lawful route by which part of the common elements can pass to anyone: a special resolution of the owners of all the parcels, executed by the management corporation. A unilateral deed by an outsider is not that route.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1973; last amended by Act No. 39 of 2003 s.21, before the matter reference date.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim in 11-1973/s16(1), and subsections (2) to (4) confirm that the management corporation executes the instrument, so the route described is the statutory one.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: The Partition Law shall not apply to any land or building comprised in any registered Condominium Plan.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Closes off the obvious fallback. Having declared himself entitled to a half share, Gihan could not follow it with a partition action over the condominium land, because the Partition Law does not apply to land comprised in a registered Condominium Plan.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1973 with no recorded amendment event; applicable at 2018-04.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim in 11-1973/s23; the Partition Law itself is not in the corpus, so what it would otherwise have permitted cannot be checked from within the corpus, as the recorded corpus gap says.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: means so much of the land parcel for the time being not comprised in any condominium parcel shown in a Condominium Plan or Semi Condominium or Provisional Condominium Plan

supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1973; last amended by Act No. 39 of 2003 s.41, before the matter reference date. The corpus text of this interpretation section has lost the defined-term lead-ins, so the excerpt reads as a bare 'means ...' clause; the verifier should confirm against the source that this clause is the definition of 'common elements'.

supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Resolves the clash the question sets up. Gihan wants to use the Registration of Documents Ordinance to achieve something the Apartment Ownership Law prohibits; this section makes the Apartment Ownership Law prevail over the Ordinance.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1973 with no recorded amendment event; applicable at 2018-04.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Wording is verbatim, but s.25 operates only where there is a conflict or inconsistency and there is none on these facts, because s.7(4) of the Ordinance itself denies the registration any curative effect, so the role is corrected from indispensable to supporting.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: any instrument registered under Chapters IE or IV is a forgery, or has been registered without due authority or in contravention of any provision of this Ordinance, or where any instrument registered as aforesaid is rectified or set aside by a competent court, the District Court may order the registration of the instrument to be cancelled or to be rectified in such manner as the circumstances may require
