legal_issues.issue: Whether a person who owns no condominium parcel can, by a unilateral Deed of Declaration, acquire or assert an undivided half share in the land parcel on which a registered condominium stands, that land being common elements.

Whether such a Deed of Declaration is an instrument that may be executed and presented for registration under the Registration of Documents Ordinance, and what registration would achieve if it were accepted.
Whether the Apartment Ownership Law or the Registration of Documents Ordinance governs where the two conflict.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Gihan de Silva, who owns no condominium parcel in the building, can execute a Deed of Declaration claiming an undivided half share of the land on which Rehan's registered condominium stands, and register it under the Registration of Documents Ordinance, and what such a deed and its registration would achieve.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Once a Condominium Plan is registered, so much of the land parcel as is not comprised in any condominium parcel is common elements (Apartment Ownership Law s.26), and the common elements are held by the owners of all the condominium parcels as tenants in common in proportion to their share parcels (s.9(1)); each parcel with its appurtenant common elements is deemed absolutely owned by the person described in the registered plan as owner (s.9(5)). Section 11 forbids any share in the common elements being disposed of or otherwise dealt with except as appurtenant to a condominium parcel of that property, and s.16 gives the only route by which part of the common elements may pass, namely a special resolution of the owners of all the parcels directing the management corporation to transfer it. The Partition Law does not apply to land comprised in a registered Condominium Plan (s.23). On the registration side, a deed purporting to declare an interest in land is an instrument affecting land (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.8(b)) which its executant may present for registration (s.26(1)), and the Registrar's grounds of refusal (s.36) go to authority to present, form of execution, stamp duty and fees rather than to the truth of the title asserted; but s.7(4) provides that registration cures no defect and confers no effect or validity the instrument would not otherwise have, beyond priority. Where the two enactments conflict, the Apartment Ownership Law prevails (s.25).
gold_answer_draft.application: Condominium Plan No. 4127 for Nelum Residencies was registered in 2011, so the 32.5 perch land parcel under the building, apart from the condominium parcels themselves, is common elements held by the owners of the parcels shown in that plan, and Rehan, named in the plan as owner, is deemed to own his parcels with their appurtenant common elements absolutely. Gihan owns no condominium parcel and holds no instrument of title to any part of the land, so there is no parcel in his hands to which a share in the common elements could be appurtenant; a deed claiming a half share of that land is exactly the dealing s.11 forbids. The owners have passed no special resolution and the management corporation has executed no transfer, so the s.16 route has not been used. As a matter of form the deed can be drawn and attested, and because the Registrar is not required to adjudicate title before accepting an instrument affecting land, it may well be accepted and entered in the register; but by s.7(4) that entry adds nothing to a deed that conveys nothing, and to the extent the Ordinance is invoked to defeat the Apartment Ownership Law, s.25 makes that Law prevail. Nor could Gihan follow the declaration with a partition action, since s.23 excludes the Partition Law. Whether the Registrar would in fact accept the deed is for the Registrar in the individual case; the point is that acceptance would not assist Gihan.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Gihan may have such a Deed of Declaration prepared and attested, and it may physically be lodged and even accepted for registration under the Registration of Documents Ordinance, but he cannot lawfully acquire what he claims. A half share of the land on which the registered condominium stands is a share in the common elements, and s.11 of the Apartment Ownership Law bars any dealing with it except as appurtenant to a condominium parcel, which Gihan does not own. Registration would give him nothing, because under s.7(4) of the Ordinance it cures no defect and confers no validity, and under s.25 the Apartment Ownership Law prevails over the Ordinance. The deed would be of no legal effect against Rehan, and its registration would be open to challenge by an interested party in the District Court.

answer_claims.claim_text: Once a Condominium Plan is registered, so much of the land parcel as is not comprised in any condominium parcel is common elements, and the common elements are held by the owners of all the condominium parcels as tenants in common in proportion to their share parcels.
On registration each condominium parcel together with the common elements appurtenant to it is deemed to be absolutely owned by the person described in the registered plan as owner.

No share in the common elements of a registered Condominium Property may be disposed of or otherwise dealt with except as appurtenant to a condominium parcel of that property, and part of the common elements can pass only on a special resolution of the owners of all the parcels directing the management corporation to transfer it.

A deed that purports to declare a right, title or interest in land is an instrument affecting land for the purposes of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, and its executant or a person claiming a benefit under it may present it for registration.

The grounds on which a Registrar may or must refuse registration go to authority to present, form and mode of execution, stamp duty and fees, and not to whether the title asserted in the instrument is good.
Registration under the Registration of Documents Ordinance cures no defect in an instrument and confers on it no effect or validity it would not otherwise have, apart from priority.
Where the Apartment Ownership Law conflicts with another written law, including the Registration of Documents Ordinance, the Apartment Ownership Law prevails.
The Partition Law does not apply to land or a building comprised in a registered Condominium Plan.

Because Condominium Plan No. 4127 was registered in 2011, the 32.5 perch land parcel on which the building stands is, apart from the condominium parcels themselves, common elements held by the owners of the parcels shown in that plan.

Gihan owns no condominium parcel in the building, so there is no parcel to which a share in the common elements could be appurtenant in his hands, and his Deed of Declaration is a dealing with a share in the common elements that section 11 forbids.

No special resolution of the owners and no transfer by the management corporation has been made, so the only lawful route by which part of the common elements could have reached Gihan has not been used.

Nothing in the Registration of Documents Ordinance obliges the Registrar to test Gihan's title before accepting the deed, so the deed may well be accepted and entered in the register, but that entry gives it no validity it lacks, and the prohibition in the Apartment Ownership Law prevails over the Ordinance in any event.
Gihan cannot follow the declaration with a partition action over the condominium land, because the Partition Law does not apply to land comprised in a registered Condominium Plan.

Gihan may have such a deed drawn and attested, and it may physically be accepted for registration under the Registration of Documents Ordinance, but it is of no legal effect: he acquires no half share in the land on which the condominium stands, and registration does not improve his position.

enrichment.original_background: Rehan de Silva is the owner of 2 Condominium properties. His brother Gihan de Silva intends to prepare a Deed of Declaration claiming 1/2 of the property, where the Condominium is situated and register the Deed under the Registration of Documents Ordinance.
enrichment.enriched_background:
Rehan de Silva is the owner of 2 Condominium properties. His brother Gihan de Silva intends to prepare a Deed of Declaration claiming 1/2 of the property, where the Condominium is situated and register the Deed under the Registration of Documents Ordinance.

The property Gihan has in mind is Nelum Residencies, a completed four-storey building at No. 118, Sri Sumangala Mawatha, Nugegoda, standing on a single land parcel of 32.5 perches. Condominium Plan No. 4127 for that land and building was registered on 5 May 2011 and has never been amended. Rehan de Silva is named in that registered plan as the owner of the whole land parcel and of the two condominium parcels he holds, Units 2B and 4A, and no share of the land parcel has at any time been transferred to Gihan. added_facts.fact: The property Gihan has in mind is Nelum Residencies, a completed four-storey building at No. 118, Sri Sumangala Mawatha, Nugegoda, standing on a single land parcel of 32.5 perches; Condominium Plan No. 4127 for that land and building was registered on 5 May 2011 and has never been amended.
added_facts.reason: The question does not say whether the Condominium Plan was ever registered, yet almost every consequence in the scenario follows from registration. Naming the property, its land parcel and the date of registration makes the scenario determinate.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If no Condominium Plan had been registered, the land would remain ordinary land, the common-elements rules would not bite and the answer would turn on ordinary conveyancing rules instead.

added_facts.fact: Rehan de Silva is named in that registered plan as the owner of the whole land parcel and of the two condominium parcels he holds, Units 2B and 4A, and no share of the land parcel has at any time been transferred to Gihan de Silva.
added_facts.reason: The background asserts Rehan's ownership but not how it appears on the plan, and says nothing about whether Gihan ever held a share. Both are needed before the claim to a half share can be assessed.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If Gihan were himself named on the plan as an owner of a condominium parcel, he would hold an undivided share in the common elements appurtenant to that parcel and the analysis would change.

added_facts.fact: Gihan de Silva owns no condominium parcel in the building and holds no deed, decree or other instrument of title to any part of the land parcel; the only document he proposes to rely on is a Deed of Declaration he intends to have attested by a notary in February 2018 and lodged at the Delkanda-Nugegoda Land Registry.
added_facts.reason: The candidate record flags a missing relevant document and missing registration status. Fixing what Gihan has, what he does not have, and when and where he proposes to lodge it removes the ambiguity.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If Gihan held a prior registered deed to an undivided half of the land predating the Condominium Plan, the question would become one of the effect of registration of the plan on an existing registered interest rather than of a bare declaration.

added_facts.fact: A management corporation for the building was constituted when the plan was registered and it has passed no resolution about transferring any part of the land or of the shared areas to anyone.
added_facts.reason: Rules out the one lawful route by which part of the common elements could have passed to Gihan, so the reader does not have to speculate about it.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the owners had passed such a special resolution and the management corporation had executed a transfer, part of the shared areas could lawfully have moved out of common ownership.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice nor authenticate or attest any deed or instrument drawn in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the only rule in section 31 that limits where a notary may attest. It restricts the area in which the act of attestation is performed and the language of the deed; it says nothing about where the land affected by the deed is situated. It is therefore the provision that answers how Lal Peiris, whose warrant covers Colombo, may lawfully attest a deed relating to land at Matara.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (22) is part of the original 1907 rules. It is not among the rules substituted, inserted or repealed by the amendments recorded against section 31 (Act No. 20 of 1976, Act No. 47 of 2011, Act No. 31 of 2022, Act No. 6 of 2024), so the text quoted stood in this form in April 2018.

legal_issues.issue: Whether the area restriction on a notary's practice bars a Colombo notary from attesting a deed of transfer of land situated in the Matara District, or whether it restricts only the place at which the act of attestation is performed.
How far the warrant of a notary who resides in Colombo extends, and what counts as the area in which he is authorised to practise.
Whether the notary's friendship with the purchaser disqualifies him from attesting the deed.
What the notary must do on the face of the deed, in particular as to language and the description of the land, in order to attest it lawfully.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Lal Peiris, a notary whose warrant authorises him to practise in Colombo and who is a friend of the purchaser, may attest a deed transferring land situated in the Matara District, and what he must do in order to attest it lawfully.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A transfer of immovable property is of no force in law unless the deed is in writing and attested by a licensed notary (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2). The area limit on a notary is imposed by Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (22), which forbids him to authenticate or attest any deed "in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice", and to attest in, or to attest a deed drawn in, a language other than that in which he is authorised to practise. The restriction is on the place at which the notary performs the attestation and on the language of the deed; rule (22) says nothing about where the land affected by the deed is situated. The area in which he is authorised to practise is fixed by his warrant, extended by Notaries Ordinance s.4A, under which a warrant authorising practice in the judicial division in which he resides is deemed to authorise practice in the judicial zone in which he resides; s.9 requires him to keep his office within the area specified in the warrant. The only disqualification in s.31 arising from the notary's own relationship to the deed is rule (13), which forbids him to attest a deed to which he is a party. Before attesting, he must have an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided (s.31 rule (6)), and the deed must embody an accurate and clear description of the land showing its boundaries, extent and situation, specifying the district (s.31 rule (16)(a)).
gold_answer_draft.application: Lal Peiris's warrant authorises him to practise in the Sinhala language in Colombo, the judicial division in which he resides, and by s.4A that authority extends to the Colombo judicial zone. The deed is drawn in Sinhala, and the vendor, the purchaser and the two witnesses are to sign it together in his presence at his Colombo office on 12 March 2018. The act of attestation is therefore performed within the area and in the language in which he is authorised to practise, and rule (22) is satisfied. That the land lies at Kumbalwella in the Matara District does not engage rule (22), because that rule looks to the area in which the notary acts and not to the situation of the land; the Matara District instead has to be stated in the description of the land under rule (16)(a). Lal Peiris is not the vendor or the purchaser, takes nothing under the deed and has no interest in the property, so rule (13) is not engaged; his friendship with Waruna Liyanage is not a matter on which s.31 fastens. He must also satisfy himself under rule (6) that the stamp duty is provided, and Waruna Liyanage has undertaken to put him in funds before the day of signing.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Lal Peiris may attest the deed. He must do so within the Colombo judicial zone, which his warrant covers by virtue of Notaries Ordinance s.4A, and in the language in which he is authorised to practise, so the parties and the two witnesses must execute the deed before him at his Colombo office and not at Matara (s.31 rule (22)). The situation of the land at Matara is no bar to his attesting; it must, however, be described in the deed with its district under s.31 rule (16)(a), and he must not attest until he has an assurance that the stamp duty is provided (s.31 rule (6)). His friendship with the purchaser does not disqualify him, since he is not a party to the deed (s.31 rule (13)).

answer_claims.claim_text: A sale or transfer of immovable property is of no force in law unless the deed is in writing and attested by a licensed notary.

A notary may not authenticate or attest any deed in an area other than that in which he is authorised to practise, nor in, nor of a deed drawn in, a language other than that in which he is authorised to practise.

The area restriction in rule (22) attaches to the place at which the notary performs the attestation and to the language of the deed, and not to the district in which the land affected by the deed is situated.
A warrant authorising a notary to practise in the judicial division in which he resides is deemed to authorise him to practise in the judicial zone in which he resides.
The only disqualification in section 31 based on the notary's own connection with the deed is rule (13), which bars him from attesting a deed to which he is a party.

A notary may not attest a deed affecting land unless the deed embodies an accurate and clear description of the land showing its boundaries, extent and situation, specifying the district, and may not attest unless he has an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided.

Lal Peiris's warrant covers the Colombo judicial division in which he resides and therefore the Colombo judicial zone, and the deed is to be executed before him in Sinhala at his Colombo office, so the attestation takes place within the area and in the language in which he is authorised to practise.
The situation of the land at Kumbalwella in the Matara District does not engage rule (22); it engages instead the requirement that the deed describe the land and specify its district.
Lal Peiris is not a party to the deed and takes no benefit under it, so rule (13) is not engaged and his friendship with the purchaser is not a statutory disqualification.

Lal Peiris may attest the deed, provided the parties and the two witnesses execute it before him within the Colombo judicial zone and in a language in which he is authorised to practise, the deed describes the Matara land with its district, and he has an assurance that the stamp duty is provided.
If Lal Peiris were instead to attest the deed at Matara, he would be attesting in an area other than that in which he is authorised to practise and would breach rule (22).

legal_issues.issue: What a notary must deliver or transmit, to whom, and by when, where the deed he attests affects land situated in a district other than that in which he resides.
Whether that duty is in substitution for, or in addition to, the ordinary monthly duty to transmit the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the notary resides.
Whether the out-of-district duty is engaged on these facts, the notary residing in the Colombo District and the land lying in the Matara District.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What duty is cast on Lal Peiris by reason of the land being situated in the Matara District, which is a district other than the Colombo District in which he resides.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Every notary must, under Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (26)(a)(i), deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which he resides, so as to reach the registrar on or before the fifteenth day of every month, the duplicate of every deed or instrument (except wills and codicils) executed or acknowledged before or attested by him during the preceding month, together with a list in duplicate signed by him in the prescribed form. Where the deed is one other than a will or codicil and affects land situated in a district other than that in which the attesting notary resides, s.31 rule (29) casts an additional duty on him: on or before the fifteenth day of the month next following that in which the deed was executed, and besides transmitting the duplicate in the manner already described, he must deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated a copy of the deed certified by him as correct, together with a list in duplicate in the prescribed form signed by him of all such deeds as relate to lands in that district. The district of the land is the district which s.31 rule (16)(a) requires to be specified in the description of the land in the deed itself. Breach of a rule set out in s.31 is an offence punishable on summary trial before a Magistrate, in addition to any civil liability the notary incurs (s.34).
gold_answer_draft.application: Lal Peiris resides in the Colombo District and attests the deed at his Colombo office on 12 March 2018. The deed is an ordinary deed of transfer, not a will or codicil, and he is the only notary before whom it is executed, so the duty of transmitting the duplicate rests on him. The land conveyed is at Kumbalwella in the Matara District, a district other than the Colombo District in which he resides, so s.31 rule (29) is engaged. His ordinary duty under rule (26)(a)(i) is to send the duplicate of the deed, with the signed list in duplicate, to the Registrar of Lands, Colombo, so as to reach that registrar on or before 15 April 2018. Rule (29) then requires him, in addition and by the same date of 15 April 2018, to deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands, Matara, a copy of the deed certified by him as correct, together with a list in duplicate signed by him of the deeds he has attested that relate to lands in the Matara District. The deed must in any event describe the land as being in the Matara District under rule (16)(a), which is what identifies the registrar to whom the certified copy must go.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Because the land lies in the Matara District and Lal Peiris resides in the Colombo District, s.31 rule (29) of the Notaries Ordinance casts on him the additional duty of delivering or transmitting to the Registrar of Lands, Matara, on or before the fifteenth day of the month next following execution, that is on or before 15 April 2018 for a deed executed on 12 March 2018, a copy of the deed certified by him as correct together with a list in duplicate in the prescribed form signed by him of the deeds relating to lands in that district. This is over and above, and does not replace, his ordinary duty under s.31 rule (26)(a)(i) to transmit the duplicate and his monthly list to the Registrar of Lands, Colombo, by the same date. Failure to observe the rule is an offence under s.34 of the Ordinance in addition to any civil liability he may incur; the fine applicable in April 2018 cannot be stated from the corpus, which carries only the later text of s.34.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary must deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which he resides, so as to reach the registrar on or before the fifteenth day of every month, the duplicate of every deed or instrument except wills and codicils executed or acknowledged before or attested by him during the preceding month.

Where a deed other than a will or codicil affects land in a district other than that in which the attesting notary resides, he must, on or before the fifteenth day of the month next following that in which the deed was executed and besides transmitting the duplicate as already required, deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated a copy of the deed certified by him as correct, with a signed list in duplicate of the deeds relating to lands in that district.
The rule (29) duty is additional to and not in substitution for the ordinary monthly duty, because it operates besides transmitting the duplicate in the manner already required.
The district in which the land is situated is the district that the deed itself must specify in its description of the land.
Breach of a rule set out in section 31 makes the notary guilty of an offence triable summarily before a Magistrate, in addition to any civil liability he may incur.

Lal Peiris resides in the Colombo District while the land conveyed is at Kumbalwella in the Matara District, so the deed affects land in a district other than that in which he resides and rule (29) is engaged.
The instrument is a deed of transfer and not a will or codicil, and Lal Peiris is the only notary attesting it, so the duty of transmission falls on him.

legal_issues.issue: What fractions of Lot A vested in Kanthi, Samantha, Rakitha and Muditha on the intestate death of Suresh Perera on 10 December 1995.
How Rakitha's fraction devolved on his death on 2 July 2022, leaving a widow Ann, a surviving mother Kanthi, a full sister Muditha and a half-sister Samantha.
How Muditha's fraction devolved on her death on 5 June 2023 unmarried and issueless, her only surviving sibling being the half-blood sister Samantha.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What fraction of Lot A each surviving heir holds as at April 2026, after the intestate deaths of Suresh Perera on 10 December 1995, Rakitha on 2 July 2022 and Muditha on 5 June 2023.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Inheritance on intestacy to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance whatever the domicile of the deceased or of an heir (s.21), and Part III reaches the estate of anyone dying after the proclamation of the Ordinance (s.20). A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the intestate's property (s.22). Subject to that half, the right of inheritance runs to descendants first, then ascendants, then collaterals (s.23). Children take equally per capita and the issue of a deceased child take per stirpes (s.24). Where the descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half and the other half goes to the full-blood brothers and sisters, the issue of deceased full-blood brothers and sisters by representation, and the half-blood brothers and sisters related to the intestate through the deceased parent (s.25). Where the only half-blood siblings are on one side, the full-blood siblings take one-half of that sibling portion in the first place and divide the balance with the half-blood siblings (s.27).
gold_answer_draft.application: Suresh Perera owned the whole of Lot A when he died intestate on 10 December 1995. Under s.22 his widow Kanthi took one-half. Under s.23 and s.24 the other half went to his children per capita. He had three children: Samantha of his first marriage, Rakitha and Muditha. Each took one-sixth. Rakitha died on 2 July 2022 leaving his widow Ann and no children on the facts stated. Ann took one-half of his one-sixth under s.22, that is one-twelfth. The remaining one-twelfth fell under s.25: his father Suresh had predeceased him and his mother Kanthi survived, so Kanthi took half of it, one twenty-fourth, and the sibling class took the other one twenty-fourth. That class was his full sister Muditha and his half-sister Samantha, who is related to him through the deceased parent Suresh and so is within s.25. Applying s.27, Muditha took one-half of the sibling portion first and then divided the balance with Samantha, giving Muditha three quarters of one twenty-fourth, that is one thirty-second, and Samantha one quarter of one twenty-fourth, that is one ninety-sixth. Muditha died on 5 June 2023 unmarried and issueless holding one-sixth plus one thirty-second, which is nineteen ninety-sixths. Under s.25 her surviving mother Kanthi took half, nineteen one hundred and ninety-seconds. The sibling half went to Samantha alone: Rakitha had predeceased Muditha and left no issue to take by representation, so under s.27 there was no full-blood sibling or issue of one to take the first half, and the only member of the class was the half-blood sister Samantha. Adding the three intestacies, Kanthi holds 96/192 plus 8/192 plus 19/192, Ann holds 16/192, and Samantha holds 32/192 plus 2/192 plus 19/192.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: As at April 2026 the shares in Lot A are Kanthi 123/192, which reduces to 41/64; Ann 16/192, which reduces to 1/12; and Samantha 53/192. Those three fractions total the whole. Two facts are open on the face of the scenario and would change the arithmetic if resolved differently: it is not stated in terms that Rakitha died without issue, and it is not stated that Kanthi is still living. The answer above assumes both, since no child of Rakitha and no death of Kanthi is mentioned.

answer_claims.claim_text: Intestate succession to Lot A is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance because Lot A is immovable property situated in Sri Lanka, and the domicile of an heir such as Samantha is irrelevant to that.
A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the intestate's property and the balance passes to descendants before ascendants and collaterals.
Children take the descendants' share equally per capita, and the issue of a deceased child take by representation.

Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half and the full-blood siblings together with half-blood siblings related through the deceased parent take the other half.
Where the only half-blood siblings are on one side, the full-blood siblings take one-half of the sibling portion first and divide the remaining half with the half-blood siblings.
On Suresh Perera's intestate death on 10 December 1995 Kanthi took one-half of Lot A and Samantha, Rakitha and Muditha took one-sixth each.
On Rakitha's death on 2 July 2022 his one-sixth passed as one-twelfth to Ann, one twenty-fourth to Kanthi, one thirty-second to Muditha and one ninety-sixth to Samantha.

On Muditha's death on 5 June 2023 unmarried and issueless her nineteen ninety-sixths passed half to Kanthi as surviving parent and half to Samantha as the only surviving member of the sibling class, Rakitha having died without issue.
Samantha is an heir of Suresh Perera even though she is a child of his first marriage, because children take equally per capita without distinction between marriages.
As at April 2026 Kanthi holds 123/192 of Lot A, being 41/64.
As at April 2026 Ann holds 16/192 of Lot A, being 1/12.
As at April 2026 Samantha holds 53/192 of Lot A.
The answer assumes Rakitha left no issue and that Kanthi is still living, neither of which is stated in terms; if either assumption fails the fractions change.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a deed of transfer is invalidated by the notary's failure to observe rules set out in section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance.
Whether the defect on the face of the deed (the notary's own particulars omitted from the front page) is a matter of form within the protection of section 33 of the Notaries Ordinance.

Whether obtaining the second attesting witness's signature on a later day, away from the executant and the other witness, breaches a requirement imposed by another written law so as to fall within the proviso to section 33.
Whether the notary's exposure to punishment under section 34 of the Notaries Ordinance is a separate question from the standing of the deed.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the Deed of Transfer attested by Saman can be invalidated because he failed to comply with rules set out in section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance, and whether the answer depends on which rule he broke.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Breach of a rule in section 31 does not of itself destroy the instrument. Notaries Ordinance s.33 provides that no instrument shall be deemed to be invalid by reason only of the failure of any notary to observe any provision of any rule set out in section 31 in respect of any matter of form. The protection is expressly limited by the proviso to s.33, which states that nothing in the section gives validity to any instrument that may be invalid by reason of non-compliance with the provisions of any other written law. Two of the rules in section 31 are engaged here. Rule (17)(c) requires the notary to write on the front page of the deed his name with initials, the number assigned to him, his office address and telephone number, and, if he is a legal officer working in an organisation, the registered address of that organisation; that requirement goes to how the face of the instrument is completed. Rule (12) forbids a notary to attest any deed unless the executant and the witnesses have signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and he has signed in their presence; the same requirement is imposed independently, and as a condition of the deed having any legal force, by the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)(a), under which no transfer of immovable property shall be in force or avail in law unless the deed is in writing and is signed by every executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another and is attested by that notary. Notaries Ordinance s.34(1)(c) makes a breach of a rule in section 31 an offence punishable on summary trial before a Magistrate by a fine, in addition to any civil liability the notary may incur; it says nothing about the validity of the instrument, so the notary's liability and the standing of the deed are separate questions.
gold_answer_draft.application: Saman's omission of his name, notary number, office address and telephone number, and of his employer's registered address, from the front page is a failure to observe rule (17)(c). It concerns the completion of the face of the instrument and not the manner in which the parties bound themselves, and no other written law makes those particulars a condition of a valid transfer. On that default alone the deed would be protected by the main limb of s.33. The second default is of a different character. The executant Nimal Perera and one witness signed at Saman's office, but the second witness signed at his own house on the following day, in the absence of the executant and of the other witness, and Saman attested that all had signed in his presence and in the presence of one another. That is a breach of rule (12); more importantly, it means the deed was not signed by the executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary present at the same time and in the presence of one another, which the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)(a) makes a condition of a transfer of immovable property being in force or availing in law. Because the deed affects a house and premises at Colombo 05, that Ordinance applies, and the proviso to s.33 withholds from this deed the protection the section would otherwise give. Saman attested at his own office at Colombo 07, within the Judicial Zone of Colombo for which he is licensed, so no separate objection arises under section 31 rule (22) as to the area of attestation. Independently of the fate of the deed, Saman remains exposed to prosecution and a fine under s.34 of the Notaries Ordinance, together with any civil liability towards the parties, and the urgency of his employer's instruction is no answer to either.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The Deed can be invalidated, but not simply because rules in section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance were broken. Defaults that are matters of form, such as the omission of the notary's particulars from the front page, do not by themselves affect the instrument, because of Notaries Ordinance s.33. The deed is at risk here because the failure to have the executant and both witnesses sign in Saman's presence and in the presence of one another is also non-compliance with the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)(a); on the terms of that provision the transfer is not in force and does not avail in law, and by the proviso to s.33 the Notaries Ordinance does not cure it. Saman is in addition liable to be punished under Notaries Ordinance s.34 and to answer civilly to the parties for the loss.

answer_claims.claim_text: No instrument is to be deemed invalid by reason only of a notary's failure to observe a rule set out in section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance in respect of a matter of form.
The proviso to section 33 of the Notaries Ordinance withholds that protection where the instrument may be invalid by reason of non-compliance with the provisions of any other written law.

Notaries Ordinance section 31 rule (12) forbids a notary to attest a deed unless the executant and the witnesses have signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and he has signed in the presence of the executant and the attesting witnesses.

Under the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance section 2(1)(a) a transfer of immovable property is not in force and does not avail in law unless the deed is in writing and signed by every executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and is attested by that notary.

Notaries Ordinance section 31 rule (17)(c) requires the notary to write on the front page of the deed his name with initials, the number assigned to him, his office address and telephone number, and, where he is a legal officer of an organisation, that organisation's registered address.

Breach of a rule in section 31 is an offence under Notaries Ordinance section 34(1)(c), punishable on summary trial before a Magistrate by a fine in addition to any civil liability the notary may incur, and that section attaches no consequence to the instrument itself.
A notary may not attest a deed in any area other than that in which he is authorised to practise.

Saman's omission of his own particulars and his employer's registered address from the front page of the deed is a breach of rule (17)(c) which concerns a matter of form, so it does not of itself invalidate the deed.

Because the second attesting witness signed on the following day at his own house, away from the executant and the other witness, the deed was not signed by the executant and both witnesses in the presence of the notary present at the same time and in the presence of one another, so both rule (12) and the condition in the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance section 2(1)(a) were left unsatisfied.

Since the deed affects immovable property at Colombo 05, the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance applies to it and the proviso to section 33 of the Notaries Ordinance prevents that section from saving the deed from the consequence of that non-compliance.
Saman attested at his own office at Colombo 07, within the Judicial Zone of Colombo for which he holds his licence, so no objection arises from the area of attestation.
Whatever happens to the deed, Saman remains liable to be tried and fined for the breaches of section 31 and to answer civilly, and his employer's instruction to act urgently is no defence.

The deed can be invalidated: not on account of the formal defect on its front page, which section 33 of the Notaries Ordinance protects, but because the signing was not carried out in the simultaneous presence required by the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance section 2(1)(a), so the transfer is not in force and does not avail in law.

legal_issues.issue: Whether knowledge that a client has executed a last will, and knowledge of its contents, is a secret confided to the notary or one of which he became possessed in the execution of his office.
Whether the testator's children can supply the 'express permission of his employer' that alone permits disclosure, or whether that permission must come from the testator who instructed the notary.

Whether an informal request by the testator's children, made while he is alive and unaccompanied by any court order or lawful demand, brings the notary within the exception for disclosure 'required to do so by law'.
What the notary is exposed to if she does divulge the information.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the notary who attested the will may tell the testator's children, during the testator's lifetime and without his permission, that he has executed a will and what it contains; and what the notary is exposed to if she does.
gold_answer_draft.rule: It is the duty of every notary, under Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (1), not to divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office. Rule (1) allows only two exceptions: the express permission of his employer, or a case where he is required to divulge by law. The Ordinance treats a will as confidential in its own record-keeping rules as well: under s.31 rule (24) the notary preserves the protocol of the will but enters only the number and date of the instrument in his register, and under s.31 rule (27)(a)(i) the duplicate of a will is not delivered to the Registrar of Lands and only the number and date of the document go into the monthly list. A notary who acts in violation of rule (1) is guilty of an offence under s.34(1)(a) and is liable, on conviction after summary trial before a Magistrate, to a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees, in addition to any civil liability he may incur.
gold_answer_draft.application: The notary learned that the will exists, and learned its contents, because the testator instructed her to draw it and executed it before her; that is information of which she became possessed in the execution of her office, and it is exactly the kind of information the Ordinance keeps out of her register and out of the monthly list. The employer for the purposes of rule (1) is the testator, who engaged her, and he is alive and has given no permission of any kind. His children are not her employers and cannot waive a secrecy owed to their father; while he lives they have no vested interest in his estate, only an expectation. Nor is she required by law to answer: no court order, summons or lawful demand by a public officer has been served on her, and an informal enquiry at her office is not legal compulsion. Neither exception in rule (1) is therefore satisfied, so the prohibition applies in full, and it applies to the bare fact that a will was executed as much as to its contents, since confirming the fact would itself divulge a secret.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: No. The notary should not divulge the information. She should decline to say whether a will was executed before her or what it provides, and direct the children to their father, who alone can authorise disclosure while he lives. She may answer only if the testator gives express permission or if she is required by law to do so, for example under a court order. If she divulges without either, she commits an offence under s.34(1)(a) and is liable to a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees on summary trial before a Magistrate, in addition to any civil liability, and the breach may also be treated as misconduct in her office as a notary.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary is under a statutory duty not to divulge secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office.
The duty of secrecy yields only in two cases: where the notary has the express permission of his employer, or where he is required to divulge by law.

The Notaries Ordinance treats wills as specially confidential: only the number and date of a will go into the notary's register, and the duplicate of a will is not sent to the Registrar of Lands, only its number and date appearing in the monthly list.
answer_claims.verifier_note: Rejected on two grounds: (a) the register limb is no longer an accurate statement of the law at 2025-10, because s.31 rule (20)(h)(ii) (inserted by 31-2022 s.16(11)(d)) requires the name of the testator, as well as the number and date, to be entered in the notary's deed register for a will; and (b) the monthly-list limb is sourced to PROV-M022-003, which cites the repealed rule (27) instead of rule (26)(a)(i). The claim is supporting only, so the conclusion is unaffected, but the gold answer's rule paragraph repeats both defects.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary who acts in violation of the secrecy rule is guilty of an offence and is liable, on conviction after summary trial before a Magistrate, to a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees in addition to any civil liability.
Both the existence of the will and its contents are information of which the notary became possessed in the execution of her office, because she drew and attested it on the testator's instructions.
The employer whose express permission could release the notary is the testator, who engaged her; he is alive and has given no such permission, and his children cannot give it in his place.
answer_claims.verifier_note: Verified on the corpus text, but flagged for the lawyer: 'employer' in rule (1) is undefined in the Ordinance (s.43 defines only 'Council of Legal Education', 'High Court Judge' and 'Registrar-General') and the word appears nowhere else in 1-1907, so reading it as the testator who instructed the notary is an interpretation the statute does not itself state.

answer_claims.claim_text: The notary is not required by law to answer, because no court order, summons or lawful demand by a public officer has been served on her and an informal enquiry at her office is not legal compulsion.
Neither exception being satisfied, the notary should not divulge the information, and should decline even to confirm whether a will was executed before her, referring the children to their father.

If she does divulge without permission or legal compulsion, she commits an offence punishable with a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees on summary trial before a Magistrate, in addition to any civil liability.

indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Inserted by the Powers of Attorney (Amendment) Act No. 28 of 2022, in force before April 2025.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Deeds and Documents (Execution before Public Officers) Ordinance
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: signed by the party making the same or by some person lawfully authorized by him, and by two or more witnesses present at the same time, in the presence of some District Judge or Commissioner of a Court of Requests* for the district in which the party making such writing, deed, or instrument, or the person signing the same as such attorney, resides

indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Added by the verifier. Excerpt checked verbatim against 17-1852/s2; the cross-reference to Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 is confirmed by the corpus edge graph.

The map cited rule (30) for the notary's protocol duty but omitted this condition on the attorney.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a lease of business premises for two years falls within section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance and must therefore be executed in notarial form.
Whether both parties must sign the instrument at the same time and place before a single notary, or whether execution may be split.
Whether a notary practising in Colombo may attest the lessor's signature taken in Galle.
Whether the lessor may instead authorise another person to sign the lease on her behalf, and what form that authority must take.

gold_answer_draft.issue: By what lawful means may a two-year lease of business premises in Galle be signed by a lessor who cannot travel to Colombo and by a lessee dealing with a notary who practises in Colombo?
gold_answer_draft.rule: A lease of immovable property for a period exceeding one month is within Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2, because the only leases excluded are a lease at will and a lease for a period not exceeding one month. Such an instrument has no force in law unless it is in writing and signed by every executant, or by a person duly authorised by the executant, and by the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and is attested by that notary. Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (12) casts the same requirement on the notary as a duty, and rule (22) forbids her from attesting in any area other than that in which she is authorised to practise; s.4A treats the warrant as authorising practice in the judicial zone in which she resides. Notaries Ordinance s.32(2) deals expressly with a deed executed by two or more parties who do not sign it at the same time and place, and s.31 rule (25) governs attestation where an instrument is executed before more than one notary, the notary who first attests complying with the whole of rule (20) and every other notary with paragraphs (a) to (e). Rule (27)(c)(ii) contemplates completion within three months of the first signature. Alternatively, s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance allows the instrument to be signed by a person duly authorised by the executant. That authority is a power of attorney within Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.2, which if executed in Sri Lanka must be executed before two witnesses and notarially attested, must satisfy s.3A because the lease is a transaction within s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, and must be registered with the Registrar General under s.3; Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (30) then requires the attesting notary to keep a true copy of the power with her protocol and forward a copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands.
gold_answer_draft.application: The proposed lease runs for two years at Rs 150,000 a month, so it is well outside the one-month exclusion and must be executed notarially. The parties cannot cure Rupa Perera's absence by exchanging the document through the post and signing it apart, because both s.2 and rule (12) require signature in the presence of the notary and of the witnesses, all present together. Malani Silva practises in Colombo, and rule (22) with s.4A stops her from attesting a signature taken in Galle, so she cannot solve the problem by travelling to the lessor. Two routes remain. First, the one instrument may be executed in parts: Rupa Perera signs in Galle with two witnesses before a notary authorised to practise in that zone, and Gamini Sirisene signs in Colombo before Malani Silva, each notary attesting the signatures taken before her. That is the situation s.32(2) addresses, and rule (25) then allocates the attestation, numbering and protocol duties between the two notaries, the notary who first attests complying with the whole of rule (20). Rule (27)(c)(ii) shows the execution is expected to be completed within three months of the first signature. Second, Rupa Perera may grant a power of attorney to a person able to attend in Colombo. Because the lease is a transaction within s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, that power must be notarially attested and comply with s.3A of the Powers of Attorney Ordinance, and must be registered with the Registrar General under s.3; the attorney then signs the lease before Malani Silva, who keeps a copy of the power with her protocol under rule (30). The facts do not say whether Rupa Perera is willing to appoint an attorney or whether a notary is readily available in the Galle zone, so the choice between the two routes is practical rather than legal.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The lease must be executed notarially. It may lawfully be signed either by the two parties executing the same instrument at different times and places before two notaries, Rupa Perera before a notary practising in the Galle zone and Gamini Sirisene before Malani Silva in Colombo, as contemplated by Notaries Ordinance s.32(2) and s.31 rule (25); or by Rupa Perera granting a notarially attested and registered power of attorney under the Powers of Attorney Ordinance to an attorney who signs on her behalf in Colombo, as permitted by Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2. What is not open to the parties is signing the agreement outside the presence of a notary and the witnesses, or having the Colombo notary attest a signature taken in Galle.

answer_claims.claim_text: A lease of immovable property for a period exceeding one month falls within section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, because the only leases excluded are a lease at will and a lease for a period not exceeding one month.

An instrument within section 2 has no force in law unless it is in writing and signed by every executant, or by a person duly authorised by the executant, and by the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and is attested by that notary.
The notary is under a corresponding duty not to attest unless the executants and the witnesses signed in her presence and in the presence of one another and she signed in their presence.
A notary may not attest a deed in any area other than the area in which she is authorised to practise, that area being the judicial zone in which she resides.
The Notaries Ordinance expressly contemplates a deed executed by two or more parties who do not sign it at the same time and place and provides how the execution rules apply in that case.

Where an instrument is executed before more than one notary, the notary who first attests it must comply with the whole of rule (20) and every other attesting notary with paragraphs (a) to (e) of that rule.

Section 2 also permits the instrument to be signed by a person duly authorised by the executant, and such authority is a power of attorney which, if executed in Sri Lanka, must be executed before two witnesses and attested by a notary public.

A power of attorney granted for a transaction falling within section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance must be notarially attested in accordance with the Notaries Ordinance and the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, and every power of attorney must be registered with the Registrar General.
A notary attesting a deed executed through an attorney must keep a true copy of the power of attorney with her protocol and forward a copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands.

An instrument executed in parts is expected to be signed by all the parties within three months of the date on which it is first signed by one of them, failing which the notary may be called on to deliver the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands.
The proposed lease runs for two years, so it is outside the one-month exclusion and must be executed in notarial form.
The parties cannot cure Rupa Perera's inability to travel by exchanging the document and signing it apart from a notary and the witnesses.
Malani Silva, practising in Colombo, cannot attest Rupa Perera's signature in Galle, because that lies outside the judicial zone in which she is authorised to practise.

Rupa Perera may sign the lease in Galle with two witnesses before a notary authorised to practise there while Gamini Sirisene signs the same instrument in Colombo before Malani Silva, each notary attesting the signatures taken before her.

Alternatively Rupa Perera may grant a notarially attested power of attorney complying with section 3A and registered under section 3, and her attorney may then sign the lease in Colombo before Malani Silva.

The agreement can therefore be signed either by both parties executing the one instrument at different times and places before two notaries, or by an attorney signing for Rupa Perera in Colombo under a duly executed and registered power of attorney.
What is not permitted is signature outside the presence of a notary and the witnesses, or attestation by the Colombo notary of a signature taken in Galle.

enrichment.original_background: Malani Silva is a Notary Practicing in Colombo .Her friend Rupa Perera who is the owner of a business premises in Galle wishes to lease out the same to a Gamini Sirisene for two (02) years at a monthly rental of Rs 150,000/. However Rupa is unable to come to Colombo to sign the Agreement

block_reason: Two grounds, neither of which the verifier can close from the corpus. First, part of the answer is conveyancing practice rather than statute: no corpus provision fixes the depth of the title search, and none creates the acquisition clearance, the street line and building limit confirmation, the bank's letter of release or the fresh survey that the answer calls for, so a complete answer does not follow from statute alone even though each document can be given a statutory reason. The nine claims marked disputed are the ones affected. Second, PROV-M026-006, an indispensable provision, exists only because of the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 4 of 2024, whose commencement date cannot be recovered from the corpus and which falls in the same year as the matter reference date. authority_requirement is left at statute_only because the missing element is practice rather than case law; a lawyer should decide whether it becomes mixed_statute_and_case, in which case the question must be reserved.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: be void as against all parties claiming an adverse interest thereto on valuable consideration by virtue of any subsequent instrument which is duly registered under this Chapter
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Priority between competing instruments turns on due registration, so the purchaser's lawyer must call for the vendor's title deeds together with a certified extract of the land registry folio to see what has in fact been registered against the land and in what order. It is the reason the search covers registered instruments and not only the deeds the vendor chooses to produce.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1927; the corpus records no amendment event on this section, and it stands in the consolidated 1990 edition. In force in October 2024.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: all duplicates and copies and all books and indexes kept under this Ordinance may be searched and examined by any person claiming to be interested therein or by his attorney-at-law or agent duly authorized thereto in writing, and certified copies of or extracts from any such duplicate, copy, or book may be obtained if required
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the statutory authority for the central document of any title examination: the certified extract of the land registry folio, obtained by the purchaser's attorney-at-law. It also authorises certified copies of registered duplicates where an original deed in the chain has been lost.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1927; no amendment event recorded on this section. In force in October 2024.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: affecting or relating to land instituted on or after the 9th day of November, 1917, shall bind a purchaser, unless and until the lis pendens is duly registered under this Chapter
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: A registered lis pendens binds a purchaser for valuable consideration. The search of the folio must therefore extend to registered lis pendens entries, and the purchaser must call for particulars of any pending action disclosed, because the company would take subject to the outcome of that action.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1927, amended in 1947. The text relied on is the consolidated text, which stood unchanged in October 2024.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim but begins after the opening negative of s.11(1) ("No lis pendens ... shall bind a purchaser, unless and until the lis pendens is duly registered"), so standing alone it states the opposite of the section; the section as a whole does support why_relevant, and the corpus OCR renders "lis" as "Us" in subsections (1) and (7).

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: shall be in force or avail in law unless - (a) the relevant deed or instrument shall be in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and the same shall be attested by such notary
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: No sale or transfer of immovable property avails in law unless it is in writing and notarially attested. Every link in the chain the vendor produces must therefore be a notarially executed deed (or its registered duplicate or a certified copy), which is why the lawyer calls for the deeds themselves and inspects the attestations rather than accepting a schedule of title.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1840; the section was replaced by Act No. 30 of 2022 and further amended by Act No. 4 of 2024, so the text quoted is the text in force in October 2024. The notarial requirement itself has stood since 1840, so the older deeds in the chain were subject to an equivalent requirement in the text then in force. A verifier should confirm the commencement date of Act No. 4 of 2024 against the matter date.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Provided further, where the transferee is a corporate body and where the Board of Directors of such corporate body is unable to be present and execute the deed or instrument, such Board shall authorise in writing, any other person to sign such deed or instrument on his behalf
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The purchaser here is a corporate body. The transferee must sign and place a thumb impression, and where the board cannot attend, a written board authority in favour of a named signatory is required. That written authorisation, together with proof of the board's constitution, is a document that must be in hand before the transfer is executed.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: This proviso is part of the section as it stood in October 2024, following the 2022 and 2024 amendments. It has no bearing on the older deeds in the chain, which were executed before it was introduced.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Wording is verbatim and is the text the corpus now prints, but subsection (2) with the corporate-transferee proviso was inserted only by the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 4 of 2024, which carries no commencement provision beyond its short title; the corpus records no certification date, so applicability at the October 2024 matter date cannot be established from the corpus and rests on the inference that an Act numbered 4 of 2024 was certified early in that year.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Proof of the undisturbed and uninterrupted possession by a defendant in any action, or by those under whom he claims, of lands or immovable property, by a title adverse to or independent of that of the claimant or plaintiff in such action
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Ten years of undisturbed adverse possession can defeat a paper title, so a deed chain alone does not settle title. The purchaser must also call for documents that evidence possession over at least that period: rates and assessment receipts, utility bills, tenancy or lease agreements and receipts for rent, and where the building is let, the tenancy records.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1871; the corpus records no amendment event on this section (Act No. 26 of 2014 amended the Ordinance but the corpus records no change to s.3). In force in October 2024.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act No. 38 of 2014
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: the transfer of title of any land situated in Sri Lanka, shall be prohibited if such transfer is- (a) to a foreigner; or (b) to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka under the Companies Act where any foreign shareholding in such company, either direct or indirect, is fifty per cent or above; or (c) to a foreign company, unless exempted as provided in section 3.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The purchaser is a company incorporated in Sri Lanka. A transfer to it is prohibited outright if direct or indirect foreign shareholding is fifty per cent or above, and s.2(2)(a) requires that the shareholding stay below that level for twenty consecutive years after the transfer. This makes the purchaser's own corporate documents part of the title examination: the share register, the latest annual return and the shareholder particulars needed to establish direct and indirect foreign holding.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 2014; the corpus records no amendment event on s.2 itself (the 2017 and 2018 amending Acts touched other sections, and s.3 was amended in 2018). In force in October 2024.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: A certificate of incorporation issued under this section in-respect of any company, shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that- (a) all the requirements under this Act relating to the incorporation of a company have been complied with
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Both parties are companies, so their existence and identity must be proved by the document the Act treats as conclusive: the certificate of incorporation. Certified copies of the certificate, the articles and the form recording the current directors and registered office are called for to show that the vendor company exists, that the persons signing for it are its directors, and that the purchaser company itself is validly incorporated.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 2007; subsections were substituted by the Companies (Amendment) Act No. 13 of 2019. The 2019 text is the text in force in October 2024.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: A company shall not enter into any major transaction, unless such transaction is- (a) approved by special resolution; (b) contingent on approval by special resolution; (c) consented to in writing by all the shareholders of the company; or (d) a transaction which the company is expressly authorised to enter into by a provision in its articles
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: A major transaction includes the acquisition of assets worth more than half the value of the company's assets before the acquisition. If the purchase price crosses that threshold for the purchaser, the transaction requires a special resolution, written consent of all shareholders or express authority in the articles. The certified special resolution or shareholders' consent, and the articles, must therefore be called for on the purchaser's side; the same test is applied to the vendor company's disposal of the building.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 2007; the corpus records no amendment event on this section. In force in October 2024.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt stops at "a provision in its articles" and omits the closing words of s.185(1)(d), "which was included in it at the time the company was incorporated", so the articles limb is stated more widely in the map and in the gold rule than the section allows.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Registration of a charge under this Part shall constitute notice to all persons of the particulars of the charge entered on the register of charges under this section, but not of the contents of the instrument which creates or is evidence of the charge
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Because registration of a charge is notice to all persons, the purchaser cannot claim ignorance of a charge registered against a corporate vendor. A search of the Registrar's register of charges, and the certificate of registration and instrument creating any subsisting charge, must be called for in addition to the land registry search, together with a letter of release or vacation of the mortgage on completion.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 2007; no amendment event recorded. In force in October 2024.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Every instrument presented for registration shall be registered in the book allotted to the division in which the land affected by the instrument is situated
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Registration counts only if it is in the correct folio or a folio opened in continuation of it with cross references. The extract called for must therefore be of the folio in which the first registered instrument affecting the land was registered and of every connected folio, otherwise the search misses registrations that still take priority.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1927, amended in 1974 (Act No. 14 of 1974). The amended text long predates the matter date and is the text relied on.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act No. 38 of 2014
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: The provisions of section 2 shall not apply to- (a) any land the title of which is transferred to a Diplomatic Mission of another State within the meaning of the Diplomatic Privileges Act
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: The exemptions qualify the prohibition, so if the purchaser were to rely on one (for instance listing on the Colombo Stock Exchange under paragraph (i)) the documents evidencing that exemption would have to be called for as well. On the facts no exemption is relied on, which is why the shareholding documents remain the operative check.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 2014, amended by Act No. 21 of 2018. The amended text is the text in force in October 2024.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Where a company creates a charge to which this section applies, it shall be the duty of the company within the time specified in subsection (3), to cause a copy of the instrument by which the charge is created or evidenced, to be delivered to the Registrar for registration under this Act.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: A charge on land or on any interest in land created by a company registered in Sri Lanka is registrable, so the register of charges is the right place to look for a mortgage granted by a corporate vendor. It tells the lawyer which company filings to call for.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 2007; no amendment event recorded. In force in October 2024.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Western Province Financial Statute No. 6 of 1990
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: No instrument chargeable with stamp duty shall be received or admitted in evidence by any person having by law or consent of parties authority to receive evidence or registered or authenticated or acted upon by any person or by any officer in a public office or corporation or bank or approved credit agency unless such instrument is duly stamped
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: The land is in Colombo, in the Western Province. An instrument that is not duly stamped cannot be registered or acted upon, so each deed in the chain must be inspected for the stamp or the endorsement of payment, and the stamp duty receipts and endorsements must be called for with the deeds.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1990; no amendment event recorded on this section in the corpus. A verifier should note that the corpus holds no later Western Province statute, so only the admissibility rule and not the current rate is relied on.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Wording is verbatim, but s.60 carries a proviso under which such an instrument may still be admitted in evidence and, where the duty chargeable is Rs. 5,000 or less, acted upon by the Registrar-General on payment of the proper duty and a penalty; why_relevant and the gold rule state the bar as absolute.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: No plan or map or copy or tracing of a plan or map shall be receivable in evidence in any court in Sri Lanka unless such plan or map has been prepared
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Ten perches has to be identified on the ground and matched to the description in the deeds. Only a plan prepared or certified by the Surveyor-General, an authorised registered surveyor or a registered licensed surveyor is receivable in evidence, so the survey plan and, where the identity of the land is in doubt, a fresh survey by a registered licensed surveyor must be called for.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 2002; no amendment event recorded. In force in October 2024.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: No building constructed after the date of the commencement of this Ordinance shall be occupied, except by a caretaker, until the Council has given a certificate that such building, as regards construction, drainage, and other respects conforms to the provisions of this Ordinance and to the by-laws made thereunder.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: The subject of the purchase is an office building in a Municipality. It cannot lawfully be occupied without the Council's certificate of conformity, so the approved building plan and the certificate of conformity are documents the purchaser must call for before parting with the price.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1947, amended in 1986. The amended text long predates the matter date.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: be a first charge on the premises in respect of which the same are incurred or made, and shall be paid to the Council by the owner of such premises and his successors in title
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Council expenses of this kind rank with the rates as a first charge on the premises and are payable by successors in title, so they pass to the purchaser. Rates and assessment receipts to date and a Council statement showing that nothing is outstanding must therefore be called for.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1947; no amendment event recorded on this section. In force in October 2024.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Urban Development Authority Law No. 41 of 1978
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: no Government agency or any other person shall carry out or engage in any development activity in any development area or part thereof, except under the authority, and in accordance with the terms and conditions, of a permit issued in that behalf by the Authority
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: If the premises are in a declared development area, the building had to be put up under a permit and in conformity with it. The permit, the approved plan and any clearance about street lines and building limits are called for both to confirm the building is authorised and to see what the company may lawfully do with the premises afterwards.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1978, amended in 1982. The amended text long predates the matter date.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Powers of Attorney Ordinance No. 4 of 1902
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Every power of attorney executed in Sri Lanka or any other country shall be registered with the Registrar General.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: One deed in the chain was signed by an attorney and not by the owner. The power of attorney under which he acted, its registration particulars and evidence that it had not been revoked at the date of that deed must be called for, because a deed signed without a subsisting authority breaks the chain.
