legal_issues.issue: Whether the purchase must be effected by a notarially attested deed and what the notary must do before drawing it.
What the notary must search for and obtain from the land registry, and what he must do about a registered encumbrance disclosed by the folio.
What corporate documents and authorisations the notary must call for where the purchaser is a private limited company, and how such a company executes a deed of transfer.
Whether the purchase is a major transaction requiring shareholder approval by special resolution.
Whether the restriction on transfer of land to a company with foreign shareholding of fifty per cent or above bars the transfer, and what proof the notary must have for the Registrar of Lands.
Whether the ceiling on agricultural land is exceeded once the estate is attributed to the company's shareholders.
What the notary must do about consideration, stamp duty, attestation and registration of the completed deed.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What must a notary instructed by Sales Plus (Private) Limited do, step by step, before, at and after executing a deed transferring a fifteen-acre planted coconut estate at Kuliyapitiya to the company?
gold_answer_draft.rule: A purchase of immovable property is of no force in law unless it is in writing and notarially attested (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2). Before drawing such a deed the notary must search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (17)(a)), and must obtain from the Registrar of the relevant Land Registry a certified extract of the folio showing ownership and registered encumbrances (rule (17)(b)(i)); the search matters because an unregistered instrument is void against a later duly registered instrument taken for value (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7). He must use his best endeavours to obtain the vendor's title deed and endorse the transaction on it (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (33)), and must embody in the deed or its schedule an accurate description of the land showing boundaries, extent and administrative situation (rule (16)(a)). Where a party is a corporate body he must retain a certified copy of the certificate of incorporation and the details of the board of directors (rule (17)(d)); at execution he must cause the seal of the corporate body to be affixed and obtain the signatures of the board or of a person authorised by board resolution (rule (14)), and attach a copy of that resolution to the protocol (rule (14), final sentence). A company enters a notarially attested obligation by a writing signed under the name of the company by two directors, by a sole director, by a class authorised by the articles, or by an appointed attorney, and notarially executed (Companies Act s.19(1)(a)). The acquisition of assets worth more than half the value of the company's assets is a major transaction which the company may not enter into without approval (Companies Act s.185(1) and (2)(a)), and that approval is exercised by special resolution (Companies Act s.92(1)(b)). Transfer of title to a Sri Lankan company in which direct or indirect foreign shareholding is fifty per cent or above is prohibited (Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2(1)(b)); the Registrar of Lands must be satisfied by documentary proof from the company secretary that foreign shareholding is below that level (s.4(3)), and an alienation in contravention of that Act is void (s.18). Agricultural land, meaning land used or capable of being used for agriculture (Land Reform Law s.66), is subject to a ceiling of fifty acres where it is not exclusively paddy (s.3(1)(b)); land owned by a private company is deemed owned by its shareholders in proportion to their shares (s.8), and land acquired in excess of the ceiling vests in the Land Reform Commission (s.5(1)). The notary must ascertain and set out the true and full consideration (Notaries Ordinance s.38(1)), must not attest until assured that the required stamp duty, charged on specified instruments under the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.3(1), is provided (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (6)), must state in the attestation whether the money was paid in his presence and the details of any bank draft (rule (20)(e)), and must submit the deed for registration within thirty days of attestation (rule (30A)).
gold_answer_draft.application: Because the company is buying immovable property the transaction has to be by notarially attested deed, so the notary is engaged from the outset. His first step is the land registry search against the vendor's chain: Mr. Piyadasa claims on Deed No. 4172 of 2009 and holds the earlier deeds back to 1985, and the certified folio extract for Delgahawatta discloses Mortgage Bond No. 2201 of 2018 in favour of a bank with no discharge entered, so the notary must require the bond to be discharged or a release executed and registered before or at the transfer rather than treat the title as clear. He must call for the vendor's title deeds and endorse the new transfer on them, and must take Plan No. 1123 and the locality particulars of Ihala Gomugomuwa village, Grama Niladhari Division 615, Kuliyapitiya East Divisional Secretary's Division, Kurunegala District, so that the schedule describes the fifteen acres accurately. On the purchaser's side he must call for and retain a certified copy of the certificate of incorporation of Sales Plus (Private) Limited, registration number PV 128654, and the particulars of its two directors. Since the price of Rupees Sixty Two Million exceeds half of the company's Rupees Ninety Five Million of assets, the acquisition is a major transaction and the notary must call for a special resolution of the shareholders as well as the board resolution authorising Ms. Ranatunga and Mr. Wickramasinghe to sign; a copy of the board resolution goes on the protocol, and the deed is signed under the name of the company by those two directors with the company seal affixed and is notarially executed. Because the purchaser is a Sri Lankan company the notary must establish its shareholding: both shareholders are Sri Lankan citizens and there is no foreign holding, so the prohibition is not attracted, but he should still obtain the secretary's documentary proof of that for the Registrar of Lands. The estate is planted with bearing coconut and so is agricultural land; treating the company's fifteen acres as belonging to the two shareholders in their equal shares gives each a further seven and a half acres, which added to Ms. Ranatunga's twenty acres and Mr. Wickramasinghe's twelve acres leaves both well under fifty acres of non-paddy agricultural land, so nothing vests in the Land Reform Commission. He must then set out the true consideration of Rupees Sixty Two Million, satisfy himself that the stamp duty on the transfer is provided, record in the attestation that payment was made in his presence together with the particulars of the bank draft, and lodge the deed for registration at the Kuliyapitiya Land Registry within thirty days of attestation. Two things remain open on the facts: whether the bank will in fact release the mortgage on payment, and whether the vendor's earlier chain of deeds is unbroken, and the notary cannot advise the company to complete until both are resolved.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary should, in order: search the registers and obtain the certified folio extract for the estate; examine the vendor's chain of deeds and require the subsisting mortgage bond to be discharged or released; obtain the survey plan and locality particulars for the schedule; call for and retain the company's certificate of incorporation and board details; obtain the special resolution approving the major transaction and the board resolution authorising the two directors to sign; draw the deed with an accurate description and the true consideration; see that the stamp duty is provided; attest the deed with the company seal affixed and the directors' signatures under the company's name, recording the bank draft payment in the attestation and attaching the board resolution to the protocol; endorse the transfer on the vendor's title deed; and submit the deed for registration within thirty days. On the facts as enriched no shareholding bar and no ceiling on agricultural land stands in the way, so the notary may complete the transaction once the mortgage is cleared and the special resolution is in hand.

answer_claims.claim_text: A sale or purchase of immovable property is of no force in law unless it is in writing and attested by a notary, so the company's purchase must be effected by notarial deed.

Before drawing a deed affecting an interest in land the notary must search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered.
The notary must obtain from the Registrar of the relevant Land Registry a certified extract of the folio containing the last entry showing ownership and the registered encumbrances.
An instrument that is not duly registered is void against a party claiming an adverse interest for valuable consideration under a later duly registered instrument.
The notary must use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed of the property transferred and endorse on it the number and date of the new deed and the nature of the transaction.
The deed or its schedule must carry an accurate and clear description of the land showing its boundaries, extent and administrative situation.
Where a party to the deed is a corporate body the notary must retain a certified copy of its certificate of incorporation and the details of its board of directors.

Where the executant is a corporate body the notary must cause the seal of the corporate body to be affixed and obtain the signatures of the board of directors or of a person authorised by board resolution, and must attach a copy of that resolution to the protocol.

A company enters into a notarially attested obligation by a writing signed under the name of the company by two directors, by a sole director, by a class of persons authorised by the articles, or by an appointed attorney, and notarially executed.

An acquisition of assets worth more than half the value of a company's assets is a major transaction which the company may not enter into unless it is approved, and that shareholder approval must be given by special resolution.

Transfer of title to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka in which direct or indirect foreign shareholding is fifty per cent or above is prohibited, the Registrar of Lands must be satisfied by documentary proof from the company secretary that the foreign shareholding is below fifty per cent, and an alienation in contravention of that Act is void.

Agricultural land means land used or capable of being used for agriculture, the ceiling on agricultural land that is not exclusively paddy is fifty acres, agricultural land owned by a private company is deemed owned by its shareholders in proportion to their shares, and land acquired above the ceiling vests in the Land Reform Commission.

The notary must endeavour to ascertain the true and full consideration and set it out in the deed, must not attest until assured that the required stamp duty, which is charged on specified instruments, is provided, and must state in the attestation whether the money was paid in his presence and the details of any bank draft.
The notary must submit the attested deed for registration within thirty days of the date of attestation.

The search of the registers and the certified folio extract for Delgahawatta disclose Mortgage Bond No. 2201 of 2018 in favour of a bank with no discharge entered, so the notary must require a discharge or release before or at the transfer instead of treating the title as clear.
answer_claims.verifier_note: No provision in the corpus obliges the notary to require a subsisting mortgage bond to be discharged or released; rules (17)(a) and (17)(b)(i) require only the search and the certified folio extract. The step is conveyancing practice, not a statutory duty.

answer_claims.claim_text: The notary must call for the vendor's deeds from Deed No. 4172 of 2009 back through the earlier chain and endorse the new transfer on the title deed.
answer_claims.verifier_note: Rule (33) requires best endeavours to obtain “the title deed” and to endorse it; calling for the vendor's earlier chain of deeds back to 1985 has no statutory source in this corpus, and the map's own corpus_gaps says the customary chain of title was to be excluded.

answer_claims.claim_text: Plan No. 1123 and the Ihala Gomugomuwa, Grama Niladhari Division 615 and Kuliyapitiya East Divisional Secretary's Division particulars are what the notary needs in order to describe the fifteen acres accurately in the schedule.
Because the purchaser is a private limited company the notary must retain a certified copy of its certificate of incorporation and the particulars of its two directors.

The price of Rupees Sixty Two Million is more than half of the company's Rupees Ninety Five Million of assets, so the acquisition is a major transaction and the notary must call for a special resolution in addition to the board resolution.

The deed must be signed under the name of the company by its two directors with the company seal affixed and notarially executed, and a copy of the board resolution authorising them must go on the protocol.

All the shares being held by two Sri Lankan citizens with no foreign holding, the prohibition on transfer to a company with fifty per cent or more foreign shareholding is not attracted, but the notary should still obtain the secretary's documentary proof of the shareholding for the Registrar of Lands.
answer_claims.verifier_note: Section 4(3) of Act No. 38 of 2014 places the duty to require the secretary's documentary proof on the Registrar of Lands; no provision requires the notary to obtain it.

answer_claims.claim_text: The estate is planted with bearing coconut and so is agricultural land, and the company's fifteen acres attributed equally to the two shareholders adds seven and a half acres to Ms. Ranatunga's twenty acres and to Mr. Wickramasinghe's twelve acres, leaving both under the fifty-acre ceiling so that nothing vests in the Land Reform Commission.

The notary must set out Rupees Sixty Two Million as the true consideration, satisfy himself that the stamp duty on the transfer is provided, and record in the attestation that payment was made in his presence by bank draft with the details of that draft.

The notary should complete the title search and folio extract, clear the subsisting mortgage, assemble the corporate documents and resolutions, draw and attest the deed with an accurate schedule, the true consideration and the company seal and directors' signatures, endorse the vendor's title deed, and lodge the deed for registration within thirty days.
answer_claims.verifier_note: The conclusion carries over the unsupported step of clearing the subsisting mortgage from CL-M041-Q01-015.

answer_claims.claim_text: On these facts no foreign shareholding bar and no ceiling on agricultural land stands in the way, so once the mortgage is discharged and the special resolution obtained the purchase may be completed.
answer_claims.verifier_note: The conclusion is made conditional on the mortgage being discharged, a condition with no statutory source in this corpus.

enrichment.original_background: Sales Plus (Private) Limited intends to purchase a coconut estate situated in Kuliyapitiya, Fifteen Acres (A15, RO, PO) in extent.
enrichment.enriched_background: Sales Plus (Private) Limited intends to purchase a coconut estate situated in Kuliyapitiya, Fifteen Acres (A15, RO, PO) in extent. Sales Plus (Private) Limited is a private limited company incorporated in Sri Lanka, registration number PV 128654, with its registered office at No. 14, Rajapihilla Road, Kurunegala. It has two directors, Ms. D. N. Ranatunga and Mr. S. B. Wickramasinghe, and its articles contain no provision expressly authorising the company to enter into transactions of this size. All the issued shares of the company are held by those two directors in equal halves; both are citizens of Sri Lanka resident in Sri Lanka, and no shares are held, directly or indirectly, by any person or body outside Sri Lanka. Apart from their shares in the company, Ms. Ranatunga owns twenty acres of coconut land at Pannala and Mr. Wickramasinghe owns twelve acres of mixed cultivation at Alawwa; neither owns any paddy land. The estate offered for sale is called Delgahawatta, depicted as Lot 1 in Plan No. 1123 dated 4 August 2007 made by A. B. legal_issues.issue: Whether a notary who does not personally know the executant may nevertheless attest the deed, and on what statutory footing.
Whether the notary's acquaintance with one attesting witness satisfies the identification requirement, or whether the executant must be known to at least two attesting witnesses.
What the notary must satisfy himself about before accepting the witnesses, and what the witnesses must do on the face of the deed.

gold_answer_draft.issue: The notary is asked to attest a deed of transfer executed by a man he does not know, in circumstances where he knows one of the two attesting witnesses. The issue is whether, and on what conditions, the rules to be observed by notaries permit him to attest a deed when the executant is a stranger to him.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (9), in the form in force in October 2021, provided that a notary shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same be known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses thereto. The statutory test therefore looks to the notary's knowledge of the executant, and failing that to the knowledge which at least two attesting witnesses have of the executant; the notary's acquaintance with a witness is not itself a substitute. Where the notary relies on the witnesses, the same rule requires that he satisfy himself, before accepting them as witnesses, that they are persons of good repute and that they are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation, and residence, and that the witnesses sign a declaration at the foot of the deed to that effect. Section 31 rule (8) forbids attestation of a deed to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters, and rule (12) forbids attestation unless the executant and the witnesses have signed in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, the notary signing before them. Rule (20) then requires the attestation to state whether the executants are known to the notary or whether the witnesses are known to him, and in the latter case to specify which executant is known to which witness. Notarial attestation of this kind is what the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 makes a condition of a valid transfer of immovable property.
gold_answer_draft.application: The notary does not know Mr. Dharmasena, so the first branch of rule (9) is unavailable and he cannot attest on the strength of his own knowledge. That he has known Mr. Silva for years does not cure this: rule (9) asks whether the executant is known to at least two attesting witnesses, not whether a witness is known to the notary. Here the second branch is satisfied, because both Mr. Silva and Mr. Fernando have been acquainted with the executant for more than twenty years and know his proper name, occupation and residence, so the executant is known to at least two of the attesting witnesses even though one of them is a stranger to the notary. Before accepting them the notary must satisfy himself that they are of good repute and that their acquaintance with the executant is real; on the facts both are of settled reputation in the executant's village and both are willing to sign the declaration at the foot of the deed, which the rule requires them to sign. Two witnesses will subscribe their signatures in letters, as rule (8) requires, and executant and witnesses can sign together before the notary as rule (12) requires. Having attested on the strength of the witnesses rather than his own knowledge, the notary must say so in his attestation and specify which of the witnesses knows the executant.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary may attest the deed, but only in these circumstances: the executant, though unknown to him, must be known to at least two of the attesting witnesses; the notary must first satisfy himself that those witnesses are persons of good repute and are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation and residence; the witnesses must sign the declaration to that effect at the foot of the deed; at least two witnesses must subscribe their signatures in letters, and executant, witnesses and notary must sign in one another's presence; and the attestation must record that the executant was not known to the notary and specify which witness knows him. Knowing one witness is not enough on its own. This states the position under section 31 as it stood at the October 2021 examination session; the rule was recast in 2022 to allow identity to be established by inspection of a national identity card, passport bio-page or driving licence, which was not an available route at that date.

answer_claims.claim_text: In October 2021 a notary could not authenticate or attest a deed unless the person executing it was known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses.

Where the notary relies on the witnesses' knowledge, he must satisfy himself before accepting them that they are persons of good repute and well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation and residence, and the witnesses must sign a declaration to that effect at the foot of the deed.
A deed may not be attested unless at least two witnesses have subscribed their signatures in letters.
The executant and the witnesses must sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and the notary must sign before them.
The attestation must state whether the executants are known to the notary or whether the witnesses are known to him, and in the latter case specify which executant is known to which witness.

Because the notary does not know the executant, he cannot attest on the first branch of the rule, and his acquaintance with one witness does not supply the missing knowledge, since the test is whether the executant is known to at least two attesting witnesses.
The second branch is satisfied on these facts, because both attesting witnesses have long been acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation and residence.
The witnesses may be accepted because they are of good repute and are willing to sign the required declaration at the foot of the deed.
Two witnesses will subscribe their signatures and executant, witnesses and notary can sign together, so the remaining execution formalities are met.

The notary may attest the deed, but only where the executant is known to at least two attesting witnesses whom he has satisfied himself are of good repute and well acquainted with the executant, who sign the declaration at the foot of the deed, with at least two witnesses subscribing and all signing in one another's presence, and with the position recorded in the attestation.
The notary's acquaintance with one witness alone does not entitle him to attest the deed.

This states the position as at October 2021; the identification rule was recast in 2022 to allow identity to be established by inspection of a national identity card, passport bio-page or driving licence, which was not available at the matter date.

enrichment.original_background: The Notary does not know the executant but he knows one witness.
enrichment.enriched_background: Mr. Sarath Wickramaratne is a notary practising in the Gampaha judicial zone. In October 2021 he is instructed to draw and attest a deed of transfer of a house and land at Ja-Ela for a consideration of Rs. 4,500,000. The intended executant, Mr. Nimal Dharmasena of Ja-Ela, is a stranger to the notary: he has never appeared before him and the notary does not know him. Mr. Dharmasena brings with him the earlier deed by which he acquired the property, and the notary has searched the land registry folio for the land. Two persons are to sign as attesting witnesses. The first is Mr. Ranjith Silva, a schoolteacher of Ja-Ela whom the notary has known personally for many years. The second is Mr. Upali Fernando, a retired postmaster of the same village, whom the notary has never met. Both witnesses live in Mr. Dharmasena's village, have been acquainted with him for more than twenty years, and know his proper name, his occupation and where he lives. Both are persons of settled reputation in the village, and both are willing to sign a declaration at the foot of the deed that they are well acquainted with Mr. Dharmasena and know his proper name, occupation and residence. All three men are able to attend at the notary's office at the same time and to sign in one another's presence and in the presence of the notary.

added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If only one witness knew the executant, the notary could not attest the deed, because the executant would be known neither to him nor to at least two attesting witnesses.

legal_issues.issue: What documents evidence the registered state of the title to Lot B and the undivided one-third share of Lot R at the Colombo Land Registry.
What documents evidence each notarially attested link in the chain, including Deed of Transfer No. 234 of 2015.
What court records evidence the partition decree and the devolution of Sunil Peiris's interest on his heirs.
What survey documentation identifies Lot B and Lot R on the ground and ties Plan No. 1125 back to Partition Plan No. 567.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Which four classes of documentation should the purchaser Anura Perera obtain from the present owners and from the Land Registry in order to establish a clear chain of title to Lot B, together with the undivided one-third share of the road reservation Lot R?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Duplicates, copies, books and indexes kept under the Registration of Documents Ordinance may be searched by an interested person or his attorney-at-law, and certified copies of or extracts from them may be obtained (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.42); such a certified copy or extract is admissible without proof of the Registrar's signature and is prima facie evidence of the contents of the folio (s.43). Registration matters, because an unregistered instrument is void against a later duly registered instrument taken for value (s.7), and an instrument must describe a divided allotment by its own boundaries and an undivided share by the proportion it bears to the whole (s.13). Every transfer of immovable property must be by a notarially attested deed (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2, executed in triplicate under s.16), and the notary who is to draw the purchaser's conveyance must himself search the land registry to ascertain the state of the title (Notaries Ordinance s.31). Where a link is a court record, the decree or a certified copy of it is the sole primary evidence of what the court decided (Civil Procedure Code s.206), certified copies of the judgment, decree or proceedings are obtainable from the Registrar of the court (s.205), a certificate of heirship is sufficient proof of the true heirs and of each heir's share on an intestacy (s.531), and a sealed duplicate or certified copy of letters of administration has the same effect as the original (s.554X). A plan is receivable in evidence only if prepared and certified as the Survey Act requires (s.13).
gold_answer_draft.application: First, certified extracts of the relevant Colombo Land Registry folios: the folio for the original land, Lot 1 in Partition Plan No. 567, and the folio opened for Lot B and Lot R after the sub-division, showing the ownership and every registered encumbrance, lis pendens, caveat, mortgage or seizure down to the date of the search. These come under s.42 and carry the evidentiary weight given by s.43, and they are what shows whether Deed No. 234 was duly registered and so protected by s.7. Second, certified copies of every notarially attested deed in the chain, taken either from the registered duplicate in the Land Registry under s.42 or from the attesting notary's protocol, beginning with Deed of Transfer No. 234 dated 23 March 2015 attested by Walter de Silva, Notary Public, and including any later deed by which an heir has dealt with a share; each must satisfy s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance and must describe Lot B by its own boundaries and the share of Lot R as an undivided one-third under s.13 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance. Third, certified copies of the court records that carry the title over the two links that are not deeds: the final decree and the partition plan filed in District Court of Colombo Partition Case No. 1256/P, obtained under s.205 and constituting under s.206 the primary evidence of the allotment of Lot 1 to Alfred Almeida; and the order, the letters of administration or certificate of heirship and the final proceedings in District Court Testamentary Case No. 345/16/T, obtained under s.205 and s.554X, the certificate of heirship being sufficient proof under s.531 of who the heirs of Sunil Peiris are and what share each takes. Fourth, a current survey plan with a superimposition, prepared and certified by a registered licensed surveyor, identifying Lot B and Lot R on the ground and tying Survey Plan No. 1125 dated 2 January 2000 back to Lot 1 of Partition Plan No. 567; a plan not so certified would not be receivable in evidence under s.13 of the Survey Act, and it is this document that shows whether the thirty perches recited in the deed match what is on the ground.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The purchaser should obtain, first, certified extracts of the relevant Colombo Land Registry folios; second, certified copies of every notarially attested deed in the chain, starting with Deed of Transfer No. 234 of 2015; third, certified copies of the final decree and plan in Partition Case No. 1256/P and of the order, letters of administration or certificate of heirship and final proceedings in Testamentary Case No. 345/16/T; and fourth, a current plan and superimposition certified by a registered licensed surveyor. Taken together these establish the chain from the partition decree to the persons who now hold Lot B and disclose any registered encumbrance. Nothing short of all four will show that Kusum Peiris cannot convey the entirety by herself.

answer_claims.claim_text: An interested person or his attorney-at-law may search the duplicates, copies, books and indexes kept under the Registration of Documents Ordinance and obtain certified copies of or extracts from them.
A copy or extract certified under the hand of a Registrar is admissible without proof of his signature or appointment and is prima facie evidence of the contents of the folio.
An unregistered instrument is void against a later instrument duly registered and taken for valuable consideration, which is why the registered state of the folio has to be checked.

A transfer of immovable property is of no force in law unless made by a deed in writing signed by the executants and witnesses before a notary and attested by him, and such deeds are executed in triplicate.
A notary must search the land registry before drawing an instrument affecting an interest in land, to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered.

A decree or a certified copy of it is the sole primary evidence of the decision of the court, and certified copies of the judgment, decree or proceedings may be obtained from the Registrar of the court.

A certificate of heirship is sufficient proof of the true heirs of the deceased and of the share each is entitled to receive on an intestacy, and a sealed duplicate or certified copy of letters of administration has the same effect as the original.

A plan is receivable in evidence only if it has been prepared and certified as the Survey Act requires, and an instrument must describe a divided allotment by its own boundaries and an undivided share by the proportion it bears to the whole.

The purchaser should obtain certified extracts of the Colombo Land Registry folios for the original land and for Lot B and Lot R, showing ownership and every registered encumbrance down to the date of the search.

The purchaser should obtain certified copies of every notarially attested deed in the chain, beginning with Deed of Transfer No. 234 dated 23 March 2015 attested by Walter de Silva, Notary Public, taken from the registered duplicate or from the notary's protocol.

The purchaser should obtain certified copies of the final decree and plan in District Court of Colombo Partition Case No. 1256/P and of the order, letters of administration or certificate of heirship and final proceedings in District Court Testamentary Case No. 345/16/T.

The purchaser should obtain a current survey plan and superimposition certified by a registered licensed surveyor, identifying Lot B and Lot R on the ground and tying Survey Plan No. 1125 back to Lot 1 of Partition Plan No. 567.
These four classes of document, taken together, establish the chain of title from the partition decree to the persons who now hold Lot B and disclose any registered encumbrance affecting it.

enrichment.original_background: Anura Perera your client wants to purchase a house and property situated in Rajagiriya said to be belonging to one Kusum Peiris and gives you a copy of a Transfer Deed No. 234 dated 23rd March, 2015 attested by Walter de Silva Notary Public and a copy of a Survey Plan No.1125 dated 2nd January, 2000 made by Anil Silva Licensed Surveyor relating to an allotment of land marked Lot B together with a Reservation for a Road marked Lot R of the Land called Dewatagahawatta in extent of 30 perches situated in Rajagiriya. On examining the documents tendered and after a search at the Colombo Land Registry you observe that Lot B and R depicted in the said Survey Plan are sub-divisions of Lot 1 containing in extent of One Rood and 10 Perches depicted in Partition Plan No. 567 dated 4th April 1998 also made by Anil Silva Licensed Surveyor (herein after referred to as the Original land). 1. The Original Land was allotted to one Alfred Almeida by Final Decree in the District Court of Colombo Partition case No. 1256/P and subsequently by Survey Plan 1125 made by Anil Silva Licensed surveyor sub-divided the said Lot 1 into 4 allotments of land marked A,B,C.and R. and by Deed of Transfer No. 234 dated 23rd March 2015 attested by Walter de Silva Notary Public sold Lot B together with undivided 1/3rd share of the Road Reservation marked Lot R to Sunil Peiris. 2. Sunil Peiris had died Intestate without children on 6th December 2016 leaving behind his widow Kusum Peiris. His estate was duly Administered in District Court Testamentary Case No. 345/16/T and proceedings terminated on 7th May 2018.On examining the Testamentary Case it was observed that the father of Sunil Peiris one Charles Peiris had pre-deceased him leaving behind 2 children named Upul and Wimal by his 1st marriage to Kamala Peiris and three children named Sunil, Kanthi and Manel by his 2nd marriage to Pushpa Peiris. Pushpa Peiris was alive and she too had a child by her 1st marriage to Lal Perera named Keerthi Perera and three children named Sunil, Kanthi and Manel by her 2nd marriage to Charles Peiris.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: to whom or to whose wife or husband any beneficial devise, legacy, estate, interest, gift, disposition, or appointment of or affecting any immovable or movable property (other than and except charges and directions for the payment of any debt or debts) shall be thereby given or made, such devise, legacy, estate, interest, gift, disposition, or appointment shall, so far only as concerns such person attesting the execution of such will, testament, or codicil, or the wife or husband of such person, or any person claiming under such person or wife or husband, be utterly null and void
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The operative provision. It avoids the beneficial gift taken by an attesting witness or that witness's spouse, preserves the witness's competence to prove the will, and carves out charges and directions for the payment of debts. Every limb of the advice turns on it.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1840; the corpus records no amendment event for this section, so the text read is the text in force at 2020-04.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: If any person who shall attest the execution of any will, testament, or codicil shall at the time of the execution thereof, or at any time afterwards, be incompetent to be admitted a witness to prove the execution thereof, such will, testament, or codicil shall not on that account be invalid.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the first half of the answer: the will itself is not struck down because of a defect in an attesting witness. Without it the advice could wrongly be that the whole will fails.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1840; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so the text applies at 2020-04.

Section 12 completes the exception already carved out in section 11 for charges and directions for the payment of debts: the charged debt survives the attestation and the creditor remains a competent witness.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a will is invalid because one of its two attesting witnesses is a beneficiary named in it.
Whether the beneficial devise and legacy given by the will to the attesting witness, and to the attesting witness's spouse, remain effective.
Whether a debt owed by the testator to the proposed witness and charged on the estate, and the witness's appointment as executor with a commission, are affected by his attesting the will.
What the attesting notary should accordingly advise the testator about the choice of attesting witnesses.

gold_answer_draft.issue: The testator wishes his nephew, who takes a devise of a house under the will and whose wife takes a legacy under it, to sign the will as one of the two attesting witnesses. The notary must advise the client on the effect of that course on the validity of the will, on what the nephew and his wife would take, on the debt charged in the nephew's favour and on his office as executor, and on what the testator should do instead.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11 provides that where a person attests the execution of a will and any beneficial devise, legacy, estate, interest, gift, disposition or appointment of movable or immovable property is thereby given to that attesting witness or to that witness's wife or husband, the gift is utterly null and void so far as concerns the attesting witness, the spouse and any person claiming under either, while the attesting witness is still admitted as a witness to prove the execution or the validity of the will. Charges and directions for the payment of debts are expressly excepted from that avoidance, and Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.12 confirms that a creditor whose debt is so charged is admitted as a witness notwithstanding the charge. Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.10 provides that a will is not invalid merely because an attesting witness is, at the execution or afterwards, incompetent to be admitted a witness to prove it. Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.13 provides that attesting does not make an executor incompetent as a witness and does not forfeit the recompense or commission payable for his trouble. Notaries Ordinance s.31(8) forbids the notary to attest an instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters, and Notaries Ordinance s.31(12) requires the executant and the witnesses to sign in the presence of the notary and of one another.
gold_answer_draft.application: The nephew is a person to whom a beneficial devise of immovable property, the house and premises at Kalutara, is given by the very will he is asked to attest, so under s.11 that devise would be utterly null and void so far as concerns him and anyone claiming under him. The legacy of Rs. 500,000 to his wife falls within the same provision, which reaches a gift to the wife or husband of the attesting witness, and would equally be void. The will would not itself fail: s.10 keeps the will valid despite any incompetency in an attesting witness, and s.11 in terms admits the attesting witness to prove the execution and validity of the will, so the second witness and the notary's attestation would still carry it. The direction that the estate be charged with and pay the Rs. 400,000 owed to the nephew on the promissory note is a charge and a direction for the payment of a debt, which s.11 expressly excepts from the avoidance, and s.12 confirms that he is admitted as a witness notwithstanding that charge, so that entitlement would survive. His appointment as executor and the commission for his trouble are preserved by s.13 and would not be forfeited by his attesting. On these facts the nephew would therefore keep only the charged debt and the executorship and would lose the house, and his wife would lose her legacy, for no gain; and since Notaries Ordinance s.31(8) requires two subscribing witnesses in any event and the testator is willing to call in another person, a disinterested witness to sign alongside the neighbour is readily available.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary should advise the testator not to have the nephew sign as an attesting witness. If he does so the will remains valid and the notary may still attest it, but the devise of the house to the nephew and the legacy to the nephew's wife would be utterly null and void so far as they are concerned, while the charged debt of Rs. 400,000 and the executorship with its commission would survive. The safe course, which the notary should press on the client, is to have the will attested by two witnesses who take no benefit under it, such as the neighbour and one other disinterested person of good repute, so that every disposition the testator intends takes effect. Who is in fact available to sign is a matter the notary must satisfy himself about at the execution.

answer_claims.claim_text: Where a person attests the execution of a will, a beneficial devise, legacy, estate, interest, gift, disposition or appointment of movable or immovable property given by that will to the attesting witness is utterly null and void so far as concerns that witness and any person claiming under him.
The same avoidance applies to a gift given by the will to the wife or husband of the attesting witness.

The will itself is not invalidated by the fact that an attesting witness is or becomes incompetent to be admitted a witness to prove its execution, and the attesting witness remains admissible to prove the execution or the validity of the will.
Charges and directions for the payment of debts are excepted from that avoidance, and a creditor whose debt is so charged is admitted as a witness notwithstanding the charge.
An executor is not rendered incompetent as a witness by attesting the will, and does not thereby forfeit the recompense or commission payable for his trouble.

The notary may not attest an instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters, and the executant and the witnesses must sign in the presence of the notary and of one another.
If the nephew attests the will, the devise to him of the house and premises at Kalutara is avoided so far as concerns him and anyone claiming under him.
The legacy of Rs. 500,000 to the nephew's wife is likewise avoided if the nephew attests the will, because she is the wife of the attesting witness.
The will would still be valid and the notary could still attest it, with the neighbour as the second subscribing witness.
The direction charging the estate with the Rs. 400,000 owed to the nephew on the promissory note survives his attestation, and he remains a competent witness notwithstanding that charge.
The nephew's appointment as executor and the commission for his trouble are not lost by his attesting the will.

The notary should advise the testator that the nephew should not sign as an attesting witness, and that the will should be attested by two witnesses who take no benefit under it, so that the devise to the nephew and the legacy to his wife take effect.

If the testator nevertheless insists, the notary may attest the will, which remains valid, but the nephew and his wife lose the devise and the legacy while the charged debt and the executorship with its commission survive.

enrichment.original_background: The testator of a Will wants one of the beneficiaries in his Will to sign as an attesting witness of the Will.
enrichment.enriched_background: Mr. Ariyaratne Peiris, a retired schoolmaster aged 76, of No. 27, Hospital Road, Kalutara, is of sound mind and has instructed his notary in March 2020 to draw and attest his last will. The will bequeaths his house and premises at No. 27, Hospital Road, Kalutara to his nephew, Mr. Sunil Peiris of Panadura, and leaves a legacy of Rs. 500,000 to Mrs. Nilanthi Peiris, who is the wife of Sunil Peiris. It also directs that the estate be charged with, and that the estate pay, a sum of Rs. 400,000 which the testator owes to Sunil Peiris on a promissory note dated 4 February 2019, and it appoints Sunil Peiris as executor with the usual commission. The testator now tells the notary that he wants Sunil Peiris to sign the will as one of the two attesting witnesses, the other being Mr. Wimalasena, a neighbour who takes nothing under the will. The testator says he is willing to call in any other person the notary suggests, and asks the notary to advise him.

added_facts.fact: The testator is Mr. Ariyaratne Peiris, a retired schoolmaster aged 76, of No. 27, Hospital Road, Kalutara, of sound mind, instructing his notary in March 2020.
added_facts.reason: Supplies the missing party identity and fixes the instructions before the April 2020 matter date; carries no legal weight of its own.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: None. Changing the name, age or town would not change any statutory consequence.

added_facts.fact: The beneficiary whom the testator wants to sign as an attesting witness is his nephew, Mr. Sunil Peiris of Panadura, and the will bequeaths to him the testator's house and premises at No. 27, Hospital Road, Kalutara.
added_facts.reason: Makes concrete that the proposed witness takes a beneficial devise of immovable property under the same will, which is the condition on which the avoidance operates.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the proposed witness took nothing under the will, nothing would be avoided and the notary could simply accept him as a witness.

added_facts.fact: The will also leaves a legacy of Rs. 500,000 to Mrs. Nilanthi Peiris, who is the wife of Sunil Peiris.
added_facts.reason: Engages the spouse limb of the avoidance, so the loss is not confined to the witness himself.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the witness were unmarried or his wife took nothing, the Rs. 500,000 legacy would stand and only the devise of the house would be avoided.

added_facts.fact: The will directs that the estate be charged with, and that the estate pay, a sum of Rs. 400,000 which the testator owes to Sunil Peiris on a promissory note dated 4 February 2019.
added_facts.reason: Brings in the express exception for charges and directions for the payment of debts and the creditor's competence as a witness, which separates the surviving entitlement from the avoided one.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Without the charged debt, everything the proposed witness took under the will would be avoided and nothing would be left in his favour.

added_facts.fact: The will appoints Sunil Peiris as its executor and provides for the usual executor's commission.
added_facts.reason: Tests whether attesting also costs the proposed witness his office and his commission, which is a distinct statutory question from the avoidance of the gift.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If a stranger were appointed executor, the commission point would not arise and the advice would be confined to the avoided gifts.

added_facts.fact: The second attesting witness is to be Mr. Wimalasena, a neighbour of the testator who takes nothing under the will, and the testator is willing to call in another person if the notary advises it.
added_facts.reason: Fixes that the second witness is disinterested and that a substitute witness is practically available, so the notary's advice has something to bite on.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the second witness were also a beneficiary, the gift to that second witness would be avoided as well; if no substitute witness were available the advice would have to address that practical difficulty.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument, other than a will or codicil, affecting land or other immovable property, unless the deed or instrument embodies therin or in a Schedule annexed therto an accurate and clear description of the said land or other property affected thereby, showing its boundaries, extent, situation specifying the district, pattu, korale, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division and the Grama Niladari Division, and the village within the District in which the land is situated
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the rule that fixes what the Schedule of the deed of transfer must contain: an accurate and clear description of the land showing boundaries, extent and situation down to the Grama Niladhari Division and village, with the assessment number and street name where the land lies in a municipality, town or development area. A deed whose Schedule is blank cannot lawfully be attested.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (16)(a) in this form was substituted by the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 47 of 2011, s.2, and was in force in April 2020. The consolidated corpus text of s.31 also carries later words on condominium parcels inserted by Act No. 31 of 2022, with further changes by Act No. 6 of 2024; those post-date the matter and are not relied on. legal_issues.issue: What particulars the Schedule of a deed of transfer of land must contain for the notary lawfully to attest the deed.
Whether what Anuk can convey out of the 45 perch portion allotted by the partition decree is a divided block or an undivided one third share, and how each must be described in the Schedule.
The consequence for attestation and for registration if the Schedule is left blank or omits the required particulars.

gold_answer_draft.issue: How the block of land must be described in the Schedule of the deed of transfer that the buyer's notary has left blank, and whether the description is of a divided block or of an undivided share of the 45 perch portion allotted by the partition decree.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Notaries Ordinance s.31(16)(a) forbids a notary to attest any deed, other than a will or codicil, affecting land unless the deed embodies in itself or in a Schedule annexed to it an accurate and clear description of the land showing its boundaries, extent and situation, specifying the district, pattu, korale, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division, Grama Niladhari Division and the village in the district in which the land is situated, and, where the land lies in a municipality, town or development area declared under s.2 of the Municipal Councils Ordinance, s.2 of the Urban Councils Ordinance or the corresponding local government law, the assessment number and the name of the street. Section 31(16)(b) adds that where the property is a share of a land the deed must state whether the share is divided or undivided and the fractional part which it is of the whole; a divided share must be clearly and accurately defined by its own particular boundaries and extent, while for an undivided share the boundaries and extent of the land of which it is a share must be stated. The same standard governs registration: s.13(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, as substituted by Act No. 48 of 2011, requires those particulars in the Schedule; s.13(2) requires a divided portion to be defined by its particular boundaries and extent; s.13(3) requires, for an undivided share, the proportion it bears to the entire land together with a description of the entire land; and s.13(5) obliges the Registrar to refuse registration of an instrument that does not state the required particulars. The description is not taken from the parties' instructions but from the land registry, since Notaries Ordinance s.31(17)(a) requires the notary to search the registers before drawing the deed.
gold_answer_draft.application: The subject matter is the divided portion of 45 perches allotted by the partition decree entered in the District Court of Ratnapura in case No. 345/P, of which the three brothers hold equal undivided shares. On the facts as given no further partition has divided that portion among them; that is precisely why the brothers are being pressed to file a partition action. What Anuk can convey as matters stand is therefore an undivided one third share, and by s.31(16)(b) and s.13(3) the Schedule must set out the whole 45 perch portion, describing it by its boundaries on the four sides and its extent of 45 perches as they appear in the partition decree and in the registered title, and locating it by district, pattu, korale, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division, Grama Niladhari Division and village, with the assessment number and street name added if the land lies within a municipality, town or development area; the deed must then state in terms that what is transferred is an undivided one third share of that land. Only if a defined block has in fact already been allotted to Anuk can the Schedule describe a divided block, and in that case s.31(16)(b) and s.13(2) require the block itself to be defined by its own particular boundaries and extent, with the extent stated in perches and each of the four boundaries given, and the deed to state that the share conveyed is a divided one and the fractional part it is of the whole. Either way the notary must verify the description against the folio by the search required by s.31(17)(a) and reproduce it in the Schedule. Because the Schedule has been left blank the deed as drafted cannot be attested at all, and if it were attested in that state registration would have to be refused under s.13(5). The papers do not show whether the land falls within a municipal, urban or Pradeshiya Sabha area, nor whether a survey has yet defined a block for Anuk, so those particulars must be settled before the Schedule is engrossed.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The draft should go back to the notary. The Schedule must carry an accurate and clear description of the land answering Notaries Ordinance s.31(16)(a) and s.13(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, stating boundaries, extent and situation down to the Grama Niladhari Division and village, with assessment number and street where applicable, and it must be framed under s.31(16)(b) and s.13(2) and (3) according to what Anuk actually owns at execution: the whole 45 perch portion described in full with the transfer expressed as an undivided one third share of it, unless a divided block has by then been allotted to him, in which case the block is described by its own particular boundaries and extent. A blank or defective Schedule leaves the notary in breach of his statutory duty and compels the Registrar to refuse registration.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary may not attest a deed affecting land unless the deed embodies, in itself or in a Schedule annexed to it, an accurate and clear description of the land showing its boundaries, extent and situation, specifying the district, pattu, korale, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division, Grama Niladhari Division and village (Notaries Ordinance s.31(16)(a)).

Where the land lies within a municipality, town or development area declared under section 2 of the Municipal Councils Ordinance, section 2 of the Urban Councils Ordinance or the corresponding local government law, the assessment number and the name of the street must also be given (Notaries Ordinance s.31(16)(a)).

Where the subject of the deed is a share of a land, the deed must state whether the share is divided or undivided and the fractional part it is of the whole; a divided share must be defined by its own particular boundaries and extent, and for an undivided share the boundaries and extent of the entire land of which it is a share must be stated (Notaries Ordinance s.31(16)(b)).

The registration law sets the same standard for the instrument presented for registration: an accurate and clear description in the Schedule with boundaries, extent and situation down to the Grama Niladhari Division, a divided portion defined by its particular boundaries and extent, and for an undivided share the proportion it bears to the entire land together with a description of the entire land (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.13(1) as substituted in 2011, and s.13(2) and (3)).
A Registrar must refuse to register an instrument that does not state those particulars (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.13(5)).

The description put into the Schedule must be taken from a search of the land registry, which the notary is bound to make before drawing a deed affecting an interest in land (Notaries Ordinance s.31(17)(a)).
The deed as forwarded cannot be attested, because a blank Schedule leaves the deed without the description of the land that Notaries Ordinance s.31(16)(a) makes a condition of attestation.

The land to be described is the divided portion of 45 perches allotted by the partition decree entered in the District Court of Ratnapura in case No. 345/P, and the Schedule must reproduce that land by its boundaries, extent and situation as it stands registered, ascertained by the notary's search of the folio.

On the facts as stated the three brothers hold equal undivided shares of that 45 perch portion and no further partition has yet divided it among them, so what Anuk can convey is an undivided one third share; the Schedule must then describe the whole 45 perch portion by its boundaries and extent and the deed must state that the interest transferred is an undivided one third share of it.

If a defined block has in fact been allotted to Anuk, the Schedule must instead define that block by its own particular boundaries and extent, giving the extent in perches and the four boundaries, and the deed must state that the share conveyed is a divided one.

The draft should be returned to the notary with instructions to complete the Schedule with an accurate and clear description of the land answering Notaries Ordinance s.31(16)(a) and (b) and s.13 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, expressed as a divided or an undivided share according to what Anuk in fact owns at execution.
If the Schedule is left blank or is inaccurate the notary is in breach of his statutory duty and the Registrar of Lands must refuse registration of the transfer.

enrichment.original_background:
Anuk de Silva, Pramuk de Silva and Dinuk de Silva are three brothers and they own equal undivided shares of a divided portion of a land in extent of 45 perches as per a Partition Decree in the District Court of Ratnapura in case No. 345/P. Anuk wishes to sell his entitlement of the land. Pramuk wishes to construct a house on his share of the land having mortgaged it to a Bank. Dinuk wants to Lease his share of land to a Company for a commercial purpose. The Bank informed Pramuk that he should have a divided and defined block of land in order to enable them to grant him a loan. Therefore, he informs his brothers that they should file a Partition Action for the division of the property. Anuk has approached you for Legal advice.

The Notary retained by the buyer of Anuk's divided block of land has drafted the deed of Transfer and forwarded it to you for perusal. You observe that he has kept the Schedule blank.

This is the direct answer to what document may be presented.

It also establishes that registration by the Registrar, not any court order, is what brings the caveat into operation.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: in an action commenced by the caveator in a competent court within thirty days from posting of the notice required by subsection (4) it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that the instrument presented for registration is or was at the time of registration void or voidable by the caveator or fraudulent as against him or in derogation of his lawful rights the court may order the instrument to be rectified or cancelled as may be necessary to preserve the rights of the caveator
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The second and decisive limb of the effect. It supplies the thirty-day time limit running from the posting of the notice, the grounds the caveator must prove (void, voidable, fraudulent as against him, or in derogation of his lawful rights) and the relief the court may give (rectification or cancellation of the instrument and correction of the register). It matches the wording of the background almost exactly.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: A caveat shall be in force for such period as may be specified therein, not being longer than the period covered by the fee paid on the caveat.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Limits how long the protection lasts and ties duration to the fee paid, which matters because s.32(5) operates only while a caveat is in force.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1927 at the matter date; replaced by a flat two-year maximum only by Act No. 32 of 2022 s.2(3).
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Confirmed verbatim and promoted from supporting to indispensable, because s.32(5) operates only "while a caveat is in force" and the duration rule in s.32(3) is therefore a necessary condition of the remedy the answer states.

legal_issues.issue: What document may a person present for registration in order to be served with notice of the presentation for registration of any instrument affecting his land?
To whom, and at which office, must that document be presented?

What is the legal effect of registering that document, including the notice it produces, the time limit and grounds for challenging the instrument, the relief available, the duration of the protection and its cancellation?

gold_answer_draft.issue: The issue is what document may be presented for registration so that the owner of the Colombo 5 property is told whenever a document affecting that land is presented for registration, to whom that document must be presented, and what legal consequences follow from its registration, including what the owner must then do to have the offending document set aside.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The document is a caveat. Under the Registration of Documents Ordinance s.32(1) any person, called in the Ordinance a caveator, may present for registration a caveat in the prescribed form requiring to be served with notice of the presentation for registration of any instrument affecting the land described in the caveat. The prescribed form is the relevant form in the Second Schedule, which s.50 directs is to be used with such variations as circumstances require. The caveat is presented for registration to the Registrar: s.32(2) obliges the Registrar on receiving a caveat to register it in the same manner as other instruments but to retain the caveat itself. The Registrar meant is a Registrar of Lands, since s.2(2) provides that the business of the land register office and its branch offices is conducted by the Registrar-General of Lands and Registrars of Lands; and because s.32(2) directs registration in the same manner as other instruments, s.14(1) places the caveat in the book allotted to the division in which the land is situated, that is, at the land registry serving the division in which the property lies. What counts as an instrument affecting the land is fixed by s.8, which deems every instrument that purports or operates to create, transfer, charge or extinguish any right, title or interest in land to affect it. The effect of registration is threefold. First, duration: by s.32(3) the caveat is in force for the period specified in it, which cannot exceed the period covered by the fee paid, and the fee item substituted by the Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act No. 21 of 2013 s.5 is charged for each land described in the caveat, for each land registry in which it is registered, and for each period of two years. Second, warning: by s.32(4) the notice to the caveator is in the prescribed form and is sent by registered letter to the address mentioned in the caveat, and by s.43(2) the Registrar's endorsement on the duplicate caveat is admissible without proof of his signature or appointment and is prima facie evidence of registration. Third, remedy: by s.32(5), if while the caveat is in force an instrument affecting the land described in it is presented for registration, and the caveator commences an action in a competent court within thirty days from the posting of that notice and proves that the instrument is or was at the time of registration void or voidable by him, fraudulent as against him, or in derogation of his lawful rights, the court may order the instrument rectified or cancelled as necessary to preserve his rights and may order the register corrected. Two limits complete the picture. legal_issues.issue: Whether knowledge that a named person has executed a will before the notary, and the contents of that will, is a secret confided to the notary or of which he became possessed in the execution of his office within rule (1) of section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance.

Whether either exception in rule (1) applies - that is, whether the testator, as the notary's employer, has given express permission to disclose, and whether the notary is required by law to disclose to the testator's children.
Whether the children of a living testator, having no authority from him, can stand in the place of the employer for the purpose of giving that permission.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the notary may tell the testator's children that he has attested a Will executed by their father, and disclose what it contains, while the testator is alive and has given no permission. The issue is whether that knowledge is a secret within the notary's statutory duty of secrecy, and whether either exception to that duty is made out.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Notaries Ordinance s.31(1) makes it the duty of every notary that he shall not divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office, unless with the express permission of his employer or when required to do so by law. The prohibition is general and the two exceptions are the only gateways out of it. That a will attested by a notary falls within this protection is borne out by the way the Ordinance itself handles wills: under s.31(24) a notary's protocol register may record only the number and date of a will or codicil, and under the proviso to s.31(26)(a)(i) the monthly list delivered to the Registrar of Lands likewise carries only the number and date of a will. Breach of rule (1) is not merely unprofessional; the s.31 rules are penally enforced by s.34 of the Ordinance, which makes a notary who disregards rule (1) guilty of an offence triable summarily before a Magistrate and liable to a fine in addition to any civil liability he may incur, although the fine figures in the consolidated text come from a 2022 amendment and were not the figures in force in October 2019.
gold_answer_draft.application: The notary learned that Mr. Wickramaratne had made a Will, and learned its contents, because the Will was executed before him and attested by him on 12 March 2017 and its protocol is in his custody. That is information of which he became possessed in the execution of his office, so s.31(1) is engaged. On the first exception, the employer for this purpose is the testator, the person at whose instance the notary acted, and he is alive and of sound mind; he has given the notary no permission, express or otherwise, to tell his children anything about the Will. The children are not the notary's employer, and holding no power of attorney or other authority from their father they cannot supply the permission on his behalf; their relationship to the testator and their expectation as prospective heirs give them no standing under the rule, and while the testator lives they have no interest in his estate at all. On the second exception, nothing requires the notary to disclose: the children come of their own accord with no court order, summons or other legal process, and no public officer has called for the information. Neither exception being made out, the general prohibition stands. It also applies to the bare fact of attestation and not only to the terms of the Will, since confirming that a named person has made a Will before him would itself divulge something the notary knows only through his office.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: No. The notary should not divulge the information. He should decline to confirm or deny whether he has attested a Will for their father and should not disclose its contents; he may properly tell the children that he is bound to keep his client's affairs secret and that they should approach their father. The position is not permanent: if the testator himself expressly permits disclosure, or if a court or some other law requires the notary to disclose, s.31(1) allows him to speak. If he were to divulge the information now, he would expose himself to prosecution under s.34 of the Ordinance in addition to any civil liability.

legal_issues.issue: To whom stamp duty on a lease of immovable property is paid, and how payment is evidenced on the instrument.
Who, as between lessor and lessee, bears the duty on this lease.

gold_answer_draft.issue: To whom the stamp duty on this lease agreement is paid, in what manner and by when, and which party bears it.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Under the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act No. 12 of 2006 s.6(c), stamp duty on a lease is payable by the lessee unless the parties agree otherwise. Section 8(1) provides that, where the duty is not compounded, it is paid by affixing adhesive stamps to the required value before or at the time of execution, with the value stated on the face of the instrument. Section 8(2) provides a distinct route for an instrument relating to a mortgage or lease of immovable property: the duty may be paid to a prescribed bank before or at the time of execution and, where that is impossible for reasons beyond the control of the person liable, within seven days of execution; the bank then issues a certificate in the prescribed form certifying that the duty has been duly paid. Section 9 provides that all stamp duty payable to a Provincial Council in respect of documents referred to in List I of the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution is paid to the Provincial Council within whose limits the instrument was executed or the property is situated.
gold_answer_draft.application: This is a lease of immovable property, the upstair floor of the house bearing assessment No. 30/1 at Nawala Road, Rajagiriya, so s.8(2) applies. Payment is made to a bank prescribed for the purpose, before or at the time the lease is executed, and the bank's certificate of payment is affixed to the instrument; only if payment before execution is prevented by reasons beyond the control of the person liable does the seven-day allowance apply. The money is not handed to the lessor and is not paid to the notary. As between the parties, s.6(c) puts the duty on Ravi Perera as lessee, so unless the lease provides otherwise he is the person who must make the payment. The premises are situated, and the lease would be executed, within the Western Province, so if lease duty falls within List I of the Ninth Schedule the Council entitled to it under s.9 is the Western Provincial Council. The Ninth Schedule itself is outside the corpus, so that last step is stated as a qualified proposition rather than a settled one.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The duty is paid to a prescribed bank, before or at the time of execution of the lease, and the bank's certificate in the prescribed form is affixed to the instrument; alternatively, in the general manner under s.8(1), by adhesive stamps of the required value affixed before or at execution and cancelled by the executant. The person who must pay is the lessee, Ravi Perera, absent agreement to the contrary. Where the duty is one payable to a Provincial Council, s.9 directs it to the Council within whose limits the instrument was executed or the property is situated, which on these facts points to the Western Provincial Council.

answer_claims.claim_text: Stamp duty on a lease is payable by the lessee unless there is an agreement to the contrary.

Stamp duty on an instrument relating to a lease of immovable property may be paid to a prescribed bank before or at the time of execution, and the bank issues a certificate in the prescribed form certifying that the duty has been duly paid.
Where the duty cannot be paid before or at execution for reasons beyond the control of the person liable, it must be paid to the prescribed bank within seven days from the date of execution.
Otherwise the duty is paid by affixing adhesive stamps to the required value before or at the time of execution, and the value paid is specified on the face of the instrument.

Stamp duty payable to a Provincial Council in respect of documents within List I of the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution is paid to the Council within whose limits the instrument was executed or the property is situated.
Because the lease concerns immovable property, the duty on it is paid to a prescribed bank and the bank's certificate is affixed to the lease agreement.
The lessee, Ravi Perera, is the party who must pay the duty unless the lease agreement provides otherwise.
The demised premises are at Nawala Road, Rajagiriya, within the Western Province, so any Provincial Council entitlement to this duty under s.9 would be that of the Western Provincial Council.

The stamp duty on this lease agreement is paid to a bank prescribed for that purpose, before or at the time of execution, by the lessee, and is evidenced on the instrument by the bank's certificate or, in the general case, by adhesive stamps.

block_reason: Verifier downgrade from proposed_gold. The conclusion is probably right, but the decisive step is not a direct statutory inference. Section 327 defines "street" inclusively and as a road over which the public HAVE a right of way, so a public right of way is a precondition of street status and not an effect of vesting; s.71(6) has to extend the word for its own section precisely because the general definition carries that requirement. The question stipulates only that Lot R1 "is vested in the Kaduwela Municipal Council" and does not say by what route, and the corpus holds no provision on the approval of a subdivision plan or on the dedication of a private road reservation to the public. The answer therefore assumes, rather than shows, that Lot R1 became a street. A lawyer should confirm that assumption before this becomes a gold item; the authority requirement remains statute_only.
