legal_issues.issue: What the legal character of Lot R1 becomes once it is vested in the Kaduwela Municipal Council.
Whether Kapila Fernando, who holds no servitude over Lot R1, may nevertheless pass over it to reach the main road once it is vested in the Council.
Whether that access is secure, and what the Council can do if it is obstructed.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Kapila Fernando, who owns the block adjoining Lot A2, has no access to the main road and holds no servitude over Lot R1, can gain access to his land over the road reservation Lot R1 if Lot R1 is vested in the Kaduwela Municipal Council.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Under the Municipal Councils Ordinance s.37(1)(b), all streets within the Municipality, together with their pavements, stones and materials, are vested in the Municipal Council, save streets specially exempted by the President. A street, for the purposes of that Ordinance, includes any road, lane or passage, whether a thoroughfare or not, over which the public have a right of way (s.327). A street so vested is a public street which the Council is under a duty to maintain and cleanse (s.46(a)); it may be sold, leased or exchanged only after it ceases to be used as a street and with the prior approval of the President (s.50); and the Council may order the removal of any obstruction or encroachment on a street under its control (s.77). Section 65 shows one route by which a road serving private owners is constituted a public road and vested in the Council.
gold_answer_draft.application: If Lot R1 is vested in the Kaduwela Municipal Council under s.37(1)(b), it is no longer a private road reservation burdened only by servitudes granted to particular lots. It is a street over which, by the definition in s.327, the public have a right of way. Kapila Fernando therefore does not need a grant from Ananda Senerath or from anyone else: he may use Lot R1 as a member of the public to reach the main road from his block. That access is protected in practice, because the Council must maintain the street under s.46(a), cannot dispose of it while it is still used as a street without the President's prior approval under s.50, and can order any obstruction or encroachment on it to be removed under s.77. The scenario does not say how the vesting came about, and s.65 is only one of the possible routes; but the question directs that vesting be assumed, and it is on that assumption that the answer proceeds.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Yes. Once Lot R1 is vested in the Kaduwela Municipal Council it is a public street over which the public have a right of way, so Kapila Fernando can gain access to his allotment over Lot R1 as a member of the public, without purchasing any right of way from Ananda Senerath, and the Council's duties and powers over the street support that access.

answer_claims.claim_text: All streets within a Municipality, other than those specially exempted by the President, together with their pavements, stones and materials, are vested in the Municipal Council.
For the purposes of the Municipal Councils Ordinance a street includes any road, lane or passage, whether a thoroughfare or not, over which the public have a right of way.

A street vested in a Municipal Council is a public street which the Council must maintain and cleanse, and which it may sell, lease or exchange only once the street has ceased to be used as a street and with the prior approval of the President.
The Council may order any person obstructing or encroaching upon a street under its control to remove or abate the obstruction, and may remove it itself if the order is not complied with.

One statutory route by which a road serving private owners becomes vested in the Council is a contract under which the road is constituted a public road and vested in the Council by an appropriate instrument.

On the assumption stated in the question, Lot R1, the road reservation giving access from the lots to the main road, is vested in the Kaduwela Municipal Council and is therefore a street vested in that Council.

Because a vested street is one over which the public have a right of way, Kapila Fernando may pass over Lot R1 as a member of the public even though he holds no servitude over it and his block was never a dominant tenement of the right of way.
Kapila Fernando can gain access to his allotment over Lot R1 once it is vested in the Kaduwela Municipal Council, and he need not purchase a right of way from Ananda Senerath.
That access is supported by the Council's duty to maintain the street, the restriction on disposing of it while it is still used as a street, and the Council's power to clear obstructions on it.

legal_issues.issue: What duties does the attesting notary owe in respect of the original of the deed: attestation, retention of the protocol, and registration.
What duties does he owe in respect of the duplicate: to whom, in what form and by what date it must be delivered or transmitted.
Whether the land being in Nuwara Eliya while the notary resides at Gangodawila alters those duties, and in particular whether a further document must go to a second Registrar of Lands.
What follows if the notary fails in these duties, and whether such a failure affects the validity of the deed.

gold_answer_draft.issue: The question is what the notary must do with the original of the deed he has attested and with its duplicate, given that he resides and practises at Gangodawila in the Colombo district while the land the deed affects lies at Nuwara Eliya, in a different land registration district.
gold_answer_draft.rule: By rule (20) of section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance the notary must without delay duly attest the deed executed before him, sign and seal the attestation and state in it the prescribed particulars, among them the number and value of the stamps affixed to the deed and to the duplicate (rule (20)(f)). By rule (24) he must carefully preserve as his protocol a draft or copy of the deed signed by the parties and witnesses to the original, and keep an indexed register of protocols. By rule (26)(a)(i) he must deliver or transmit the duplicate of every deed other than a will or codicil attested by him in a month to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which he resides, so that it reaches the registrar on or before the fifteenth day of the following month, together with a signed list in duplicate in the prescribed form; on transmission he tenders two lists, one of which the registrar signs and returns, the other being filed and kept with the duplicate (Notaries Ordinance s.42; Registration of Documents Ordinance s.5(1)). Rule (29) adds a further duty where the deed affects land in a district other than the one in which the attesting notary resides: by the fifteenth day of the month next following execution he must also deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated a copy of the deed certified by him as correct, with a list in duplicate of the deeds relating to lands in that district. The original goes forward for registration, and by section 14(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance an instrument is registered in the book allotted to the division in which the land affected is situated; an instrument not duly registered is void against a later instrument duly registered for value (s.7(1)). Where the notary has been instructed to register the deed and given a sufficient sum for that purpose, section 37 of the Notaries Ordinance makes it an offence for him to fail to use due diligence in effecting registration. Section 32(1) exempts certain classes of instrument from rules (20), (24) and (26), and section 33 provides that non-observance of a rule of section 31 in a matter of form does not by itself invalidate the instrument.
gold_answer_draft.application: The instrument is a deed of transfer of land in Sri Lanka, executed on 8 March 2019 before this notary alone; it is not a will or codicil and falls within none of the classes exempted by section 32(1), so rules (20), (24), (26) and (29) apply to it in full. On the original, the notary must complete his attestation at once, stating the matters required by rule (20), including the stamps borne by the original and by the duplicate, and must retain the signed protocol under rule (24). On the duplicate, because he resides at Gangodawila, within the Colombo land registration district, rule (26)(a)(i) requires the duplicate to reach the Registrar of Lands of the Colombo district on or before 15 April 2019, with the list in duplicate signed by him and two lists tendered to the registrar under section 42. Because the land is at Nuwara Eliya, in a different district, rule (29) is engaged: by the same date, 15 April 2019, he must deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the Nuwara Eliya district a copy of the deed certified by him as correct, with a list in duplicate of the deeds he attested relating to lands in that district. As the parties instructed him in writing to register the deed and paid him the registration charges, section 37 obliges him to use due diligence in effecting registration, and section 14(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance means that the original must be presented at the land registry for the Nuwara Eliya division, not at the registry of his own district; delay in registering the original carries the risk under section 7(1) that a later registered instrument taken for value will gain priority.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary's duties divide between the two documents. On the original he must attest it fully and without delay, keep his protocol of it, and, having been instructed and put in funds, use due diligence to have it registered in the land registry of the Nuwara Eliya division where the land lies. On the duplicate he must transmit it, with the lists in duplicate, to the Registrar of Lands of the Colombo district, the district in which he resides, so that it reaches that registrar by 15 April 2019; and because the land lies in another district he must in addition send to the Registrar of Lands of the Nuwara Eliya district, by the same date, a copy of the deed certified by him as correct with a like list. Failure in these duties exposes him to prosecution, but where the default is one of form it does not of itself make the deed invalid.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary must without delay duly attest every deed executed or acknowledged before him, sign and seal that attestation, and state in it the matters set out in rule (20) of section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance, including the number and value of the stamps affixed to the deed and to its duplicate.

He must carefully preserve as his protocol a draft or copy of every deed executed before him, carrying his signature and the signatures of the parties and witnesses to the original, and keep an indexed register of protocols, so that the protocol is a third document distinct from the original and the duplicate (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (24)).

He must deliver or transmit the duplicate of every deed other than a will or codicil attested by him during a month to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which he resides, so that it reaches the registrar on or before the fifteenth day of the following month, together with a list in duplicate signed by him in the prescribed form (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (26)(a)(i)).
answer_claims.verifier_note: Supported by the text of rule (26)(a)(i); note only that the prescribed form was "Form F" in April 2019 and became "Form F 1" in 2024.

answer_claims.claim_text: When the duplicate is transmitted the notary must tender two lists to the registrar, who signs the lists, returns one to the notary and files and preserves the other with the duplicate among the records of his office, the duplicates being bound into volumes (Notaries Ordinance s.42; Registration of Documents Ordinance s.5(1)).

Where the deed affects land situated in a district other than the district in which the attesting notary resides, he must, besides transmitting the duplicate, deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated a copy of the deed certified by him as correct, together with a list in duplicate signed by him, on or before the fifteenth day of the month next following that in which the deed was executed (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (29)).
answer_claims.verifier_note: Supported by the text of rule (29); the form was "Form F" at the matter date.

answer_claims.claim_text: The original is the instrument that goes forward for registration, and it must be registered in the book allotted to the division in which the land affected by it is situated (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.14(1)); an instrument that is not duly registered is void against a later instrument duly registered for value (s.7(1)).
answer_claims.verifier_note: The section 7(1) limb and the registration-in-the-proper-book limb from section 14(1) are supported, but the opening assertion that the original is the instrument that goes forward for registration is contradicted by section 26(2) of the same Ordinance (PROV-M091-901), under which either the original or a duly attested or certified copy may be presented for registration.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary who has received instructions to register a deed drawn or attested by him, and a sum sufficient to meet the expense of registration, commits an offence if he fails to use due diligence in effecting that registration (Notaries Ordinance s.37).

Rules (20), (24) and (26) of section 31 do not apply to the classes of instrument listed in section 32(1) of the Notaries Ordinance, and non-observance of a rule of section 31 in a matter of form does not by itself render the instrument invalid (s.33).
answer_claims.verifier_note: Accurate on its own terms. Note that section 32(1) disapplies rules (20), (23), (24), (25) and (26) only; rule (29) is not among them.

answer_claims.claim_text: This deed of transfer of land in Sri Lanka is neither a will nor a codicil and falls within none of the excluded classes, so rules (20), (24), (26) and (29) apply to it in full.
answer_claims.verifier_note: Correct in result, but the citation is incomplete: section 32(1) says nothing about rule (29), so the application of rule (29) rests on rule (29)'s own words, which exclude only wills and codicils, not on the section 32(1) exception.

answer_claims.claim_text: Having attested the deed on 8 March 2019, the notary must complete the attestation on the original at once, stating among other things the stamps borne by the original and by the duplicate, and must retain his signed protocol of it.

Because the notary resides at Gangodawila, within the Colombo land registration district, the duplicate of the deed executed in March 2019 must reach the Registrar of Lands of the Colombo district on or before 15 April 2019, with the signed list in duplicate and against two lists tendered to the registrar.
answer_claims.verifier_note: Turns on the enriched fact that Gangodawila lies within the Colombo land registration district; nothing in the corpus fixes that, as corpus_gaps already records.

answer_claims.claim_text: Because the land is at Nuwara Eliya, in a district other than the district in which he resides, the notary must in addition deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the Nuwara Eliya district, on or before 15 April 2019, a copy of the deed certified by him as correct together with a list in duplicate of the deeds he attested that relate to lands in that district.

Since the parties instructed him to register the deed and put him in funds, he must use due diligence to present the original for registration in the land registry for the division in which the Nuwara Eliya land lies, and not in the registry of his own district.
answer_claims.verifier_note: The registry is right, since section 14(1) fixes it by the situation of the land, and the section 37 duty of diligence is right, but "present the original" overstates section 26(2), which permits a duly attested or certified copy to be presented instead.

answer_claims.claim_text: The notary's duties therefore divide between the two documents: on the original, to attest it fully and without delay, to keep his protocol of it, and to have it registered with due diligence in the Nuwara Eliya land registry; on the duplicate, to transmit it to the Registrar of Lands of the Colombo district by 15 April 2019 with the lists in duplicate, and, because the land lies elsewhere, to send a copy certified by him as correct with a like list to the Registrar of Lands of the Nuwara Eliya district by the same date.
answer_claims.verifier_note: Subject to the same qualification on the original as CL-M091-Q01-006 and CL-M091-Q01-013.

answer_claims.claim_text: Neglect of these duties exposes the notary to prosecution, but where the default is one of form it does not of itself invalidate the deed.
answer_claims.verifier_note: Prosecution is verifiable only for failure to register under section 37; for breach of rules (24), (26) and (29) the penal provision in force in April 2019, section 34 before its replacement in 2022, is not in the corpus. The section 33 saving is also subject to a proviso the map does not quote.

Perera, and two attesting witnesses in his presence and in the presence of one another. Stamps to the value of the duty payable were affixed to the original and to the duplicate. On the day of execution the parties instructed him in writing to attend to the registration of the deed and paid him a sum sufficient to cover the registration charges.

block_reason: The decisive step is not settled by the corpus. Section 4A of the Notaries Ordinance, read with sections 3(1) and 4(2), deems a warrant expressed for a judicial division to authorise practice throughout the judicial zone in which the notary resides, so whether a warrant expressed as ‘Colombo’ held by a notary residing at Battaramulla reaches Mount Lavinia turns on the delimitation of judicial zones under the Judicature Act and the orders made under it, none of which is in the corpus. The researcher supplied the answer to that question as a synthetic decisive fact (FACT-M092-Q01-002), which pre-decides the issue the examiner poses. Two further provisions the answer relies on, Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4(2) and Notaries Ordinance s.34, exist in the corpus only in text enacted after the matter date. A lawyer must settle the judicial-zone point and the April 2019 wording before this question can stand as gold.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: No will, testament, or codicil containing any devise of land or other immovable property, or any bequest of movable property, or for any other purpose whatsoever, shall be valid unless it shall be in writing and executed subject to the provisions specified in subsection (2);
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Sets the validity condition for every will: it must be in writing and executed in the prescribed manner. It is the provision that makes the mode of execution a question of validity rather than of good practice.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1840. The corpus text is the version substituted by the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022, which post-dates 2019-04; the requirement that a will be in writing and executed in the prescribed manner was, however, the substance of the section long before the matter date.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim of the current text, but the renumbering as subsection (1) and the closing words ‘subject to the provisions specified in subsection (2)’ were made by Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.3(1)-(2); in April 2019 the section read ‘executed in the manner hereinafter mentioned’ and that repealed wording is not in the corpus.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: The testator shall - (a) sign; and (b) affix his left or right thumb impression, at the foot or end of the will, testament or codicil referred to in subsection (1), before a notary public and two witnesses who shall be present at the same time
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the three actors who must be together at one time for a valid will: the testator signing at the foot or end, a notary public, and two witnesses. This is why execution cannot happen by post, by proxy or in stages, and therefore why someone must travel to the bedridden testator.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: The requirement of signature at the foot or end before a notary public and two witnesses present at the same time was in force in April 2019. The additional thumb-impression requirement in paragraph (b) and its proviso were introduced by Act No. 30 of 2022 and did NOT apply at the matter date; the excerpt is relied on only for the signature, notary and two-witnesses-present-together elements.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Confirmed against 30-2022 s.3(3): the whole of subsection (2) was added in 2022 and the pre-2022 words prescribing the manner of execution were repealed by the same section, so the April 2019 requirement of signature at the foot or end before a notary and two witnesses present together is a reconstruction that cannot be read anywhere in the corpus.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The decisive constraint. A notary's competence to attest is territorial: he may not attest anywhere outside the area named in his warrant. A will attested at the testator's home outside that area is attested in breach of this rule.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (22) is part of the original 1907 rules and is not among the rules recorded as substituted by the 2011, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts; treated as in force in April 2019.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same and the witnesses shall have signed the same in his presence and in the presence of one another, and unless he shall have signed the same in the presence of the executant and of the attesting witnesses.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Makes simultaneous physical presence of testator, both witnesses and the notary a notarial duty as well as a validity requirement, so the whole signing must happen in one sitting at the testator's bedside.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Original 1907 rule, not recorded as substituted by any amending Act in the corpus; treated as in force in April 2019.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Requires two witnesses who sign in letters, which matches the two witnesses demanded by the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance and settles that a mark alone from a witness is not enough.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Original 1907 rule, not recorded as substituted by any amending Act in the corpus; treated as in force in April 2019.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall without delay duly attest every deed or instrument which shall be executed or acknowledged before him, and shall sign and seal such attestation. In such attestation he shall state- (a) that the said deed or instrument was signed by the party and the witnesses thereto in his presence and in the presence of one another;
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Requires the notary to draw, sign and seal an attestation recording that the testator and both witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another. The attestation is the instrument's own proof that the statutory mode of execution was followed.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: The rule (20) chapeau and paragraph (a) are long-standing; the corpus records substitutions to parts of rule (20) by Act No. 31 of 2022 and Act No. 6 of 2024, so the exact 2019 wording of the later paragraphs is uncertain and is not relied on here.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall correctly insert in letters in every deed or instrument executed before him the day, month, and year on which and the place where the same is executed, and shall sign the same.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The notary must state the true place of execution in letters. He cannot cure a territorial problem by recording a place inside his own area when the will was in fact signed elsewhere, so this rule locks rule (22) in place.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Original 1907 rule, not recorded as substituted by any amending Act in the corpus; treated as in force in April 2019.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: The Minister may on application made in that behalf grant to a notary, having a warrant authorizing him to practice within a judicial zone, a fresh warrant authorizing him to practice within another judicial zone.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The only route in the corpus by which this notary himself could become competent to attest in the testator's area, and the reason the answer is either a fresh warrant or a different notary rather than a flat impossibility.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Substituted by the Notaries (Amendment) Law No. 20 of 1976, well before the matter date; in force in April 2019.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Every warrant issued to a notary under the provisions of section 3* or section 4* authorizing him to practice as a notary in any judicial division in which he resides, shall be deemed to authorize him to practice as a notary in the judicial zone in which he resides.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Measures the area that rule (22) protects. Read with section 3(1) and section 4(2), which entitle a notary to a warrant for the judicial zone in which he resides, this section deems a warrant expressed for a judicial division to authorise practice throughout the judicial zone of the notary residence. It is therefore the provision that decides whether a warrant expressed as "Colombo", held by a notary residing at Battaramulla, reaches Mount Lavinia, and the researcher treated that question as a scenario fact instead.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Inserted by the Notaries (Amendment) Law No. 20 of 1976 s.4 and not amended since; in force in April 2019.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Added by the verifier; excerpt checked as a verbatim substring of 1-1907/s4A.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: unless and until he shall have read over and explained the same, or caused the same to be explained, in the presence and hearing of such person and, except in the case of wills and codicils, in the presence of the attesting witnesses.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Governs reading over where the executant cannot read or asks for it, and carries the express exception for wills and codicils: the reading need not be done in the presence of the attesting witnesses, which protects the confidentiality of the testator's dispositions.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Original 1907 rule with the wills exception; not recorded as substituted by any amending Act in the corpus; treated as in force in April 2019.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: he shall satisfy himself, before accepting them as witnesses, that they are persons of good repute and that they are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation, and residence
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Constrains who may be used as the two witnesses at a bedside execution: people of good repute who genuinely know the testator, not whoever happens to be in the house.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: The good-repute and acquaintance limb quoted here is long-standing. The identity-document limb of rule (9), covering the national identity card, passport bio-page and driving licence, was introduced by later amendments recorded in the corpus and is not relied on for April 2019.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: In April 2019 the quoted duty was introduced by the words ‘and in the latter case, he shall satisfy himself’, which Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(3) replaced with ‘he shall’; at the matter date the good-repute and acquaintance duty therefore applied where the executant was known to the notary through the two attesting witnesses, not unconditionally as the excerpt now reads.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Every such attestation shall be substantially in the form E in the Second Schedule, and shall be legibly signed by him in the language in which the deed or instrument is written
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Prescribes the form and language of the attestation the notary must sign at the bedside.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Original 1907 rule, not recorded as substituted by any amending Act in the corpus; treated as in force in April 2019. Form E itself is not reproduced as a searchable section in the corpus.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall carefully preserve as his protocol a draft or copy of every deed or instrument executed or acknowledged before him, to which shall be attached his signature and those of the party and witnesses to the original deed or instrument
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: The protocol obligation applies to wills as well, and the same rule limits the register entry for a will to its number and date, which is how the notary's record-keeping duty is reconciled with testamentary secrecy.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Original 1907 rule, not recorded as substituted by any amending Act in the corpus; treated as in force in April 2019.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: any other rule set out in section 31, shall be guilty of an offence, and shall, on conviction after summary trial before a Magistrate, be liable to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, in addition to any civil liability he may incur thereby.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Shows the consequence for the notary personally if he attests outside his area: rule (22) is not in the lighter penalty lists in paragraphs (a) and (b), so it falls into the residual paragraph (c).
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: The corpus carries the consolidated text including fine levels raised by later amendments; the fine figures may differ from those in force in April 2019, so the provision is used for the fact of criminal liability, not for the amount.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Section 34 was repealed and replaced by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.17, so the paragraph lettering, the rule lists in paragraphs (a) and (b) and the fine levels are all 2022 text; the April 2019 section is not in the corpus, so the inference that rule (22) falls into the residual paragraph (c) cannot be read off the law in force at the matter date.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: No instrument shall be deemed to be invalid by reason only of the failure of any notary to observe any provision of any rule set out in section 31 in respect of any matter of form
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Separates the two consequences that this scenario mixes together. Breach of a section 31 rule of form does not by itself void the instrument, but the proviso keeps intact any invalidity arising under another written law, which is where the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance requirements bite.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Original 1907 section, not recorded as amended in the corpus; treated as in force in April 2019.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: If any person shall attest the execution of any will, testament, or codicil to whom or to whose wife or husband any beneficial devise, legacy, estate, interest, gift, disposition, or appointment of or affecting any immovable or movable property (other than and except charges and directions for the payment of any debt or debts) shall be thereby given or made, such devise, legacy, estate, interest, gift, disposition, or appointment shall, so far only as concerns such person attesting the execution of such will
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: A bedside execution tempts the notary to use family members present in the house as witnesses. This section makes any benefit under the will void as against an attesting witness or that witness's spouse, so the choice of witnesses is a substantive matter, not a formality.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Original 1840 section, not recorded as amended in the corpus; treated as in force in April 2019.

legal_issues.issue: What formalities must be satisfied for the client's last will to be validly executed.
Whether a notary whose warrant covers one area may attest a will at the testator's home in another area, and what follows for the notary and for the instrument if he does.
By what lawful means the will can still be executed when the testator is bedridden and cannot travel to the notary.
What the notary must do at the bedside signing itself: choice of witnesses, simultaneous presence, reading over, attestation, place and date, and protocol.

gold_answer_draft.issue: How, if at all, can the client's last will be lawfully executed when the notary employed to draw it holds a warrant for an area that does not extend to Mount Lavinia, while the testator is bedridden at Mount Lavinia and cannot travel to the notary? Three questions follow: what the statutory mode of executing a will is; whether this notary may attest at the testator's bedside; and what the correct course is if he may not.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A will is valid only if it is in writing and executed in the prescribed manner (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4(1)), and the prescribed manner is that the testator signs at the foot or end of the instrument before a notary public and two witnesses who are all present at the same time (s.4(2)). The Notaries Ordinance then regulates the sitting. The notary may not attest unless at least two witnesses have subscribed their signatures in letters (s.31 rule (8)); the testator and the witnesses must sign in his presence and in the presence of one another, and he must sign in their presence (rule (12)); he must satisfy himself that the witnesses are of good repute and well acquainted with the testator (rule (9)); where the testator cannot read or asks for the instrument to be read, it must be read over and explained to him, though in the case of a will this need not be done in the presence of the attesting witnesses (rule (11)); he must insert in letters the day, month and year and the place of execution (rule (18)); and he must without delay attest, sign and seal the instrument, stating that the testator and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another (rule (20) and (20)(a)), substantially in Form E of the Second Schedule (rule (21)), keeping the draft or copy as his protocol (rule (24)). Cutting across all of this, a notary shall not authenticate or attest any instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorised to practise (s.31 rule (22)). The Minister may grant a notary holding a warrant for one judicial zone a fresh warrant for another (s.11). Breach of rule (22) is an offence punishable on summary trial in addition to civil liability (s.34(1)(c)), and although an instrument is not void merely for a notarial failure in a matter of form (s.33), that saving does not cure invalidity arising under another written law. Finally, a beneficial gift to an attesting witness or to that witness's spouse is void as against that person (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11), and the alternative of executing before a District Judge or an authorised Justice of the Peace under the Deeds and Documents (Execution before Public Officers) Ordinance s.2 is offered only for instruments required to be executed under s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance and so is not available for a will.
gold_answer_draft.application: Because the testator must sign before the notary and two witnesses all present together, and because he cannot be moved from his house, the signing must take place at his bedside at Mount Lavinia; there is no statutory route by which the notary can attest from a distance or in stages. That fixes the place of execution outside the area specified in this notary's warrant, and rule (22) forbids him to attest there. He cannot escape the difficulty by recording a place inside his own area, because rule (18) obliges him to insert the true place of execution in letters, and the attestation he must sign under rule (20) records the same. His residence at Battaramulla makes no difference, since it is the area named in the warrant, and not where he lives, that measures his competence to attest; s.9 regulates his residence only through the location of his office. If he nevertheless attests at the bedside he commits an offence under s.34(1)(c), and while s.33 would protect the will from being treated as void for a mere matter of form, the breach is of his territorial competence rather than of form, so the safe course cannot rest on that saving. Two lawful routes remain. Either he applies to the Minister under s.11 for a fresh warrant covering the area in which Mount Lavinia lies, which changes his competence prospectively but not in time for a signing fixed for 15 May 2019, or the will he drew is executed before a notary whose warrant covers that area, such as Mrs. Perera. At that bedside sitting the testator, being alert and able to sign, signs at the foot or end of the will; the two neighbours, who have known him for over twenty years and take nothing under the will, sign as witnesses in letters in his presence and in the presence of one another and of the notary, who then signs in their presence. The daughter and the son should not be used as witnesses even though they are in the house, because a gift to an attesting witness is void as against that witness. The will is read over and explained to the testator, which for a will need not be done in front of the witnesses, and the notary then attests without delay in Form E, stating the true date and place of execution, and preserves the protocol.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The will can be executed, but not by this notary at the testator's bedside. Since the testator cannot travel and the signing must therefore occur at Mount Lavinia, which lies outside the area specified in his warrant, the notary who drew the will is barred by s.31 rule (22) of the Notaries Ordinance from attesting it there and would be criminally liable if he did. The will he has drawn should be executed at the bedside before a notary whose warrant covers the area in which Mount Lavinia lies, with two disinterested witnesses who know the testator, all four present at the same time and signing in one another's presence, followed by a Form E attestation stating the true date and place; alternatively the notary may first obtain a fresh warrant for that area under s.11. Whether Mount Lavinia in truth falls outside a warrant expressed as Colombo depends on the delimitation of judicial zones, which is outside the statutes examined here, so this analysis holds on the facts as stated and remains unverified.

answer_claims.claim_text: A will is valid only if it is in writing and executed in the manner prescribed by the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance.
The prescribed manner is that the testator signs at the foot or end of the will before a notary public and two witnesses who are all present at the same time.

The notary may not attest unless at least two witnesses have subscribed their signatures in letters, and the testator and the witnesses must sign in his presence and in the presence of one another, he signing in theirs.
The notary must satisfy himself that the witnesses are of good repute and well acquainted with the testator before accepting them.

Where the instrument must be read over, it must be read and explained in the presence and hearing of the executant, but in the case of a will this need not be done in the presence of the attesting witnesses.

The notary must insert in letters the day, month and year on which and the place where the instrument is executed, must attest it without delay under his signature and seal stating that the party and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, substantially in Form E of the Second Schedule, and must preserve the draft or copy as his protocol.
A notary shall not authenticate or attest any instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorised to practise.
The Minister may grant a notary who holds a warrant for one judicial zone a fresh warrant authorising him to practise in another judicial zone.

Breach of the territorial rule is an offence triable summarily before a Magistrate, in addition to any civil liability, and the protection given to instruments defective only in a matter of form does not extend to invalidity arising under another written law.
A beneficial gift under a will to a person who attests its execution, or to that person's spouse, is void so far as concerns that attesting witness or spouse.

Execution before a District Judge or an authorised Justice of the Peace is available only for instruments required to be executed under section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, and so cannot be used for a will.
Because the testator cannot be moved from his house and all four persons must be present together at the signing, the will must be executed at his bedside at Mount Lavinia.
That place lies outside the area specified in the notary's warrant, so he is forbidden to attest the will there.
He cannot avoid that bar by recording a place of execution inside his own area, because he is bound to insert the true place in letters and to record it in his attestation.

His residence at Battaramulla does not enlarge his competence, because it is the area named in the warrant that measures where he may attest, residence being regulated only through the location of his office.

If he attested at the bedside he would commit an offence, and the saving for defects of form would not be a safe answer because the defect would be in his territorial competence rather than in the form of the instrument.

The will he drew can instead be executed at the bedside before a notary whose warrant covers the area in which Mount Lavinia lies, or he may first apply to the Minister for a fresh warrant for that area.

At that sitting the testator, being alert and able to sign, signs at the foot or end, and the two neighbours who have long known him sign as witnesses in letters in his presence and in the presence of one another and of the notary, who then signs in their presence.
The daughter and the son should not be used as attesting witnesses, because the benefits given to them under the will would be void as against them.

The will is read over and explained to the testator, which for a will need not be done in the presence of the witnesses, and the notary then attests without delay in Form E stating the true date and place and preserves the protocol.

The last will can lawfully be executed, but not by the notary who drew it: it must be signed at the testator's bedside before a notary authorised to practise in the area in which Mount Lavinia lies, with two disinterested witnesses, all present at the same time, unless that notary first obtains a fresh warrant for that area.

Whether Mount Lavinia in fact falls outside a warrant expressed as Colombo turns on the delimitation of judicial zones, which is not settled by the statutes examined here, so the conclusion holds on the stated facts and remains unverified.

enrichment.original_background: The notary is licensed to practice in Colombo. He lives in Battaramulla. He is employed to draw up the Last Will of his client who lives in Mt Lavinia. The client is not able to leave Mt lavinia as he is bedridden.

His warrant authorises him to practise as a notary in Colombo, and the area specified in that warrant does not extend to Mount Lavinia. In March 2019 he was employed by Mr. Piyasena Silva, aged 74, of No. 12, Sea Breeze Lane, Mount Lavinia, to draw up Mr. Silva's last will. block_reason: Verification left three claims disputed and eight provisions partially verified. (1) CL-M093-Q01-013 and the conclusion treat obtaining a certified extract of the folio as a step the notary must take; that duty was created by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s 16(10)(a) (rule (17)(b)(i)) and did not exist in April 2019, when Registration of Documents Ordinance s 42 gave only a right to obtain extracts. (2) No cited provision requires the notary to insist that the registered 2016 bond be discharged or the block released before the deed is drawn; that step is practice, not statute. (3) CL-M093-Q01-018 puts approval of the blocking out plan before drafting, whereas s 23A(1) only forbids a local authority to approve such a plan without the Board's certificate. (4) CL-M093-Q01-008 reads Survey Act s 13, an admissibility rule, as requiring a survey. The verifier may not rewrite the gold answer prose, so a lawyer must decide whether to correct these limbs or reserve the question.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Before any deed or instrument (other than a will or codicil) affecting any interest in land or other immovable property is drawn by him, he shall search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title in regard to such land and whether any prior deed affecting any interest in such land has been registered
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The only provision that speaks directly to what a notary must do before the deed is drawn: search the land registry registers for the state of the title and for prior registered deeds. It is the statutory core of the answer.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (17)(a) was in force in April 2019. Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022, s 16(10) repealed and replaced only paragraph (b) of rule (17) and added new paragraphs (c) to (e); paragraph (a) was not touched by the 2022 or the 2024 amendment. The proviso allowing the parties to dispense with the search in writing was also in force.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument, other than a will or codicil, affecting land or other immovable property, unless the deed or instrument embodies therin or in a Schedule annexed therto an accurate and clear description of the said land or other property affected thereby, showing its boundaries, extent, situation specifying the district, pattu, korale, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division and the Grama Niladari Division
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The notary cannot draft the schedule until he has the material for an accurate description of the land by boundaries, extent and situation. Gathering that material is a pre-drafting step.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force in April 2019. Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022, s 16(9)(a) only substituted the closing words of rule (16)(a) to add condominium parcels; the words quoted here are the pre-2022 text (the spellings 'therin' and 'therto' are as printed in the corpus).

If it be a divided share, such share shall be clearly and accurately defined by its particular boundaries and extent
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Wimal is buying a portion, not the whole estate. Rule (16)(b) requires the deed to say whether the share is divided or undivided and, if divided, to define it by its own boundaries and extent, which in practice requires a survey plan of the portion before drafting.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: The transfer of ownership of a tea or rubber estate on or after the appointed day shall, subject to the provisions of subsections (2) and (3), be null and void unless- (a) a certificate of consent of the Board to such transfer has been previously obtained by the transferor, and (b) such transfer is effected in accordance with the conditions, if any, subject to which such consent has been granted.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: If the land is a rubber estate within the meaning of the Act, the transfer of a portion of it is null and void unless the transferor has previously obtained the Board's certificate of consent. Checking whether the Act applies, and seeing the certificate, is an indispensable pre-drafting step.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force since the appointed day, 11 December 1957 (s 2), and unamended as at April 2019.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: means a rubber estate of not less than one hundred acres in extent which, under the Rubber Control Act is or is deemed to be an estate registered under that Act
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The consent requirement in s 3(1) only bites if the land answers this definition. The notary must therefore establish the extent of the estate and whether it is registered under the Rubber Control Act before he can know whether a certificate of consent is needed.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force in April 2019. The corpus body of s 25 prints the defined terms in a separate list, so the definition reads as a bare 'means ...' clause; the term defined is 'rubber estate'. indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act

indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This definition is what brings the sale of a portion of the estate, and not merely a sale of the whole, within s 3(1). Without it the Fragmentation Act would look irrelevant to a purchase of part of an estate.
