legal_issues.issue: What investigation of title must a notary carry out before he draws a deed affecting an interest in land, and where must that investigation be made when the land lies outside his own district?
Does the sale of a portion of a rubber estate require the prior consent of the Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Board, and what must the notary see and do before drafting if it does?

What material must the notary have in hand before drafting so the deed can describe a divided portion accurately, and what other pre-drafting checks (identity and status of the parties, the ceiling on agricultural land, consideration and stamp duty, place of execution) does the law require?

gold_answer_draft.issue: What must a notary licensed to practise in Colombo do before he draws a deed by which his client is to buy a divided fifteen-acre block out of a 212-acre registered rubber estate at Kuruwita in the Ratnapura District: what title investigation the law requires of him, whether the fragmentation control regime applies to the sale of a portion of such an estate, and what other checks and materials he must have in hand before he starts drafting.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (17)(a) provides that before any deed affecting an interest in land is drawn by him the notary shall search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed affecting an interest in the land has been registered. The registers are open to search and certified extracts may be obtained under Registration of Documents Ordinance s.42, and the search must be made in the registry for the division in which the land lies (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.14(1)), because an unregistered instrument is void against a subsequent registered instrument taken for valuable consideration (s.7(1)). Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (33) requires the notary to use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed of the property. Rule (16)(a) forbids attestation unless the deed embodies an accurate and clear description showing boundaries, extent and situation, and rule (16)(b) requires a divided share to be defined by its own particular boundaries and extent, which calls for a survey plan; a plan is receivable in evidence only if prepared as Survey Act s.13 requires. Under Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act s.3(1) the transfer of ownership of a rubber estate is null and void unless a certificate of consent of the Board has been previously obtained by the transferor and the transfer follows any conditions attached to it; by s.25 a rubber estate is one of not less than one hundred acres registered under the Rubber Control Act, and transfer of ownership covers the transfer of such an estate or any portion of it by sale. The application for consent is made in writing by the proprietor to the Chairman of the Board (s.11), no officer of a local authority may approve a blocking out plan of such an estate without the certificate (s.23A(1)), and where a certificate is issued it must be attached to the deed and its number and date recited in the attestation (s.3(4)). Notaries Ordinance s.38(1) obliges the notary to ascertain the true and full consideration and set it out in the deed; stamp duty is charged on the instrument under Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.3(1) and, absent agreement, falls on the person executing it under s.6. Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2(1) prohibits a transfer of title to a foreigner, that is a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka (s.25). Land Reform Law s.3(1) fixes a ceiling of fifty acres of agricultural land other than paddy, and s.5(1) vests the excess in the Commission where a person becomes owner beyond the ceiling. Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (22) forbids the notary to attest in any area, or in any language, other than that in which he is authorised to practise.
gold_answer_draft.application: Because the estate is 212 acres and registered for rubber control purposes, and the sale is of a portion of it, the transaction is a transfer of ownership of a rubber estate within Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act s.25, so s.3(1) applies and the notary must first satisfy himself that the vendor has applied to and obtained from the Board a certificate of consent (s.11, s.3(1)); without it the deed he draws would be null and void, and the local authority could not approve a blocking out plan for the fifteen-acre block (s.23A(1)). He must call for Deed No. 4211 of 3 March 1996 and the earlier title deeds (rule (33)) and cause a search of the registers at the Ratnapura Land Registry, the registry for the division in which the land lies (rule (17)(a); Registration of Documents Ordinance s.42 and s.14(1)), obtaining a certified extract of the relevant folio. That search should disclose the 2016 bond in favour of the bank, and since that bond is registered it will take priority (s.7(1)); the notary must therefore require its discharge, or a release of the fifteen acres, to be arranged before the deed is drawn. As the block is a divided portion that has never been surveyed, he must have a plan prepared for it so that the schedule can define it by its particular boundaries and extent (rule (16)(a) and (b); Survey Act s.13). He should verify from the purchaser's identity documents that Wimal is a citizen, so that Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2(1) does not prohibit the transfer, and check that fifteen acres added to his existing eight acres of coconut land leaves him inside the fifty-acre ceiling in Land Reform Law s.3(1). He must record the true consideration of Rs. 21,000,000 (Notaries Ordinance s.38(1)) and settle with the parties the stamp duty payable on that value and who is to bear it (Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.3(1) and s.6); the rate is fixed by Order and is not stated here. Being licensed for Colombo, he may act although the land is in Ratnapura, but execution must take place within his own area, which the parties' proposal to sign at his Colombo office satisfies (rule (22)).
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Before drafting, the notary should take instructions and verify the parties' identity and the purchaser's citizenship; call for and examine the vendor's title deeds; cause a search of the registers at the Ratnapura Land Registry and obtain a certified extract of the folio, and require the undischarged 2016 bond to be released or discharged; satisfy himself that the estate is a rubber estate within the Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act and that the vendor has obtained the Board's certificate of consent to the transfer of the portion under s.3(1), so that the certificate can be attached to the deed and recited in the attestation under s.3(4); have the fifteen-acre block surveyed and the blocking out plan approved; ascertain the true consideration and provide for stamp duty; check the purchaser against the fifty-acre agricultural ceiling; and arrange execution within the area in which he is authorised to practise. If the Board's consent is not forthcoming he should decline to draw the deed, because the transfer would be null and void. How far back beyond the registered folio the title ought to be traced is a matter of practice on which the statutes are silent.

answer_claims.claim_text: Before drawing any deed affecting an interest in land, a notary must search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed affecting an interest in the land has been registered.
The search must be made in the registry for the division in which the land is situated, and the registers may be searched and certified extracts obtained by a person interested or his agent.
The search matters because an instrument that is not duly registered is void against a subsequent duly registered instrument taken for valuable consideration.
The notary must also use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed of the property being transferred.

The transfer of ownership of a rubber estate is null and void unless the transferor has previously obtained a certificate of consent of the Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Board and the transfer conforms to any conditions of that consent.

A rubber estate for this purpose is one of not less than one hundred acres registered or deemed registered under the Rubber Control Act, and a transfer of ownership includes the sale of any portion of such an estate.

The certificate of consent is applied for in writing by the proprietor to the Chairman of the Board, must be attached to the deed with its number and date stated by the attesting notary, and without it no officer of a local authority may approve a blocking out plan of such an estate.

The deed must embody an accurate and clear description of the land showing boundaries, extent and situation, and a divided share must be defined by its own particular boundaries and extent, which requires a survey plan prepared as the Survey Act allows.

The notary must endeavour to ascertain the true and full consideration and set it out in the deed, and stamp duty is charged on the instrument and, absent agreement to the contrary, borne by the person executing it.

A transfer of title to a foreigner, meaning a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka, is prohibited, and no person may own agricultural land other than paddy in excess of fifty acres, the excess vesting in the Land Reform Commission.
A notary may not attest a deed in any area, or in any language, other than that in which he is authorised to practise.

Because the estate is 212 acres and registered for rubber control purposes and the sale is of a portion of it, the transaction is a transfer of ownership of a rubber estate, so the Board's prior certificate of consent must be obtained by the vendor before the deed is drawn.

The notary must call for Deed No. 4211 of 1996 and search the registers at the Ratnapura Land Registry, obtaining a certified extract of the folio, which will disclose the undischarged 2016 bond in favour of the bank; he must require that bond to be discharged or the block released before drafting.
As the fifteen-acre block is a divided and unsurveyed portion, a survey plan must be obtained before drafting so that the schedule can define the block by its particular boundaries and extent.

The notary must verify from identity documents that the purchaser is a citizen of Sri Lanka, and check that fifteen acres added to his existing eight acres of coconut land leaves him within the fifty-acre ceiling.
He must record the true consideration of Rs. 21,000,000, compute the stamp duty on that value and settle who bears it before the deed is engrossed.
Being licensed for Colombo, the notary may act although the land lies in Ratnapura, provided the deed is executed and attested within his own area, which signing at his Colombo office satisfies.

The steps to be taken before drafting are therefore to take instructions and verify identity and citizenship, call for and examine the title deeds, search the Ratnapura Land Registry and obtain a certified extract, clear the registered bond, obtain the Board's certificate of consent, have the block surveyed and the blocking out plan approved, ascertain the true consideration and provide for stamp duty, check the agricultural ceiling, and arrange execution within his own area.
If the Board's certificate of consent is not obtained, the notary should decline to draw the deed, because the transfer would be null and void.

enrichment.original_background: Wimal wishes to purchase a portion of a Rubber Estate Situated in Ratnapura. He requests you to attest the Deed.
enrichment.enriched_background: Wimal Nandasena, aged 46, a citizen of Sri Lanka living at No. 118, Kirula Road, Colombo 5, wishes to purchase a portion of a Rubber Estate Situated in Ratnapura. The estate is Kirimetiyana Estate, 212 acres in extent, at Kuruwita in the Ratnapura District, and it stands registered as an estate for rubber control purposes. What Wimal wants is a divided block of about fifteen acres on the northern side of the estate; no surveyor has yet been put on the ground and no plan of that block exists. The owner is Malani Wijesinghe of Ratnapura, who holds the whole estate on Deed of Transfer No. 4211 dated 3 March 1996, attested by a notary of Ratnapura and registered in the Ratnapura Land Registry, and who says she still has the original deed. She also mentions that in 2016 she mortgaged the estate to a commercial bank and that the bond has not been discharged. The price agreed for the fifteen acres is Rs. 21,000,000, to be paid in full on the day of signing. Wimal already owns eight acres of coconut land at Polgahawela. The parties propose to come to your office in Colombo to sign. He requests you to attest the Deed.

added_facts.fact: The purchaser is Wimal Nandasena, aged 46, a citizen of Sri Lanka, of No. 118, Kirula Road, Colombo 5.
added_facts.reason: The original scenario gives only a first name, so the purchaser's status could not be tested. Citizenship and address make the identity and status checks determinate without changing the result.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If Wimal were not a citizen of Sri Lanka the transfer of title would be prohibited outright and the notary could not draw the transfer at all.

added_facts.fact: The vendor is Malani Wijesinghe of Ratnapura, who owns the whole estate.
added_facts.reason: The original scenario names no vendor. A single owner keeps the question on pre-drafting steps rather than on co-ownership or partition.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the estate were co-owned, a partition by deed would engage a separate consent regime and the pre-drafting steps would differ.

added_facts.fact: The land is Kirimetiyana Estate at Kuruwita in the Ratnapura District, 212 acres in extent, registered as an estate for rubber control purposes.
added_facts.reason: Whether the fragmentation control regime applies turns on extent and registration, neither of which the original scenario gave.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the estate were under one hundred acres or not registered, no certificate of consent would be needed and the transfer would not be void for want of it.

added_facts.fact: The subject of the sale is a divided block of about fifteen acres on the northern side of the estate, and no survey plan of that block exists.
added_facts.reason: The original scenario says only 'a portion'. Making it a divided, unsurveyed block is what brings the description and survey steps into play.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If an undivided share were being sold, no blocking out plan would be needed and the deed would state the fraction of the whole instead of separate boundaries.

added_facts.fact: The vendor holds on Deed of Transfer No. 4211 dated 3 March 1996, attested by a notary of Ratnapura and registered in the Ratnapura Land Registry, and she still holds the original deed.
added_facts.reason: The registration status of the vendor's title was missing, and the search step cannot be applied without it.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the vendor's deed were unregistered, the search would not disclose her title and the priority risk to the purchaser would be materially greater.

added_facts.fact: The estate was mortgaged to a commercial bank in 2016 and the bond has not been discharged.
added_facts.reason: The original scenario disclosed no encumbrance, so nothing turned on the search. An undischarged bond makes the search result operative.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the title were unencumbered, the search would confirm a clear title and no release or redemption would have to be arranged before the deed is drawn.

added_facts.fact: The agreed price for the fifteen acres is Rs. 21,000,000, payable in full on the day of signing.
added_facts.reason: Consideration was missing, and the duty to ascertain the true consideration and to provide for stamp duty cannot be applied without a figure.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the price stated to the notary were understated against the real one, he would be bound to insist on the true figure before drafting.

added_facts.fact: Wimal already owns eight acres of coconut land at Polgahawela.
added_facts.reason: Existing agricultural holdings decide whether the ceiling is a live problem. Eight acres plus fifteen keeps the purchaser well inside the ceiling.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If Wimal already owned more than thirty-five acres of agricultural land, the purchase would push him over the ceiling and the excess would vest in the Commission.

added_facts.fact: The parties propose to come to the notary's office in Colombo to sign the deed.
added_facts.reason: The original scenario left the place of execution open, which is what the area restriction on a Colombo notary turns on.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the parties insisted on signing at the estate in Ratnapura, the notary could not attest there and would have to arrange execution within his own area.

block_reason: Two matters need a lawyer before this can stand as gold. First, the ground on which the answer refuses the nurse as a witness is disputed: on the October 2018 wording of rule (9), recovered only from Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(6) and Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(3), the vetting and declaration duty attached where the notary relied on the attesting witnesses' knowledge of the executant, and this Notary knows the testator himself; rule (20)(c) requires the witnesses' own full names and residences, not their knowledge of the testator's particulars, so it does not carry the weight the answer puts on it. Second, completeness cannot be established from the corpus: rule (10) of section 31 was in force in October 2018 and was repealed only by Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(4) without being reproduced, and the pre-2022 wording of rule (20)(b), the witness-facing attestation paragraph, is likewise not recoverable, so a question asking for the precautions relating to witnesses cannot be answered exhaustively from the corpus text.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: It is and shall be the duty of every notary strictly to observe and act in conformity with the following rules
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Makes each numbered rule in section 31 a mandatory duty of the notary rather than a matter of good practice, so every witness rule relied on below is owed by this notary when he attests the will at the hospital.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section 31 has been in force since 1907. The corpus edition is consolidated to 2024 and prints the text as altered by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 47 of 2011, Act No. 31 of 2022 and Act No. 6 of 2024. No amendment event is recorded for the chapeau by any of those Acts, so these words also stood at October 2018.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The first precaution about witnesses: there must be at least two of them and each must subscribe his signature in letters rather than make a mark. It fixes both the minimum number of witnesses and the form of their subscription.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. Neither Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 nor Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3 touches rule (8), so this text stood unchanged at October 2018.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: he shall satisfy himself, before accepting them as witnesses, that they are persons of good repute and that they are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation, and residence, and the witnesses shall sign a declaration at the foot of the deed or instrument that they are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation, and residence.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The central witness-vetting rule: before he accepts anyone as a witness the notary must satisfy himself that the person is of good repute and well acquainted with the executant and knows his proper name, occupation and residence, and he must obtain the witnesses' signed declaration to that effect at the foot of the instrument.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: The words quoted are unaltered, but their opening context differed at the matter date. In October 2018 rule (9) began 'He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same be known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses thereto;' (those words were replaced by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(6), recorded at PROV-M100-017) and the quoted duty was introduced by the words 'and in the latter case,' (deleted by Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(3), recorded at PROV-M100-018). At the matter date the quoted duty therefore attached in terms to the case where the notary relies on the attesting witnesses' knowledge of the executant rather than on his own.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Wording is verbatim and the temporal reconstruction is right, but the role needs a correction: because Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(3) shows that in October 2018 the vetting and declaration duty was introduced by the words "and in the latter case", that duty attached in terms to the case where the notary relied on the attesting witnesses' knowledge of the executant, and this Notary knows the testator himself, so on these facts the rule (9) duty is a prudent precaution rather than one the corpus shows to be owed.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same and the witnesses shall have signed the same in his presence and in the presence of one another, and unless he shall have signed the same in the presence of the executant and of the attesting witnesses.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Governs the manner of signing: the testator and both witnesses must sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and the notary must sign in front of all of them. This is the precaution that requires nobody to leave the bedside until every signature is on the will.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. No amendment event is recorded for rule (12) in Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3, so the rule stood in this form at October 2018.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: that the said deed or instrument was signed by the party and the witnesses thereto in his presence and in the presence of one another
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Requires the notary to state in his attestation the very fact that rule (12) obliges him to secure, so the precaution taken at the bedside must also appear on the face of the will.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11) and Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(7) alter paragraphs (b), (e) and (g) of rule (20) and add paragraph (h); paragraph (a) is untouched and stood in this form at October 2018.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: the day, month, and year on which and the place where the said deed or instrument was executed or acknowledged, and the full names of the attesting witnesses and their residences
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Requires the full names and residences of the attesting witnesses, and the place of execution, to appear in the attestation. Here the place is a hospital ward, so the notary must know and record where each witness lives.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. Paragraph (c) of rule (20) is not among the paragraphs amended by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11) or Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(7); it stood in this form at October 2018.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: such devise, legacy, estate, interest, gift, disposition, or appointment shall, so far only as concerns such person attesting the execution of such will, testament, or codicil, or the wife or husband of such person, or any person claiming under such person or wife or husband, be utterly null and void
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The disqualification that matters most in choosing witnesses to a will: a beneficiary, or the spouse of a beneficiary, who attests the will loses the gift. The notary's precaution is to ensure that neither witness, nor either witness's spouse, takes anything under the will.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section 11 has been in force since 1840. No amendment event is recorded for it in the corpus, and neither Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 nor Act No. 4 of 2024 touches it, so this is also the October 2018 text.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any case in which the person executing or acknowledging the same shall be or profess to be unable to read the same, or in which such person shall require him to read over the same, unless and until he shall have read over and explained the same, or caused the same to be explained, in the presence and hearing of such person and, except in the case of wills and codicils, in the presence of the attesting witnesses.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Qualifies what the witnesses must be present for. Where the testator cannot read the will or asks for it to be read, the notary must read and explain it to him, but wills and codicils are expressly excepted from the requirement that this be done in the presence of the attesting witnesses.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. No amendment event is recorded for rule (11) in Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3; it stood in this form at October 2018. Section 34(1)(b) treats a breach of rule (11) as an offence.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Rule (11) itself is verified verbatim and was unamended at the matter date, but the temporal note's reference to section 34(1)(b) reads the post-2022 penalty section: section 34 was substituted in its entirety by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.17, so the corpus does not show how a breach of rule (11) was punished in October 2018.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: whether the same was read over by the person executing the same, or read and explained by him, the said notary, to the said person in the presence of the attesting witnesses
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: The attestation must record whether the will was read over by the testator himself or read and explained to him in the presence of the attesting witnesses, so the notary must settle which course was followed and then state it.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. Paragraph (d) of rule (20) is untouched by the 2022 and 2024 amendments and stood in this form at October 2018.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall carefully preserve as his protocol a draft or copy of every deed or instrument executed or acknowledged before him, to which shall be attached his signature and those of the party and witnesses to the original deed or instrument
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: The witnesses' task does not end with the original: the same two witnesses must also sign the protocol copy the notary keeps, so the notary must have the protocol ready at the bedside before they disperse.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. No amendment event is recorded for rule (24) in Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3; in force in this form at October 2018.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: the attesting witnesses having appeared personally before him at the time when such deed was executed or acknowledged
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Attesting without the attesting witnesses having appeared personally before the notary at the time of execution is a criminal offence, not merely a breach of a rule. It is the sanction that makes the presence requirement in rule (12) a real precaution.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Section 39 has been in force since 1907. Act No. 31 of 2022 s.19(1) altered other words of paragraph (c) ('signature or mark' became 'signature, and the left or right thumb impression or any other finger impression or toe impression, as the case may be') and s.19(2) raised the penalty; the words quoted here fall outside both substitutions and stood in this form at October 2018.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which he is a party.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Keeps the notary himself out of the instrument. He cannot make up the number by acting as one of the two witnesses to a will he attests, and cannot attest a will in which he takes an interest.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. No amendment event is recorded for rule (13) in Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3; in force in this form at October 2018.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: If any person who shall attest the execution of any will, testament, or codicil shall at the time of the execution thereof, or at any time afterwards, be incompetent to be admitted a witness to prove the execution thereof, such will, testament, or codicil shall not on that account be invalid.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Limits the consequence of a bad choice of witness: incompetency of an attesting witness does not by itself invalidate the will. It shows that the sanction for a poorly chosen witness lies elsewhere, chiefly in section 11.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force since 1840; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so this is also the October 2018 text.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: before a notary public and two witnesses who shall be present at the same time
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Sets the number of witnesses and the requirement that they be present at the same time as the notary when the testator signs. It is the source of the two-witness requirement that the notarial rules then work out in detail.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: The corpus text of section 4 is the text as renumbered and substituted by Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.3, which is after the October 2018 matter date, so the wording quoted is not the wording in force at the matter date. The corpus does not carry the pre-2022 text: Act No. 30 of 2022 s.3(2) repeals the words from 'in the manner hereinafter mentioned;' to the end of the section without reproducing them. The requirement of a notary and two witnesses present at the same time is common to the corpus text and to the surviving description of the older text, but for this reason the provision is treated as supporting and not as indispensable.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: No obliteration, interlineations, or other alteration made in any will, testament, or codicil after the execution thereof shall be valid or have any effect, except so far as the words or effect of the will, testament, or codicil before such alteration shall not be apparent, unless such alteration shall be executed in like manner as herein before is required for the execution of the will
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Extends the witness requirement to any alteration made after execution: an alteration has no effect unless executed in the same manner as the will itself, which means before the same class of witnesses.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Section 7 has been in force since 1840. Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.4 substituted words later in the section ('signature of the testator or testatrix') and added a proviso, both after the matter date; the words quoted here fall outside both changes and stood in this form at October 2018.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall, before any executant or witness signs or makes a mark and before any executant affixes his left or right thumb impression or any other finger impression or toe impression, ascertain the full names of the executant and witnesses to such deed or instrument
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Requires the notary to ascertain the full names of the witnesses before anyone signs, and to describe a witness by both names where the name signed differs from the name in his identification documents.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (14) as printed in the corpus is the rule substituted by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(7), which is after the matter date, so this wording was not in force in October 2018 and the provision is treated as supporting only. The corpus does not carry the pre-2022 text, because s.16(7) substitutes the rule without reproducing what it replaced.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: in rule (9) thereof, by the substitution for the words, "He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same be known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses thereto;"
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Recovers the opening words of rule (9) as they stood before 2022, and therefore as they stood at the matter date: the notary could proceed either because he himself knew the executant or because at least two of the attesting witnesses knew him. This is the wording against which the facts of this matter, where the notary knows the testator, have to be tested.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Act No. 31 of 2022 is later than the October 2018 matter date and is not applied as operative law here. It is recorded because the words it repeals are the words that were in force at the matter date, and the corpus preserves them only in this amending section.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: in rule (9) thereof, by the substitution for the words "and in the latter case, he shall", of the words, "he shall"; (4) by the repeal of rule (10) thereof;
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Shows two things about the October 2018 text of section 31. First, the witness-vetting duty in rule (9) was then introduced by the words 'and in the latter case, he shall', so it attached in terms to the case where the notary relies on the attesting witnesses' knowledge of the executant. Second, a rule (10) existed at the matter date and was repealed only in 2024, so the consolidated text used here is missing a rule that was in force when this will would have been executed.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Act No. 6 of 2024 is later than the October 2018 matter date and is not applied as operative law. It is recorded because it identifies wording and a whole rule that were in force at the matter date but are absent from the consolidated corpus text of section 31.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: whether the executants of the said deed or instrument are known to him or whether he has identified them by the inspection of the national identity card, bio-page of the passport or the driving licence or whether the witnesses thereto are known to him and in the latter case he shall specify which of the executants or the person acknowledging are known to the said witness
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Added by the verifier. Paragraph (b) of rule (20) is the attestation paragraph that turns on the witnesses: the notary must state whether he knows the executants himself or whether the witnesses know them, and in the latter case which executant each witness knows. It is the counterpart in the attestation of the identification limb of rule (9), and the researcher's map records paragraphs (a), (c) and (d) of rule (20) but not (b).
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: The text quoted is paragraph (b) as substituted by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(a), which is after the October 2018 matter date, so this wording was not then in force. Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(a) repeals the old paragraph (b) without reproducing it, so the October 2018 wording of the one attestation paragraph that turns on the witnesses' knowledge of the executant is not recoverable from the corpus. Recorded as a supporting provision and as a corpus gap.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt checked verbatim against 1-1907/s31. Added because the map covered rule (20)(a), (c) and (d) but not the witness-facing paragraph (b); it is recorded as inapplicable at the matter date because only the post-2022 wording survives in the corpus.

legal_issues.issue: How many witnesses must attest the will and in what form must they subscribe it.
Whom the notary may accept as a witness: what he must satisfy himself about before accepting a person, and who is disqualified by taking a benefit under the will.
In whose presence the testator, the witnesses and the notary must sign, and whether the witnesses must be present when the will is read over.

What the notary must obtain from the witnesses and record about them: the declaration at the foot of the will, their signatures on the protocol, and their full names and residences in the attestation.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What precautions must the Notary take with regard to the witnesses when the testator, who is warded in hospital, executes his last Will: how many witnesses are needed, whom he may accept and whom he must refuse, in whose presence the Will and the protocol must be signed, and what he must obtain from the witnesses and state about them in his attestation.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance makes each of its rules a duty of the notary. Rule (8) forbids him to attest any instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters. Rule (9), in the form it bore in October 2018, allowed him to proceed either because he himself knew the executant or because at least two of the attesting witnesses knew him, and where he relied on the witnesses he had first to satisfy himself that they were persons of good repute, well acquainted with the executant and knowing his proper name, occupation and residence, and had to take their declaration to that effect signed at the foot of the instrument. Rule (12) requires the executant and the witnesses to sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another and the notary to sign in the presence of them all; attesting without the attesting witnesses having appeared personally before him at the time of execution is an offence under Notaries Ordinance s.39(c). Rule (13) forbids him to attest an instrument to which he is himself a party. Rule (11) obliges him to read over and explain the instrument where the executant cannot read it or asks for it to be read, but expressly excepts wills and codicils from the requirement that this be done in the presence of the attesting witnesses. Rule (20) requires the attestation to state that the party and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another (paragraph (a)), the date and place of execution and the full names of the attesting witnesses and their residences (paragraph (c)), and whether the instrument was read over by the executant or read and explained by the notary in the presence of the attesting witnesses (paragraph (d)). Rule (24) requires the protocol copy to carry the signatures of the party and the witnesses to the original. Outside the Notaries Ordinance, Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11 makes a beneficial gift utterly null and void so far as concerns an attesting witness, that witness's spouse and anyone claiming under them, though by s.10 the will is not invalidated by an attesting witness's incompetency, and by s.12 and s.13 a charged creditor or a named executor is not disqualified. Section 7 of the same Ordinance requires any alteration made after execution to be executed in the same manner as the will.
gold_answer_draft.application: Two witnesses are needed and each must sign in letters. Of the two people first offered at the ward, the nephew Ranjith Kumara takes an undivided half share of the coconut land under the Will; if he attests it, that bequest becomes null and void so far as he and anyone claiming under him are concerned (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11), so the Notary must not accept him. The nurse Kumudini Silva met the testator only on his admission four days earlier and does not know his occupation or his residence. The Notary's own knowledge of the testator satisfies the identification limb of Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (9) as it stood in October 2018, so the Will is not exposed on that ground, but she cannot make the declaration of acquaintance that the rule contemplates and cannot speak to the particulars the Notary must record under rule (20)(c), so she should not be accepted either. The two neighbours, Gunapala and Nandawathie, meet the conditions: they are two, they are literate in Sinhala and can subscribe in letters as rule (8) requires, each has known the testator for over twenty years and knows his proper name, occupation and residence, and neither they nor their spouses take under the Will. Since the ward allows all of them to remain at the bedside, the Notary should have the testator and both neighbours sign the original and the protocol in his presence and in the presence of one another and then sign himself in front of them, as rules (12) and (24) require, which also keeps him clear of s.39(c). He should take the witnesses' declaration of acquaintance at the foot of the Will. Because the testator can read the Sinhala Will himself, rule (11) requires no reading over, and wills are in any event excepted from reading over in the witnesses' presence, but under rule (20)(d) the attestation must record which course was taken, and under rule (20)(a) and (c) it must state that all signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and give the date, the hospital ward as the place of execution and the full names and residences of both neighbours. If anything in the Will has to be altered after signing, s.7 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance requires the alteration to be executed in the same manner, so the witnesses are needed again.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The Notary should use two witnesses and no fewer; refuse anyone who takes a benefit under the Will or whose spouse does, and so refuse the nephew; choose witnesses of good repute who are well acquainted with the testator and know his proper name, occupation and residence, which the nurse is not and the two neighbours are; satisfy himself that each witness can and does subscribe his signature in letters; not act as a witness himself; keep the testator and both witnesses together at the bedside so that all sign the original and the protocol in his presence and in the presence of one another before he signs; take the witnesses' signed declaration of acquaintance at the foot of the Will; and set out in his attestation that all signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, with the date, the place and the full names and residences of both witnesses. This list is drawn from the provisions recorded in this map. Rule (10) of Notaries Ordinance s.31, which was in force in October 2018 and was repealed in 2024, is not reproduced in the corpus, so the possibility of a further witness-related requirement in that rule cannot be excluded from the corpus text.

answer_claims.claim_text: Section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance imposes on every notary a duty strictly to observe the rules set out in that section, so the requirements about witnesses are duties and not matters of practice.
A notary may not attest a will unless at least two witnesses have subscribed their signatures to it in letters, so there must be two witnesses and each must sign his name rather than make a mark.

Under rule (9) as it stood at the matter date the notary could proceed either because he himself knew the person executing the instrument or because at least two of the attesting witnesses knew him, and where he relied on the witnesses he had to satisfy himself before accepting them that they were persons of good repute, well acquainted with the executant and knowing his proper name, occupation and residence, and had to take their signed declaration to that effect at the foot of the instrument.
The testator and both witnesses must sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and the notary must sign in the presence of the testator and of the attesting witnesses.
Attesting a deed without the attesting witnesses having appeared personally before the notary at the time of execution is an offence under section 39 of the Notaries Ordinance.

The attestation must state that the instrument was signed by the party and the witnesses in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and must give the place of execution and the full names and residences of the attesting witnesses.

Where a will gives a beneficial interest to a person who attests it, or to that person's spouse, section 11 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance makes the gift utterly null and void so far as concerns the attesting witness, the spouse and anyone claiming under them, although by section 10 the will itself is not invalidated by the incompetency of an attesting witness.
The notary himself may not be a party to the instrument he attests, so he cannot make up the two witnesses by signing as one of them.
The witnesses to the original will must also sign the protocol copy that the notary preserves.

Where the testator cannot read the will or asks for it to be read, the notary must read and explain it to him, but for wills and codicils this need not be done in the presence of the attesting witnesses, and the attestation must record which course was followed.
Any alteration made to the will after execution has no effect unless it is executed in the same manner as the will itself, which requires the witnesses again.

The nephew who takes an undivided half share of the coconut land under the Will must not be accepted as an attesting witness, because if he attests the Will that bequest becomes null and void so far as he and anyone claiming under him are concerned.

The nurse who met the testator four days earlier and does not know his occupation or his residence is not a witness the Notary can safely accept, because she cannot make the declaration of acquaintance that rule (9) contemplates and cannot supply from her own knowledge the particulars of the testator that the attestation must carry; the Notary's own knowledge of the testator meets the identification limb of rule (9) as it stood in October 2018, but it does not cure her inability to speak to those matters.

The two neighbours are suitable witnesses: there are two of them, each is literate in Sinhala and can subscribe his signature in letters, each has known the testator for over twenty years and knows his proper name, occupation and residence, and neither they nor their spouses take anything under the Will.

Because the ward allows the Notary and both witnesses to remain at the bedside throughout, the Notary can secure that the testator and both neighbours sign the original and the protocol in his presence and in the presence of one another and that he then signs in front of all of them, which also protects him from the offence of attesting without the attesting witnesses appearing personally before him.

Because the testator can read the Sinhala Will himself, the Notary need only record in his attestation that it was read over by the testator, and he must in any event enter in the attestation the date, the hospital ward as the place of execution and the full names and residences of the two neighbours.

The precautions the Notary should take about witnesses are therefore: use two witnesses and no fewer; refuse anyone who takes a benefit under the Will or whose spouse does, and so refuse the nephew; use witnesses of good repute who are well acquainted with the testator and know his proper name, occupation and residence, and so refuse the nurse and use the two neighbours instead; satisfy himself that each can and does subscribe his signature in letters; not act as a witness himself; keep the testator and both witnesses together at the bedside so that all sign the original and the protocol in his presence and in the presence of one another before he signs; take the witnesses' declaration of acquaintance at the foot of the Will; and record in his attestation that all signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, with the date, the place and the full names and residences of both witnesses.

block_reason: Verification confirmed every indispensable provision, but two defects need a lawyer before this stands as gold. First, the gold answer's rule paragraph states s.31(14) (ascertaining full names before signing) as law applicable in October 2018, while the corpus holds only the wording substituted by 31-2022 s.16(7); claim CL-M101-Q01-008 is marked disputed for the same reason, and the pre-2022 wording of rule (14), like the repealed rule (10), cannot be recovered from the corpus. Second, the enriched background states that the executant's left thumb is intact and an impression can be taken, and that the witnesses can write their names, which telegraphs the left thumb impression step in rule (15) and the rule (8) requirement that witnesses subscribe in letters; the enrichment should be reworded to remove that leak before the question is used.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice nor authenticate or attest any deed or instrument drawn in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The notary is licensed in English only, so the deed of transfer must be drawn in English and attested in English. This rule is what makes a Sinhala signature a signature in a language other than the notary's language of practice, and it is the reason the executants must be instructed that the instrument itself will be in English.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (22) is original 1907 text; it is not amended by 47-2011, 13-2013, 31-2022 or 6-2024, so the corpus text is the text in force in October 2018.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any case in which the person executing or acknowledging the same shall be or profess to be unable to read the same, or in which such person shall require him to read over the same, unless and until he shall have read over and explained the same, or caused the same to be explained, in the presence and hearing of such person and, except in the case of wills and codicils, in the presence of the attesting witnesses.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: One executant cannot sign in any language and cannot read; the other reads only Sinhala while the deed is in English. Both are therefore unable to read the instrument, so the notary must read it over and explain it, or cause it to be explained, in their presence and hearing and in the presence of the attesting witnesses before he attests.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (11) is original 1907 text; not amended by 47-2011, 31-2022 or 6-2024. In force in October 2018.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same and the witnesses shall have signed the same in his presence and in the presence of one another, and unless he shall have signed the same in the presence of the executant and of the attesting witnesses.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the manner of execution the notary must instruct the parties to follow: both brothers and both witnesses must sign, or in the case of the illiterate brother make his mark, in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and the notary must sign in their presence.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (12) is original 1907 text; not amended by 47-2011, 31-2022 or 6-2024. In force in October 2018.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: If any deed or instrument executed or acknowledged before him be signed by any of the parties or witnesses thereto with a mark, or with a signature in a language other than that in which the notary is authorized to practice, he shall write over such mark or signature in his own handwriting and at the time of execution the words "This is the mark (or signature, as the case may be) of A. B."
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the certification rule the question asks about. It covers both executants at once: the brother who cannot sign signs with a mark, and the brother who signs in Sinhala signs in a language other than English, the language of the notary's warrant. In each case the notary must write over the mark or signature, in his own hand and at the time of execution, the words prescribed, inserting the name of the person signing.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (15) is original 1907 text. Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(8) inserted a new rule (15A) after it but did not alter rule (15) itself. In force in October 2018.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: and in the case of a mark he shall besides require such person to affix to the deed or instrument the impression of his left thumb and shall write over such impression at the time and in the manner aforesaid the words "This is the left thumb impression of A. B."
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Adds the extra step required only for the executant who signs with a mark: the notary must require the left thumb impression and write the prescribed words over it. This is the step that distinguishes the treatment of the brother who cannot sign from the treatment of the brother who signs in Sinhala.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Part of the original rule (15); not amended by 31-2022 or 6-2024. In force in October 2018. The general obligation on every executant of a deed affecting immovable property to affix a thumb impression comes from rule (15A), inserted only in 2022, and is therefore not applied here.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall without delay duly attest every deed or instrument which shall be executed or acknowledged before him, and shall sign and seal such attestation. In such attestation he shall state- (a) that the said deed or instrument was signed by the party and the witnesses thereto in his presence and in the presence of one another;
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The second half of the question is how the notary certifies. Rule (20) requires an attestation, signed and sealed without delay, which states that the parties and witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, and (paragraph (d)) whether the deed was read over by the executant or read and explained by the notary in the presence of the attesting witnesses. That last statement is what records compliance with rule (11) on the face of the deed.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: The opening words of rule (20) and paragraphs (a), (c), (d) and (f) are original text. Paragraphs (b) and (e) were substituted and (h) added by 31-2022 s.16(11), and (g) was substituted by 6-2024 s.3(7); none of those later paragraphs is relied on here.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Wording and 2018 applicability confirmed against 31-2022 s.16(11) and 6-2024 s.3(7), but the subsection label reads "(20)(a) and (20)(d)" while the excerpt covers only the opening words of rule (20) and paragraph (a); paragraph (d) is carried separately by PROV-M101-007, and the label should be read as rule (20) opening words and paragraph (a).

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (d) whether the same was read over by the person executing the same, or read and explained by him, the said notary, to the said person in the presence of the attesting witnesses;
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Requires the attestation itself to record that the deed was read over and explained to these executants in the presence of the attesting witnesses, which is the certification counterpart of the rule (11) duty triggered by an executant who cannot read.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Paragraph (d) of rule (20) is original text and was not touched by 31-2022 s.16(11) or 6-2024 s.3(7). In force in October 2018.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Every such attestation shall be substantially in the form E in the Second Schedule, and shall be legibly signed by him in the language in which the deed or instrument is written, and also with his usual signature if the language or form of that signature be different from that in which such deed or instrument is written.

indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (21) is original 1907 text; not amended by 47-2011, 31-2022 or 6-2024. In force in October 2018. Form E itself is not in the corpus.

legal_issues.issue: In what language must the deed of transfer be drawn and attested, given that the notary holds a licence to practise in English only, and what does that mean for an executant who signs in Sinhala.

What must the notary do before execution where one executant cannot sign or read in any language and the other cannot read the English deed: reading over and explaining, ascertaining names, and arranging witnesses.
How must the executant who cannot sign execute the deed, and what additional step (the left thumb impression) does the notary have to require of him.

In what words and in whose handwriting must the notary certify the mark of the one brother and the Sinhala signature of the other, and what must the attestation itself state and in what form and language.

gold_answer_draft.issue: The issue is what instructions the notary, who is licensed to practise in English, must give two brothers executing an English deed of transfer where one of them cannot sign or read in any language and the other signs in Sinhala, and in what words and form he must then certify their respective signatures.
gold_answer_draft.rule: By Notaries Ordinance s.31(22) a notary may not attest a deed in any language other than that in which he is authorised to practise, nor attest a deed drawn in any other language, so an English licence means an English deed and an English attestation. By s.31(11) he may not attest where an executant is or professes to be unable to read the deed, or asks him to read it, unless he has first read it over and explained it, or caused it to be explained, in the presence and hearing of that executant and in the presence of the attesting witnesses. By s.31(12) the executants and the witnesses must sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and the notary must sign in their presence; by s.31(8) at least two witnesses must subscribe their signatures in letters, and by s.31(18) the day, month, year and place of execution must be inserted in letters. Section 31(14) requires the full names of executants and witnesses to be ascertained before any signature or mark is made. Section 31(15) governs certification: where a party signs with a mark, or with a signature in a language other than that in which the notary is authorised to practise, the notary must write over the mark or signature, in his own handwriting and at the time of execution, the words "This is the mark (or signature, as the case may be) of A. B.", inserting the name of the person signing; and in the case of a mark he must besides require that person to affix the impression of his left thumb and write over it, at the same time and in the same manner, the words "This is the left thumb impression of A. B.". Section 31(20) then requires him without delay to attest the deed, signing and sealing the attestation, and to state in it among other things that the deed was signed by the party and the witnesses in his presence and in the presence of one another, and whether it was read over by the executant or read and explained by the notary in the presence of the attesting witnesses; and by s.31(21) the attestation must be substantially in Form E of the Second Schedule and must be legibly signed by him in the language in which the deed is written, and also with his usual signature if that differs.
gold_answer_draft.application: The deed is drawn in English, which is the language of the notary's licence, so under s.31(22) he may properly draw and attest it. Because neither Ranjith, who cannot read at all, nor Nimal, who reads only Sinhala, can read the English instrument, s.31(11) obliges the notary to read the whole deed over and explain it, or cause it to be explained, in Sinhala in the presence and hearing of both brothers and in the presence of the two attesting witnesses, before anything is signed. He must instruct them that nothing is to be signed until the deed has been fully engrossed and read over, that the two witnesses must be present throughout and must sign their names in letters, and that under s.31(12) both brothers and both witnesses must sign in his presence and in the presence of one another, after which he will sign himself; he must also ascertain their full names beforehand, as s.31(14) requires, so that the correct names can be written into the certification. Ranjith, who does not know to sign in any language, must be instructed to make his mark on the deed, the duplicate and the protocol, and then to affix the impression of his left thumb. Nimal, who can write, is to sign in Sinhala, which he may do even though the deed and the attestation are in English. Certifying the signatures then follows s.31(15). Over Ranjith's mark the notary must write, in his own handwriting and at the time of execution, the words "This is the mark of Ranjith Weerasinghe", and over the left thumb impression the words "This is the left thumb impression of Ranjith Weerasinghe". He must insert the date, 12 March 2018, and the place, Gampaha, in letters under s.31(18), and then attest the deed under s.31(20), stating that the brothers and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and that the deed was read over and explained by him to the executants in the presence of the attesting witnesses, and he must sign and seal that attestation, substantially in Form E and legibly signed in English as s.31(21) requires.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary may not attest a deed in, or a deed drawn in, any language other than that in which he is authorised to practise.

Where an executant is or professes to be unable to read the deed, or requires the notary to read it, the notary may not attest until he has read it over and explained it, or caused it to be explained, in the presence and hearing of that executant and in the presence of the attesting witnesses.

The executants and the witnesses must sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and the notary must sign in their presence; at least two witnesses must subscribe their signatures in letters.

Where a party signs with a mark, or with a signature in a language other than that in which the notary is authorised to practise, the notary must write over the mark or signature in his own handwriting and at the time of execution the words "This is the mark (or signature, as the case may be) of A. B.", inserting the name of the person signing.

In the case of a mark the notary must besides require that person to affix the impression of his left thumb and write over it, at the same time and in the same manner, the words "This is the left thumb impression of A. B.".

The notary must without delay attest the deed, sign and seal the attestation, and state in it that the party and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and whether the deed was read over by the executant or read and explained by the notary in the presence of the attesting witnesses.

The attestation must be substantially in Form E of the Second Schedule and must be legibly signed by the notary in the language in which the deed is written, and also with his usual signature if that differs.

The notary must insert the day, month and year and the place of execution in letters and sign the deed, and must ascertain the full names of the executants and witnesses before any signature or mark is made.
answer_claims.verifier_note: The first half (day, month, year and place in letters, and the notary signing the deed) is verified against rule (18); the second half, on ascertaining full names before any signature or mark, rests on PROV-M101-011, whose corpus text is the wording substituted by 31-2022 s.16(7) and is therefore not shown to be the law in October 2018.

Since neither brother can read the English deed, the notary must instruct them that he will read the whole deed over and explain it in Sinhala in their presence and hearing and in the presence of the two attesting witnesses before anything is signed.

The brothers must be instructed to execute in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another and of two witnesses who will sign their own names in letters, and the notary will then sign in their presence.
Ranjith, who does not know to sign in any language, must be instructed to make his mark and then to affix the impression of his left thumb.

Nimal may sign in Sinhala even though the deed and the attestation are in English, because the rule on signatures in a language other than that of the notary's warrant provides for that signature to be certified rather than refused.

The notary must write in his own handwriting at the time of execution the words "This is the mark of Ranjith Weerasinghe" over the mark, "This is the left thumb impression of Ranjith Weerasinghe" over the thumb impression, and "This is the signature of Nimal Weerasinghe" over the Sinhala signature.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office, unless with the express permission of his employer or when required to do so by law.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the notarial secrecy rule and it decides the question. Whether a named person executed a will before the notary, and the date and number of that will, is knowledge the notary came by in the execution of his office. Rule (1) forbids him to divulge it and admits only two exits: the express permission of his employer, or a legal compulsion to disclose. Neither is present where the testator is alive, has given no permission, and no court order or statutory demand has been made.

legal_issues.issue: Whether the fact that a named person executed a will before the notary, together with its date and number, is a secret confided to the notary or of which he became possessed in the execution of his office.

Whether either statutory exception to the duty of secrecy is available - express permission of the notary's employer, or a legal requirement to disclose - where the testator is alive, has not authorised disclosure, and the request comes from his children without any court order or statutory demand.
Whether the children's relationship to the testator, as persons who may later take under the will, gives them any entitlement to the information during the testator's lifetime.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether a notary may tell the adult children of a living testator that he has attested a will executed by their father, and disclose its particulars, when the testator has given no permission and no legal process compels disclosure.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (1) makes it the duty of every notary not to divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office, unless with the express permission of his employer or when required to do so by law. The two exceptions are exhaustive: consent must come from the person who employed him, and the alternative is a legal requirement to disclose, not a moral or family claim. The Ordinance treats a will as peculiarly confidential even in the notary's own compliance duties. Under s.31 rule (24) he must preserve the will as his protocol and keep a register of his instruments, but for wills and codicils only the number and date go into the register; and under the proviso to s.31 rule (26)(a)(i) the duplicate of a will is not sent to the Registrar of Lands, only its number and date appearing in the monthly list. Breach of rule (1) is an offence punishable on summary trial before a Magistrate, in addition to any civil liability, under s.34(1)(a).
gold_answer_draft.application: The notary learned that Mr. Wickramaratne had executed a will, and learned what it says, because the will was executed before him and he holds the protocol; that is knowledge of which he became possessed in the execution of his office and it falls squarely within s.31 rule (1). His employer for this purpose is the testator, the person at whose instance he attested the instrument, and the testator is alive and has given no permission, express or otherwise, for the matter to be disclosed. The children are not his employer; their expectation of inheriting gives them no present interest in the document, because nothing passes under a will until the testator's death, and no authority from their father is produced. Nor is the second exception engaged: no court has ordered production and no officer entitled under the Ordinance to inspect his records has called for them, so he is not required to do so by law. Confirming even the bare fact that a will exists would divulge the substance of what the testator confided, and the Ordinance's own treatment of wills, which keeps their particulars out of both the notary's register and his return to the Registrar of Lands, tells against any narrower reading. Should the notary answer, he would expose himself to prosecution and civil liability under s.34.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: No. The notary should not divulge the information. He should decline, politely and without hinting at the answer either way, and tell the children that he is not at liberty to say whether he has attested any instrument for their father and that they must ask their father himself; if the testator authorises disclosure, or if the notary is later required by law to disclose, the position changes, and it changes again on the testator's death, when the will falls to be dealt with in the ordinary way.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary is under a statutory duty not to divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office.
That duty yields only in two cases: where the notary has the express permission of his employer, or where he is required by law to disclose.
A will executed before a notary is preserved by him as his protocol, and only the number and date of a will are entered in the register he is obliged to keep.
In the monthly return a notary makes to the Registrar of Lands, wills and codicils are identified by number and date alone.
A notary who acts in breach of the duty of secrecy commits an offence triable summarily before a Magistrate, in addition to any civil liability he may incur.
The notary's knowledge that the testator executed a will, and of its contents, was acquired in the execution of his office, because the will was executed before him and he holds its protocol.
The testator, and not his children, is the notary's employer for the purposes of the permission exception, and the testator is alive and has given no permission.
The second exception is not engaged either, because no court order and no lawful demand requiring disclosure has been made on the notary.
Confirming that a will exists would itself divulge what the testator confided, and the statutory practice of recording wills by number and date alone tells against a narrower reading of the duty.
The notary should not divulge the information and should decline the children's inquiry, referring them to their father.
If the notary were to answer the inquiry he would expose himself to prosecution and to civil liability.
The position would change if the testator gave express permission, or if the notary were later required by law to disclose.
