legal_issues.issue: What particulars must the schedule to Deed No. 429 contain to satisfy section 13 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance?
Lot C4 being a divided portion carved out of Lot C, what additional description does section 13(2) require over and above the general requirement in section 13(1)?
How should the schedule be drafted so that the Registrar cannot refuse registration under section 13(5)?

gold_answer_draft.issue: What must the schedule to Deed of Gift No. 429 dated 4th June 2001, by which Nimal gifted Lot C4 of 10 perches to Waruni, contain in order to satisfy section 13 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, and how should that schedule be drafted?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Registration of Documents Ordinance s.13(1) requires every instrument other than a will presented for registration to contain, embodied in it or in a schedule annexed to it, an accurate and clear description of the land affected, giving its boundaries, its extent, and its situation specifying the district and the village, pattu, korale or other division of the district, and, where the land is in a town, the name of the street. Section 13(2) adds that where the land is a divided portion of a land or allotment, that portion must be clearly and accurately defined by its own particular boundaries and extent. Section 13(3), which requires the fractional proportion and a description of the entire land, applies only to an undivided share and is not engaged. By s.3 of the same Ordinance 'land' includes things attached to the earth, so any building standing on the lot forms part of what is described. Section 13(5) requires the Registrar to refuse registration of an instrument that does not state these particulars, subject to the appeal in s.13(5A) and (5B), and s.13(7) requires a reference to the volume and folio of the earlier registered instrument relating to the same land to be written at the head of the deed. Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (16) imposes the same description duty on the attesting notary and in its present form calls in addition for the Divisional Secretary's Division, the local authority division and the Grama Niladhari Division.
gold_answer_draft.application:
Lot C4 is a divided portion of Lot C, cut out by the sub-division of Lot C on Plan No. 450B dated 18th May 2000 made by Anil Silva, Licensed Surveyor, so both s.13(1) and s.13(2) apply and the lot must be defined by its own four boundaries and its own extent of 10 perches, not merely by reference to the 32-perch parent lot. The land lies at Akuregoda Road, Pelawatta, Battaramulla, so the street name must appear. A compliant schedule may be drafted as follows.

THE SCHEDULE ABOVE REFERRED TO

All that divided allotment of land marked Lot C4 depicted in Plan No. 450B dated 18th May 2000 made by Anil Silva, Licensed Surveyor, of the land called Dawatagahawatta, situated at Akuregoda Road, Pelawatta, Battaramulla, in the Grama Niladhari Division of [.....], in the [.....] pattu / korale, within the Divisional Secretary's Division of [.....] and within the administrative limits of the [.....] local authority, in the District of [.....], [.....] Province; and which said Lot C4 is bounded on the North by [.....], on the East by [.....], on the South by [.....] and on the West by [.....], and containing in extent Ten Perches (0A. 0R. 10P.) according to the said Plan No. 450B, together with the buildings, trees, plantations and everything else standing thereon.

Registered in Volume [.....] Folio [.....] of the [.....] Land Registry.

The bracketed particulars are the ones the facts given do not supply: the four boundaries of Lot C4, the district and the administrative divisions, and the volume and folio of the earlier registered deed. They must be taken from Plan No. 450B and from the folio in which Lot C stands registered before the deed is engrossed; without them the description is not accurate and clear within s.13(1) and the divided portion is not defined by its particular boundaries within s.13(2). The facts also do not state whether either building, No. 400 or No. 400A, stands on the 10 perches of Lot C4; if one does, its assessment number must be recited in the schedule, because by s.3 the building is part of the land conveyed. Whether Nimal in fact retained Lot C4 to gift after Deed No. 409 is a separate question and does not affect the form of the schedule.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The schedule set out above states the particulars required by s.13(1) and s.13(2) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance: the lot number and the plan with its date and surveyor, the name of the land, the situation with the street, the administrative divisions and the district, the four boundaries of the divided portion, its extent of 10 perches, and what stands on it. On those particulars being completed the Registrar has no ground to refuse registration under s.13(5), and the volume and folio reference required by s.13(7) must also be written at the head of Deed No. 429. This draft is unverified and awaits a lawyer's review.

answer_claims.claim_text: Every instrument other than a will presented for registration must contain, in the instrument or in a schedule annexed to it, an accurate and clear description of the land affected, its boundaries, its extent and its situation specifying the district and the village, pattu, korale or other division of the district, and where the land is in a town the name of the street.
Where the land is a divided portion of a land or allotment, that portion must be clearly and accurately defined by its own particular boundaries and extent.
The requirement to state a fractional proportion and to describe the entire land applies only where the subject of the instrument is an undivided share, and so does not apply to a defined lot.
'Land' under the Registration of Documents Ordinance includes things attached to the earth, so a building standing on the lot is part of what the schedule describes.
The Registrar must refuse to register an instrument that does not state the particulars required by section 13.
A reference to the volume and folio in which an earlier instrument relating to the same land is registered must be written at the head of the deed presented for registration.

The attesting notary is separately forbidden to attest a deed affecting land unless the deed or an annexed schedule carries an accurate and clear description showing boundaries, extent and situation with the administrative divisions, and unless a divided share is defined by its particular boundaries and extent.

Lot C4 is a divided portion of Lot C created on Plan No. 450B dated 18th May 2000 by Anil Silva, Licensed Surveyor, so the schedule to Deed No. 429 must define Lot C4 by its own four boundaries and its own extent of 10 perches rather than by reference to the 32-perch parent lot.
Because the land lies at Akuregoda Road, Pelawatta, Battaramulla, the schedule must give the street name as well as the district and the division of the district in which the land is situated.

The four boundaries of Lot C4, the district and administrative divisions, and the volume and folio of the earlier registered deed are not supplied by the facts and must be taken from Plan No. 450B and the land registry folio before the deed is engrossed; the schedule is left with marked blanks for them.

If either building, Assessment No. 400 or No. 400A, stands within Lot C4, its assessment number must be recited in the schedule, since the building forms part of the land described; the facts do not state where the buildings stand relative to Lot C4.

A schedule to Deed No. 429 describing all that divided allotment of land marked Lot C4 in Plan No. 450B dated 18th May 2000 made by Anil Silva, Licensed Surveyor, of the land called Dawatagahawatta, situated at Akuregoda Road, Pelawatta, Battaramulla, within the stated division and district, bounded on the North, East, South and West as shown on that plan, containing in extent ten perches, together with the buildings and everything standing thereon, states the particulars required by section 13(1) and section 13(2).

Once those particulars are completed the Registrar has no ground under section 13(5) to refuse registration, and the volume and folio reference required by section 13(7) must in addition be written at the head of Deed No. 429.

enrichment.original_background:
By a Deed of Gift bearing No.409 dated 4th June 2001 attested by G.W. de Silva Notary Public Nimal the Donor gifted his son Asanka No. 400A, "Waters Edge" Akuregoda Road, Pelawatta, Battaramulla a house and property. The relevant clauses in the Deed of Gift are as follows. Recital All that building called "Waters Edge" bearing Assessment No.400A together with the land whereon the said building is situated free of all encumbrances whatsoever. Operative Clause All that allotment of land with the building standing thereon bearing Assessment No.400A situated in the said lot marked "C" and which said Lot "C" is morefully described in the schedule hereto.. Two enrichment-created problems need a lawyer. First, FACT-M110-Q01-004 has the executant identified by his Japanese passport and the gold answer takes his full name from it, but identification by the bio-page of a passport only entered rule (9) through Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(6); the April 2018 rule (9) required the executant to be known to the notary or to at least two attesting witnesses, and the enriched facts do not say he was. The corpus holds only the post-2022 text of rule (9), so whether the notary could lawfully attest at all on these facts in April 2018 cannot be resolved here, and the conclusion "the notary may attest the deed" rests on that unresolved point. Second, FACT-M110-Q01-005 (the executant cannot read English) imports rule (11) and turns a one-mark question about a foreign-language signature into a two-duty answer; enrichment should not enlarge the legal issue. A lawyer should decide whether to drop that fact and confine the gold answer to rule (15).

B." (here insert the name of the person signing with the mark or signature);
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the rule that governs the exact situation: an executant has signed in a language (Japanese) other than the language in which the notary is authorized to practise. It fixes the notary's positive duty - to write over the signature, in his own handwriting and at the time of execution, the words "This is the signature of A. B.", inserting the signatory's name.

Neither Act No. 47 of 2011, nor Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16, nor Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3 substituted rule (15); Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(8) only inserted a new rule (15A) immediately after it. Rule (15A) (compulsory thumb impression alongside the signature) came into force after April 2018 and is deliberately not relied on.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Every appointment to the office of notary shall be by warrant granted by the Minister, and shall specify the area within which, and the language or languages in which, the person appointed is authorized to practice.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Rule (15) is triggered only by a signature "in a language other than that in which the notary is authorized to practice". Section 2 is what settles that authorized language: it is the language specified in the notary's warrant. Without it there is no way to say that a Japanese signature is in another language for this notary.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (22) He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice nor authenticate or attest any deed or instrument drawn in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Marks the boundary of the problem. Rule (22) bars the notary from attesting a deed drawn in a language outside his warrant, but it says nothing about the language of a party's signature. So a Japanese signature on a deed drawn in the notary's own language does not disable him from attesting; it only brings rule (15) into play.

legal_issues.issue: What must a notary do when an executant signs a deed before him with a signature in a language other than the language in which the notary is authorized to practise?
Does a signature in such a language prevent the notary from attesting the deed at all?
What further duty arises where the executant who signs in that language is unable to read the deed?

gold_answer_draft.issue: The executant has signed the deed in Japanese, a language other than English, which is the only language the notary's warrant authorises him to practise in. The issue is what the Notaries Ordinance requires the notary to do about such a signature, whether it stops him from attesting the deed, and what follows from the executant's inability to read the deed.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A notary's warrant specifies the area and the language or languages in which he is authorized to practise (Notaries Ordinance s.2). Where a deed executed before him is signed by a party or a witness with a mark, or with a signature in a language other than that in which the notary is authorized to practise, s.31(15) requires the notary himself to write over that signature, in his own handwriting and at the time of execution, the words "This is the signature of A. B.", inserting the name of the person signing. Rule (15) attaches to the signature; it is rule (22) that deals with the language of the instrument, barring the notary from attesting a deed drawn in a language outside his warrant. Separately, s.31(11) forbids him from attesting where the executant is, or professes to be, unable to read the deed, or asks him to read it over, unless he has first read over and explained it, or caused it to be explained, in that person's presence and hearing and, except for wills and codicils, in the presence of the attesting witnesses.
gold_answer_draft.application: The deed is drawn in English, which is the language of the notary's warrant, so s.31(22) is satisfied and the Japanese signature does not disqualify him from attesting. Because the signature is in Japanese and his warrant is limited to English, s.31(15) is engaged. He must therefore write over the Japanese signature, in his own handwriting and at the time of execution rather than afterwards, the words "This is the signature of Kenji Watanabe", using the full name he has taken from the passport produced to him. The requirement of a left thumb impression in rule (15) applies to a mark and not to this signature. Since the executant says he cannot read English and asks for the document to be explained, s.31(11) also requires the notary to read over and explain the deed, or cause it to be explained, in the executant's presence and hearing and in the presence of the two attesting witnesses, before he attests it.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary may attest the deed, but he must write over the Japanese signature in his own handwriting at the time of execution the words "This is the signature of Kenji Watanabe" under s.31(15), and, because the executant cannot read English, he must first read over and explain the deed, or cause it to be explained, to the executant in the presence of the attesting witnesses under s.31(11).

answer_claims.claim_text: The language in which a notary is authorized to practise is the language specified in the warrant of appointment granted by the Minister.

Where a deed executed before a notary is signed by a party or witness with a signature in a language other than that in which the notary is authorized to practise, the notary must write over that signature, in his own handwriting and at the time of execution, the words "This is the signature of A. B.", inserting the name of the person signing.

The additional requirement in rule (15) that the signatory affix his left thumb impression, over which the notary writes a corresponding endorsement, applies where the person signs with a mark, not where he signs with a signature.

A notary may not attest a deed drawn in a language other than the language in which he is authorized to practise; that prohibition is directed at the language of the instrument and not at the language of a party's signature.

A notary must not attest a deed where the executant is, or professes to be, unable to read it, or asks him to read it over, unless he has read over and explained it, or caused it to be explained, in the executant's presence and hearing and, except for wills and codicils, in the presence of the attesting witnesses.
Because the deed is drawn in English and the notary's warrant authorises English, the Japanese signature does not prevent him from attesting the deed.
The signature is in Japanese while the notary's warrant is limited to English, so the signature is in a language other than that in which he is authorized to practise and rule (15) is engaged.

The notary must accordingly write over the Japanese signature, in his own handwriting and at the time of execution, the words "This is the signature of Kenji Watanabe", using the full name taken from the passport produced to him.

Because the executant states that he cannot read English and asks for the document to be explained, the notary must read over and explain the deed, or cause it to be explained, in his presence and hearing and in the presence of the two attesting witnesses before attesting it.

The notary may attest the deed, but only after writing over the Japanese signature at the time of execution the words "This is the signature of Kenji Watanabe" and after reading over and explaining the deed to the executant in the presence of the attesting witnesses.

added_facts.fact: The notary's warrant authorises him to practise in the English language only, and the deed has been drawn in English.
added_facts.reason: Rule (15) bites only where the signature is in a language other than the one the notary is authorized to practise in, and that language comes from the warrant under section 2. Rule (22) also has to be cleared, which requires knowing the language the deed is drawn in.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the warrant had authorised the notary to practise in Japanese, the signature would be in his own authorised language and rule (15) would not be engaged. If the deed itself had been drawn in Japanese, rule (22) would bar him from attesting it at all.

added_facts.fact: The executant produces his Japanese passport, from which the notary notes his full name as it appears there.
added_facts.reason: The matter file records relevant_document as a missing fact type. Rule (15) requires the notary to insert the signatory's name, so the scenario must show where that name comes from.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: None on the outcome; without an identity document the notary would have to establish the full name by other means before the deed is signed.

added_facts.fact: The executant states that he cannot read English and asks the notary to explain the contents of the document to him.
added_facts.reason: Determines whether the second duty, to read over and explain before attesting, is engaged. Without it the scenario leaves open whether the executant could read the deed.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the executant read the deed himself and did not profess inability to read it, the reading-over and explanation duty would not arise and only the writing-over duty would apply.
